They benefited from access to a local supply of skilled workers shared among firms in the district.
They competed with one another less intensely than small furniture makers in other Italian regions did.
They were harmed when large furniture firms in the district closed.

explanation.passage: Firms in one industry often bunch together in one area, even though that puts them near rivals. Ruiz found a reason it can pay off: when a big furniture firm in Valdera closed, its skilled workers looked for jobs at nearby small firms, which could then hire quickly. Firms outside the district saw no such benefit. So being in the cluster gives firms access to a shared local pool of skilled labor.
choices: Incorrect. This is outside the scope. Wages are never mentioned.

Correct. Skilled woodworkers released by the closed firm went to nearby firms, which filled jobs twice as fast, while firms outside the district saw no change. That shows a shared local labor pool benefiting firms in the cluster.
Incorrect. This is outside the scope. The passage doesn't measure how intensely firms competed.
Incorrect. This contradicts the evidence. The closure helped the small firms by giving them more skilled applicants.

passage.text: Ballads passed down orally are often assumed to change gradually with each retelling, much like a message in a game of telephone. Ethnomusicologist Siobhan Carey compared recordings of the same ballads made in 1958 and again in 2009 in a village in western Ireland, where many of the 2009 singers had learned their songs directly from the 1958 singers. The melodies and the order of events in each ballad's story were nearly identical across the two sets of recordings. Ornaments, however, small decorative notes added around the main melody, differed considerably, even between two performances of the same ballad by a single singer recorded a week apart.

question: Which statement about the ballads is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: They changed gradually from one generation of singers to the next, just as the telephone-game comparison would predict.
Their ornaments were deliberately simplified by the 2009 singers to make them easier to learn.
Their narrative order changed more between 1958 and 2009 than their ornaments did.
Some of their elements remained stable across generations, while others varied even within one singer's performances.

explanation.passage: The common assumption is that orally passed-down songs slowly drift with each retelling. Carey compared the same ballads recorded fifty years apart, with the later singers having learned from the earlier ones. The tune and the story's order stayed nearly the same. But the ornaments (small decorative notes) varied a lot, even when the same singer sang the same song a week apart. So the ballads are a mix: core parts stay fixed, while decoration changes every time.
choices: Incorrect. This contradicts the passage. Melodies and story order were 'nearly identical' after fifty years, which goes against the gradual-drift model.
Incorrect. This is unsupported. The ornaments 'differed,' but nothing says they were simplified or that this was deliberate.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Narrative order stayed nearly identical while ornaments differed considerably.
Correct. Melodies and story order stayed stable across the generations, while ornaments varied even between two performances by the same singer a week apart.

passage.text: Ancient Latin texts survive mainly in medieval handwritten copies, each made from an earlier copy. Philologists, scholars who study the history of texts, group manuscripts into families by their shared errors: if two manuscripts contain the same unusual mistake, it is likely that one was copied from the other or that both descend from a common source. Philologist Giulia Marchetti examined all 43 surviving manuscripts of a first-century poem and found that every one of them omits the same two lines, whose absence is revealed both by a gap in the poem's logic and by a fourth-century grammar book that quotes the missing lines.

question: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about the 43 manuscripts?
choices: They likely all descend from a single earlier copy that already lacked the two lines.
They were each copied directly from the fourth-century grammar book that quotes the missing lines.
They were produced by scribes who each independently chose to remove the same two lines.
They preserve every other part of the poem exactly as its author wrote it.

explanation.passage: Medieval scribes copied ancient texts from earlier copies, and mistakes got passed along. The passage gives a rule: if manuscripts share the same unusual mistake, they probably come from the same source. Marchetti found that all 43 copies of a poem are missing the same two lines, and we know the lines once existed because an old grammar book quotes them. Apply the rule: all 43 likely descend from one ancestor copy that had already lost those lines.
choices: Correct. A shared unusual error points to a shared source, according to the method described. Since all 43 manuscripts share the same omission, they most likely all trace back to one earlier copy that already lacked the lines.
Incorrect. This misreads the passage. The grammar book contains the missing lines, so copies made from it would include them, not omit them. It also only quotes lines, not the whole poem.
Incorrect. This is the explanation the method treats as unlikely. The passage's logic is that the same unusual mistake points to a common source, not to coincidence.
Incorrect. This is outside the scope. The passage discusses one omission and gives no evidence that the rest of the poem is error-free.

passage.text: In eighteenth-century England, more than 200 crimes, including many forms of theft, carried a mandatory death sentence; stealing goods worth 40 shillings or more from a house was one such crime. Legal historian Martin Okoye examined trial records from London's central criminal court and found that juries frequently convicted defendants of stealing goods worth exactly 39 shillings, just below that threshold, even when witnesses had testified that the stolen goods were worth far more. Such verdicts were especially common when the defendant had no previous convictions.

question: Which statement about these juries is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: They were generally unable to judge the value of stolen goods accurately and so often relied on rough guesses instead.
They opposed punishing theft at all, regardless of a defendant's criminal history.
They sometimes shaped their verdicts to spare defendants from execution rather than strictly following the evidence.
They acquitted most defendants with no previous convictions who were charged with theft.

explanation.passage: In this period, stealing 40 shillings' worth of goods from a house meant automatic death. Okoye found juries often declared the stolen goods worth exactly 39 shillings, one below the death threshold, even when witnesses said they were worth much more. This happened especially for first-time offenders. The pattern points to juries choosing a value that avoided a death sentence, while still finding the defendant guilty.
choices: Incorrect. Honest mistakes in estimating value would scatter in all directions; they wouldn't land at exactly 39 shillings so often. The pattern looks intentional, not inaccurate.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The juries still convicted the defendants of theft; they lowered the value, not the guilt.

Correct. Setting the value just below the death threshold despite contrary testimony, especially for first offenders, suggests juries were shaping verdicts to avoid execution rather than simply following the evidence.
Incorrect. This contradicts the passage. These defendants were convicted, just of stealing a lower value.

passage.text: Educational researcher Noor Haddad returned sixth graders' written work with either a numerical grade only, written comments only, or both a grade and the same kind of written comments. On a later writing task, students who had received comments only improved more than students in either of the other groups, and students who had received both a grade and comments improved no more than those who had received a grade alone. In interviews, many students in the grade-and-comments group said they had looked at their grade and then put the paper away.

question: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about the students who received both grades and comments?
choices: They received less detailed written comments than the students in the comments-only group received.
The grade may have drawn their attention away from comments that could have helped them improve.
They improved more on the later task than the students who received comments only.
They considered numerical grades more useful than written comments.

explanation.passage: Haddad gave students one of three kinds of feedback: a grade only, comments only, or both. Comments alone led to the most improvement, but adding a grade to comments wiped out that benefit: those students did no better than grade-only students. Interviews explain why: many saw the grade and put the paper away without reading the comments. So the grade seems to have pulled attention away from the useful comments.
choices: Incorrect. This contradicts the setup, which says the grade-and-comments group received 'the same kind of written comments.'

Correct. The comments helped when given alone, but students who also got a grade improved no more than grade-only students, and many said they looked at the grade and put the paper away. That suggests the grade distracted them from the comments.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The comments-only group improved more than both other groups.
Incorrect. This is unsupported. Students' behavior (putting the paper away) doesn't tell us they judged grades more useful; they may simply have stopped after seeing the grade.

passage.text: In Solomon Asch's classic experiments, participants judged which of three lines matched a reference line after hearing several other people, secretly working with the researcher, all give the same wrong answer. Many participants went along with the group. Psychologist Keiko Arai repeated the design with one change. In some trials, one of the researcher's helpers gave the correct answer, and conformity dropped sharply. In other trials, one helper gave a wrong answer different from the rest of the group's, one even further from correct; conformity dropped almost as much as when the helper had given the correct answer.

question: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred from Arai's results?
choices: Participants conformed mainly because they genuinely came to believe the group's wrong answer was correct.
Participants resisted the group only when someone else voiced the answer the participants themselves believed was correct.
A dissenter who gives a different wrong answer makes participants more likely to agree with the majority.
The group's pressure appears to depend largely on its unanimity, not on whether anyone supports the correct answer.

explanation.passage: In Asch's studies, people often gave an obviously wrong answer because everyone else in the room did. Arai changed one thing: one group member disagreed. When that person gave the right answer, people conformed much less, as you might expect. The surprise: when that person gave a different wrong answer, even more wrong, conformity dropped almost as much. So simply breaking the group's unanimity, not having an ally for the right answer, did most of the work.
choices: Incorrect. This is outside the scope. The passage measures how often people went along, not what they privately believed.
Incorrect. This contradicts the results. Conformity dropped almost as much when the dissenter gave a different wrong answer, so participants resisted even without anyone voicing the correct answer.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. A dissenter with a different wrong answer made conformity drop, not rise.

Correct. Any break in the group's agreement, even one that gave no support to the correct answer, cut conformity almost as much as a correct dissenter did. That suggests unanimity itself is a major source of pressure.

passage.text: In Kyoto, many traditional townhouses called machiya have narrow street frontages, often only five or six meters wide, but extend deep into the block. Architectural historian Kenji Morita notes that during the Edo period (1603 to 1868), property taxes in Kyoto were assessed according to the width of a building's street frontage rather than its total floor area. Morita also observes that in nearby towns that taxed buildings by floor area, merchants' houses built in the same period were typically wider and shallower.

question: Which statement about machiya is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: Their narrow, deep shape likely reflects in part a response to the way property was taxed in Kyoto.
They were built mainly for Kyoto merchants who could not afford the wider houses common in nearby towns.
Their total floor area was smaller than that of merchants' houses in nearby towns.
Their design was later copied in nearby towns that taxed buildings by floor area.

explanation.passage: Kyoto's machiya are narrow at the front and long from front to back. In this period Kyoto taxed buildings by how wide their street front was, so a narrow front meant a lower tax. In nearby towns that taxed by total floor area instead, houses were wider and shallower. The comparison suggests the tax rule shaped the buildings.
choices: Correct. Taxing frontage width rewards narrow fronts, and towns with a different tax rule built differently shaped houses. That links the machiya shape to Kyoto's tax system. 'Likely' and 'in part' keep it cautious.
Incorrect. This is outside the scope. The passage says nothing about owners' wealth; the tax rule offers a reason even wealthy owners would prefer narrow fronts.
Incorrect. This is unsupported. The passage compares shape (narrow and deep vs. wide and shallow), not total floor area.
Incorrect. This contradicts the passage. Houses in those towns were 'wider and shallower,' not copies of the machiya design.

passage.text: In the late 1970s, new schools for deaf children in Nicaragua brought together children who had previously communicated only through simple gestures developed with their hearing families. A sign language soon emerged among the students. Linguist Elena Park compared signers who had entered the schools in the first years with signers who entered about a decade later, when the language was already in use. The later group, who learned the language from older students, consistently used locations in the space in front of them to indicate which person in a story performed an action, a grammatical device the first group used only rarely and inconsistently, even though the first group had been signing for longer.

question: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about the grammatical device?
choices: It originated in the simple gestures that the children had developed at home with their hearing families before entering the schools.
It was used more consistently by the first group because that group had been signing for longer.
It became a regular part of the language through younger learners rather than being handed down complete by the first signers.
It appears in every sign language that has emerged among deaf communities.

explanation.passage: When deaf children in Nicaragua were brought together in new schools, they created a new sign language. Park compared the first students with students who arrived a decade later and learned from the older ones. The later group used a grammar tool (pointing to places in space to show who did what) consistently, while the first group used it only rarely, even though they had more years of practice. So the younger learners didn't simply copy a finished system; they turned an occasional, inconsistent habit into a regular rule.
choices: Incorrect. This is outside the scope. The home gestures are described as 'simple,' and nothing links the device to them.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The later group used the device consistently; the first group used it 'only rarely and inconsistently' despite signing longer.

Correct. The first signers, the later group's models, used the device only rarely and inconsistently, yet the later group used it consistently. So the device became a regular rule through the younger learners rather than being handed down complete.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The passage discusses only one sign language.

passage.text: At Wadi Hammeh 27, a site in present-day Jordan occupied by the Natufian culture around 12,000 years ago, archaeologist Hana Mutlaq and colleagues examined "sickle gloss," a distinctive polish that forms on the edges of flint blades when they are used to cut silica-rich plant stems. The proportion of blades bearing this gloss rose from 9 percent in the site's earliest occupation layer to 31 percent in its latest. The team argues that the rise reflects a growing reliance on harvesting wild cereals such as barley, a shift often regarded as a precursor to farming.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team's argument?
choices: Wild barley grew in greater abundance near Wadi Hammeh 27 during the site's latest occupation than during its earliest occupation.
Reeds, whose stems are also rich in silica and leave an identical gloss when cut, were increasingly used for roofing at Wadi Hammeh 27 during the site's later occupation.
Flint blades from the latest occupation layer were more often made from stone obtained from distant quarries than were blades from the earliest layer, according to geochemical sourcing.
Other Natufian sites show a smaller increase in the proportion of glossed blades over the same period than Wadi Hammeh 27 does.

explanation.passage: The passage is about a kind of polish, called sickle gloss, that forms on stone blades when people cut plant stems containing silica (a hard, glassy mineral). At one ancient site, the share of blades with this gloss more than tripled over time. The researchers take that rise as a sign that people were harvesting more wild cereals. Notice the gap in the reasoning: the gloss comes from cutting silica-rich stems in general, but the team assumes those stems were cereals. To weaken the argument, look for a finding showing that the rise in gloss could have come from cutting something other than cereals.
choices: Incorrect. If more wild barley grew nearby later on, people would have had more cereal to harvest, which fits the team's argument. This choice supports the conclusion rather than weakening it.

Correct. The team's evidence is only that more blades were used on silica-rich stems. If reeds leave the exact same gloss and people were cutting more reeds for roofs in the later period, the rise in gloss is just as well explained by roof building as by cereal harvesting. This breaks the link between the evidence and the conclusion.
Incorrect. Where the flint came from says nothing about what the blades were used to cut. This is true-but-irrelevant: it is about the blades, but not about the source of the gloss.

Incorrect. The argument is only about what happened at Wadi Hammeh 27. A smaller increase at other sites does not show that the increase at this site came from something other than cereals; it compares a detail the argument does not depend on.

passage.text: Eggshell porosity, the proportion of a shell's surface occupied by tiny pores, governs how readily gases and water vapor pass between an embryo and its surroundings. Eggs buried in soil or in mounds of vegetation, where the air is humid and oxygen is scarce, tend to have highly porous shells, whereas eggs laid in open nests tend to have less porous shells that limit water loss. Analyzing fossil eggs of the sauropod *Ampelosaurus* recovered from ancient marshland deposits in southern France, paleontologist Corinne Dufresne found porosity values similar to those of modern crocodilians, which bury their eggs. She concludes that *Ampelosaurus* likely buried its eggs rather than leaving them in open nests.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Dufresne's conclusion?
choices: The porosity of *Ampelosaurus* eggs varied less from one egg to another than does the porosity of eggs laid by modern crocodilians.
Modern crocodilians that bury their eggs in mounds of rotting vegetation have more porous eggshells than do the crocodilians that bury their eggs in dry, sandy riverbanks.
Fossil eggs of several other sauropod species from the same period have porosity values lower than those of *Ampelosaurus* eggs.
Modern birds that lay eggs in open nests on waterlogged marsh ground, where the air is constantly saturated with moisture, have shells as porous as those of crocodilians.

explanation.passage: Porosity means how many tiny holes an eggshell has. The passage explains a pattern: buried eggs (in humid, low-oxygen places) usually have very porous shells, while open-nest eggs usually have less porous shells so they do not dry out. Dufresne found that *Ampelosaurus* eggs were very porous and concluded the dinosaur buried them. But notice the detail that the fossils come from marshland. The real driver of high porosity may be humidity, not burial itself. A finding that weakens her conclusion would show high porosity is also found in open nests under humid, marshy conditions like the ones *Ampelosaurus* lived in.
choices: Incorrect. How much porosity varied from egg to egg does not tell us whether the eggs were buried or left in the open. This is true-but-irrelevant.
Incorrect. This compares two kinds of buried nests. It says nothing about whether an open-nesting animal could have eggs as porous as *Ampelosaurus* eggs, so it does not touch Dufresne's reasoning.

Incorrect. Other sauropods having less porous eggs is about different species. It does not show that *Ampelosaurus* eggs, which are very porous, could have been laid in open nests. This is a comparison the argument does not depend on.

Correct. Dufresne reasons 'high porosity, therefore buried.' If open-nesting birds in waterlogged marshes also have highly porous shells, then high porosity can come from humid surroundings alone. Since *Ampelosaurus* fossils come from marshland, its porous eggs are just as consistent with open marsh nests as with burial, which breaks the link between her evidence and her conclusion.

passage.text: In the 1950s, the golden rain tree, an ornamental species from Asia, was widely planted in central Florida. Its seedpods are much flatter than those of the balloon vine, the native plant on which the soapberry bug had long fed by piercing pods with its beak to reach the seeds inside. Surveying bugs in the 1990s, entomologist Ruth Delgado-Kerr found that those collected from golden rain trees had beaks about 25 percent shorter than those collected from balloon vines, a length well suited to the shallower pods. She argues that within just a few decades, bug populations feeding on the introduced tree underwent genetic evolution toward shorter beaks.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Delgado-Kerr's argument?
choices: When soapberry bug eggs taken from balloon vines are raised on golden rain tree seeds, the resulting adults develop beaks as short as those of bugs collected from golden rain trees.
Soapberry bugs with beaks too short to reach the seeds inside balloon vine pods have rarely been found feeding on balloon vines in central Florida.
Golden rain trees in central Florida produce seeds over a longer portion of the year than balloon vines in the same region do.

In parts of Florida where golden rain trees were never planted, the beak length of soapberry bugs feeding on balloon vines has remained nearly unchanged since the 1950s, according to museum specimens.

explanation.passage: A new tree with flatter seedpods arrived in Florida, and bugs living on that tree now have shorter beaks than bugs on the native plant. Delgado-Kerr argues this difference is genetic evolution, meaning the bugs' genes changed over generations. The key word is 'genetic.' A difference in body shape could also be caused by the environment an animal grows up in, not its genes. To weaken her argument, find a finding showing the shorter beaks could appear without any genetic change.
choices: Correct. If bugs from balloon-vine parents grow short beaks simply because they were raised on golden rain tree seeds, then beak length is shaped by diet during development. The short beaks on golden rain trees could therefore come from what the bugs eat, not from changed genes, which directly undercuts the claim of genetic evolution.

Incorrect. This suggests that short-beaked bugs do poorly on balloon vines, which fits the idea that beak length matters for feeding and could be shaped by natural selection. It does not weaken the argument; if anything it supports it.
Incorrect. How long each plant produces seeds is unrelated to whether the beak difference is genetic. This is a true-but-irrelevant detail about the plants.
Incorrect. Beaks staying the same where the new tree is absent is exactly what Delgado-Kerr's argument predicts, since it links the change to the tree. This supports her conclusion.

passage.text: On many Caribbean coral reefs, small patch reefs are ringed by halos of bare sand, created where herbivorous fish such as parrotfish leave the shelter of the reef to graze on seagrass and algae but rarely venture far. Marine ecologist Talia Brennan and colleagues found that after fishing for reef sharks was banned in a reserve off Belize in 2008, the halos there grew narrower over the following decade. The team argues that the herbivores, perceiving open sand as more dangerous once sharks had returned, began grazing closer to the reef, and that this change in behavior, rather than a decline in the number of herbivores, caused the halos to shrink.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team's argument?
choices: Tagged parrotfish in the reserve grazed just as far from the reef after sharks returned as before, but counts of herbivorous fish on the reserve's reefs fell by nearly half.
Herbivorous fish in the reserve spent a smaller share of their feeding time on open sand after the fishing ban than they had in the years before the ban was enacted.
Halos around patch reefs outside the reserve, where sharks continued to be fished and remained scarce, stayed about the same width throughout the same decade.
Reef sharks in the reserve were frequently observed hunting near patch reefs, and the remains of parrotfish were found in the stomachs of several sharks caught and examined there.

explanation.passage: A 'halo' is the ring of bare sand around a small reef: plant-eating fish swim out to graze there, but they stay close to the reef so they can hide. After sharks came back to a protected area, the halos got narrower. The team gives a specific reason: the fish became more afraid and stopped swimming as far, so they grazed a smaller ring. They also rule out the other possible reason: it was NOT that sharks simply ate so many fish that fewer were left to graze. To weaken the argument, look for evidence that the fish did not change how far they swim, and that the fish population dropped instead.
choices: Correct. The argument has two parts: behavior changed, and fish numbers were not the cause. This finding hits both. If tagged fish still grazed just as far from the reef, their behavior did not change; and if fish numbers fell by nearly half, the explanation the team ruled out (fewer grazers) is the one the evidence points to.
Incorrect. Fish spending less of their feeding time on open sand is exactly the kind of fear-driven behavior change the team describes, so this supports the argument rather than weakening it.

Incorrect. If halos stayed the same where sharks stayed scarce, that links the narrowing to the return of sharks. This fits the team's argument. It does not help decide between 'fish became fearful' and 'fish became fewer,' and it certainly does not weaken the argument.

Incorrect. This is a topic match that misses the claim. Sharks eating some parrotfish is expected under both explanations: frightened fish can still be eaten. It does not show that fish numbers dropped enough to matter or that fish behavior stayed the same, so it does not directly weaken the argument.

passage.text: Many Tibetans carry a version of the gene *EPAS1* that helps the body cope with the low oxygen levels found at high altitudes. Geneticist Ling Zhao and colleagues found that this version closely matches the corresponding DNA sequence recovered from a Denisovan, an extinct relative of modern humans known from fossils in Siberia. The researchers conclude that the ancestors of Tibetans acquired the variant by interbreeding with Denisovans, rather than inheriting it from the earlier population that gave rise to both Denisovans and modern humans.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' conclusion?
choices: The variant is also found at low frequencies in several African populations whose ancestors are not thought to have interbred with Denisovans.
The variant is considerably more common among Tibetans living above 4,000 meters than among Tibetans whose families have lived at lower elevations for generations.
Denisovan fossils have been found mainly at sites in Siberia that lie at relatively low elevations.
Other gene variants thought to have been inherited from Denisovans are present in some populations of Papua New Guinea.

explanation.passage: A gene version that helps with high altitude is common in Tibetans, and it closely matches Denisovan DNA. The researchers weigh two ways Tibetans could have gotten it: (1) interbreeding with Denisovans, or (2) inheriting it from a much older shared ancestor of both groups. They pick option 1. To weaken that, look for evidence that the variant could have come from the shared ancestor instead, such as finding it in people who never mixed with Denisovans.
choices: Correct. If African populations with no Denisovan ancestry also carry the variant, they could not have gotten it from Denisovans. The likeliest source would be the older population ancestral to everyone, which is exactly the explanation the researchers rejected. This makes the interbreeding conclusion less likely.
Incorrect. This shows the variant is useful at high altitude, but it says nothing about where the variant came from. It is about the gene's effect, not its origin.
Incorrect. Where Denisovan fossils were found does not tell us whether Tibetans got the variant from Denisovans or from an older ancestor. This is outside the scope of the argument.
Incorrect. This shows that interbreeding with Denisovans happened in other populations, which if anything makes interbreeding more believable. It does not weaken the conclusion.

passage.text: Because few ordinary people in eighteenth-century England left diaries or letters, historians often estimate literacy from marriage registers, which brides and grooms either signed with their names or marked with an X. In the registers of the parish of Thornbury, the share of grooms who signed their names rose from 38 percent in the 1750s to 67 percent in the 1790s. Historian Gwen Ashdown argues that this rise reflects a substantial increase in the proportion of men in the parish who could read.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ashdown's argument?
choices: In the 1790s, brides in Thornbury signed the marriage registers less often than grooms in the parish did.
Several grooms who married in Thornbury in the 1790s are known from estate records to have owned books.
The number of marriages recorded in Thornbury each year was roughly the same in the 1750s as in the 1790s, despite modest growth in the parish's overall population.
Beginning in the 1760s, a Thornbury charity school taught local boys to write their own names but provided almost no instruction in reading.

explanation.passage: Historians use marriage records to guess how many people could read: signing your name counts as literate, marking an X counts as not. In one parish, the share of grooms who signed rose a lot over forty years. Ashdown concludes that more men could read. The weak link is the assumption that being able to sign your name means being able to read. A finding that weakens her argument would show the rise in signatures could happen without a rise in reading.
choices: Incorrect. Ashdown's argument is only about men (grooms). How often brides signed does not affect whether the grooms' signatures show reading ability.
Incorrect. Grooms owning books, if anything, suggests they could read, which supports her argument. And 'several' grooms is too few to say much either way.
Incorrect. The number of marriages each year does not affect the percentage of grooms who signed, so it does not challenge her reasoning. This is true-but-irrelevant.

Correct. If a local school taught boys to write their names but barely taught reading, then the boys who grew up and married later could sign the register without being able to read. That would explain the jump in signatures without any rise in reading, cutting the link between Ashdown's evidence and her conclusion.

passage.text: Among the Aché, a forest-dwelling people of eastern Paraguay, hunters who kill large game typically distribute most of the meat to other households rather than keeping it for their own families. Anthropologist Tomás Ibarra argues that this sharing is best understood as a form of delayed exchange: a hunter gives meat now with the expectation that the recipients will share with him when he returns empty-handed, so that over time each household receives roughly as much as it gives.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ibarra's argument?
choices: Aché hunters who pursue large game succeed in making a kill on only about 40 percent of their hunting trips.
Households of Aché hunters who seldom share their kills receive just as much meat from other households as do households of hunters who share generously.
Plant foods gathered by Aché women are shared mostly within the gatherer's own household rather than distributed to others.
Aché hunters share meat with a larger number of households during the rainy season, when hunting is more difficult and less predictable, than during the dry season.

explanation.passage: Aché hunters give away most of the meat from big kills. Ibarra explains this as delayed exchange, or 'reciprocity': I give you meat today because you will give me meat later, so in the long run everyone gets back about what they gave. If that is true, how much a household gives should affect how much it gets back. To weaken his argument, look for evidence that giving and receiving are not connected.
choices: Incorrect. Frequent failed hunts mean a hunter often comes home with nothing, which is exactly when he would need others to share with him. This fits Ibarra's argument rather than weakening it.

Correct. Ibarra's idea depends on receiving being tied to giving. If stingy hunters' households get just as much meat as generous hunters' households, then giving earns nothing extra in return, so the sharing cannot be explained as an exchange.
Incorrect. Ibarra's argument is specifically about meat from large game. How plant foods are shared is a different practice, so this is a topic match that misses the claim.

Incorrect. Sharing more widely when hunting is hard is consistent with an exchange system: when the risk of coming home empty-handed is higher, building up future obligations is more valuable. This does not weaken the argument.

passage.text: Granite boulders scattered across the Kessel Plateau in central Canada are unlike any rock found nearby: the closest granite outcrops lie some 200 kilometers to the north. Geologist Annika Forsberg notes that ice sheets can pluck boulders from bedrock and carry them great distances before depositing them as the ice melts. On the basis of the boulders' presence, she concludes that the margin of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the vast glacier that covered much of North America during the last ice age, must have reached at least as far south as the plateau.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Forsberg's conclusion?
choices: Chemical analysis shows that the boulders on the plateau most closely match granite from the outcrops 200 kilometers to the north rather than granite from any of the outcrops located farther away.
The plateau also contains scattered boulders of limestone that match bedrock found roughly 50 kilometers to the north of the plateau.
The plateau lay beneath a large lake at the end of the last ice age, and icebergs that broke off glaciers far to the north drifted across such lakes, dropping rocks as they melted.
The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its greatest southern extent several thousand years earlier in some regions of North America than in others.

explanation.passage: Big granite boulders sit on a plateau where no granite is found nearby; the closest source is 200 km north. Forsberg knows ice sheets can carry boulders far, so she concludes the ice sheet itself must have reached the plateau. Her reasoning assumes the ice sheet is the only way the boulders could have arrived. To weaken her conclusion, find another way granite could have traveled 200 km south without the ice sheet's edge reaching the plateau.
choices: Incorrect. This only tells us where the boulders came from, which Forsberg already assumes. It does not offer any way for them to arrive without the ice sheet, so it does not weaken her conclusion.
Incorrect. More boulders from the north is what you would expect if ice carried rocks south, so this fits Forsberg's conclusion rather than weakening it.

Correct. If the plateau was under a lake and icebergs from distant glaciers floated over it and dropped rocks as they melted, the granite boulders could have arrived by iceberg. The ice sheet itself would not have needed to reach the plateau, so the boulders no longer prove where the ice sheet's edge was.
Incorrect. When the ice sheet peaked in different regions is a timing detail. It does not affect whether it reached this plateau, so it is true-but-irrelevant.

passage.text: In 2018, the state of Corvana raised its tax on gasoline by 20 cents per gallon, one of the largest such increases in the country. Economist Marisol Duarte examined fuel distributors' sales records and found that the total volume of gasoline sold in Corvana in 2019 was virtually the same as it had been in 2017. She concludes that the tax increase did not reduce gasoline consumption in the state.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Duarte's conclusion?
choices: Gas station owners across Corvana publicly campaigned against the tax increase in the months before the state legislature approved it in 2018.
The average price of a gallon of gasoline at Corvana's stations rose by roughly the amount of the tax in the months after the increase took effect.
Corvana's population grew by about 9 percent from 2017 to 2019, largely because a new factory district drew thousands of workers who commute by car.
Neighboring states that did not raise their gasoline taxes during this period also saw little change in the total volume of gasoline sold there between 2017 and 2019.

explanation.passage: Corvana raised its gas tax. Two years later, the state was selling about the same amount of gas as before. Duarte concludes the tax did not make people use less gas. The hidden assumption is that, without the tax, gas sales would also have stayed flat. To weaken her conclusion, find something else that would have pushed gas use UP during the same years; then 'flat' would actually mean the tax held consumption down below where it would otherwise have been.
choices: Incorrect. Whether station owners opposed the tax says nothing about how much gas people actually bought afterward. This is true-but-irrelevant.
Incorrect. A price rise is what you would expect from a tax. It does not tell us whether people bought less gas than they otherwise would have, so it does not weaken the conclusion.

Correct. If thousands of new car commuters arrived, gas use should have risen noticeably. Sales staying flat despite 9 percent more people means each person was using less gas, which suggests the tax did reduce consumption, just enough to cancel out the growth.

Incorrect. This is a reversal trap. Flat sales in states with no tax suggest flat sales are normal even without a tax, which makes Corvana's flat sales look like 'no effect.' That supports Duarte's conclusion instead of weakening it.

passage.text: More than 180 polished axeheads made of jadeite, a rare green stone quarried high on Monte Viso in the Italian Alps, have been found across Neolithic Europe, some as far away as Scotland and Denmark, roughly 1,800 kilometers from their source. Archaeologist Pierre Lavalle notes that jadeite is tougher than the flint most Neolithic farmers used for their axes, and he argues that the jadeite axeheads were carried so far because communities clearing forests for farmland valued them as unusually effective woodcutting tools.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Lavalle's argument?
choices: Neolithic communities across western Europe were clearing forests on a large scale to create fields and pastures during the period when the jadeite axeheads circulated.
Most jadeite axeheads found far from the Alps are thin, mirror-polished, and free of chips or wear, and many were deposited unbroken in bogs.
Jadeite axeheads found within a short distance of Monte Viso greatly outnumber those that have been found in distant regions such as Scotland, Denmark, and northern France.
Laboratory tests confirm that jadeite resists chipping and fracturing better than flint does when it is struck repeatedly against wood and other hard materials.

explanation.passage: Axeheads made of a special Alpine stone, jadeite, turn up all over Europe, sometimes 1,800 km from where the stone was dug out. Lavalle explains the long journeys by usefulness: jadeite is tough, so people wanted these axes for chopping down trees. His argument depends on the axeheads actually being used (or usable) as tools. To weaken it, look for evidence that the distant axeheads were not working tools at all.
choices: Incorrect. Large-scale forest clearing would create demand for good woodcutting axes, which fits Lavalle's argument. It supports rather than weakens it.

Correct. A real chopping tool would get chipped and worn. If the distant axeheads are too thin for chopping, have a mirror polish, show no wear, and were placed unbroken in bogs (a common way of making offerings), they look like prized display or ritual objects, not woodcutting tools. That breaks the link between 'tough stone' and 'carried far because useful.'
Incorrect. It is unsurprising that more axeheads are found near the quarry. This says nothing about why the far-traveled ones were carried, so it is true-but-irrelevant.

Incorrect. This confirms jadeite's toughness, the very fact Lavalle builds his argument on, so it supports the argument. Note that it shows the stone could make a good tool, not whether these axeheads were used as tools.

passage.text: Pollen grains preserved in lake sediments are often used to reconstruct ancient vegetation, since plants growing near a lake shed pollen that settles to the bottom year after year. In a sediment core from Lake Brezina in the Carpathian foothills, palynologist (a scientist who studies pollen) Hana Dvořák found that pine pollen made up nearly 70 percent of all the grains in a layer deposited about 9,000 years ago. She concludes that the land around the lake was then covered mainly by pine forest.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Dvořák's conclusion?
choices: Layers of the same core that were deposited about 6,000 years ago contained far less pine pollen and much more pollen from oak and elm trees.
Pine pollen made up a similar share of the grains in sediment cores that were taken from both the northern and the southern ends of the lake.
Pine forests in the Carpathian region today support a wide variety of insects, birds, and mammals that are uncommon in the region's oak and elm forests.
Pine pollen, which has air-filled sacs, can drift hundreds of kilometers on the wind, and it dominates the pollen in lakes on today's treeless tundra.

explanation.passage: Scientists can learn what plants grew long ago by counting pollen in old lake mud, on the idea that pollen in the mud came from plants near the lake. In one 9,000-year-old layer, most of the pollen is pine, so Dvořák concludes there was a pine forest around the lake. Her reasoning assumes that lots of pine pollen in the mud means lots of pine trees nearby. To weaken it, look for evidence that pine pollen can be abundant in lake mud even when pine trees are not growing nearby.
choices: Incorrect. A later layer having different pollen shows the vegetation changed by 6,000 years ago. It says nothing about whether the 9,000-year-old layer is a reliable record, so it is true-but-irrelevant.
Incorrect. Getting the same result from two parts of the lake makes the measurement look consistent. That, if anything, strengthens the conclusion.
Incorrect. What animals live in pine forests today is outside the question. It does not affect whether a pine forest grew around the lake 9,000 years ago.

Correct. If pine pollen floats for hundreds of kilometers and makes up most of the pollen even in lakes where no trees grow at all, then a high share of pine pollen does not show that pines grew around the lake. The pollen could have blown in from far away, which breaks the link between the evidence and the conclusion.

passage.text: Great tits living in European cities sing at noticeably higher pitches than great tits living in forests. Because city noise, much of it produced by traffic, is concentrated at low frequencies, biologist Hans Verbeek argues that urban great tits raise the pitch of their songs so that their songs will not be drowned out by the low rumble of traffic.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Verbeek's argument?
choices: Traffic noise in European cities is generally louder during the early morning, when great tits sing most, than during the afternoon.
Great tits in quiet city parks far from any roads sing at pitches just as high as those of great tits living beside busy roads.
Female great tits are more likely to approach males whose songs can be clearly heard over background noise than males whose songs cannot.
Great tits living in forests sing a greater variety of distinct song types than great tits living in European cities do.

explanation.passage: City great tits sing higher than forest great tits. Verbeek's explanation is traffic noise: traffic makes low sounds, so birds sing higher to be heard over it. If he is right, the amount of traffic noise around a bird should matter: birds in loud spots should sing higher than birds in quiet spots. To weaken his argument, look for evidence that pitch stays high even where there is no traffic noise.
choices: Incorrect. Traffic being loudest when the birds sing most makes noise a bigger problem for them, which supports Verbeek's argument.

Correct. If birds in quiet parks, away from traffic, sing just as high as birds next to busy roads, then traffic noise does not seem to be what raises their pitch. Something else about city life is likely responsible, which undercuts Verbeek's explanation.
Incorrect. This gives a reason why being heard over noise would matter to a male, which supports the idea that birds adjust their songs to noise.
Incorrect. Song variety is a different feature from pitch. This is a topic match that does not address Verbeek's claim about pitch.

passage.text: Populations of the Mexican tetra that live in dark caves have tiny, nonfunctional eyes or none at all, whereas members of the same species living in surface rivers have fully formed eyes. Because eye tissue and the brain regions that process vision consume large amounts of energy, biologist Elena Ruiz argues that eye loss in cave populations was driven by the scarcity of food in caves: individuals that invested less energy in useless eyes had more energy left for survival and reproduction.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ruiz's argument?
choices: Cave populations of the Mexican tetra living in caves regularly flooded with plentiful organic debris have lost their eyes to the same degree as populations in food-poor caves.
Cave populations of the Mexican tetra have a more sensitive sense of taste than surface populations, allowing them to locate food in complete darkness.
Surface-dwelling Mexican tetras raised from eggs in total darkness in the laboratory still develop fully formed and functional eyes by the time they reach adulthood, just as river fish do.
The visual system of surface-dwelling Mexican tetras uses a larger share of each fish's energy than does any of the fish's other organ systems.

explanation.passage: Cave-dwelling Mexican tetras have lost their eyes, while river-dwelling ones still have them. Ruiz says the reason is food scarcity: eyes use a lot of energy, so in caves with little food, fish that skipped making eyes had more energy for surviving and breeding. Her explanation depends on food being scarce. So if eye loss happened just as much in caves where food was plentiful, her explanation would be in trouble.
choices: Correct. Ruiz says scarce food is what made eyes too costly. If fish in food-rich caves lost their eyes just as completely, then food scarcity cannot be the driving force, since those fish had energy to spare. This directly undercuts her explanation.
Incorrect. A better sense of taste helps explain how cave fish find food without eyes, but it says nothing about why the eyes were lost. It does not weaken her argument.

Incorrect. This shows that eye development is built into the fish's genes rather than caused by darkness during one fish's life. That fits the idea that cave fish evolved eye loss, so it does not weaken Ruiz's argument.
Incorrect. If eyes are the most energy-hungry system, losing them would save a lot of energy. This supports Ruiz's argument.

passage.text: On the Atlantic island of Isla Pellar, about 1 in 20 residents carries a gene variant that, when inherited from both parents, causes a rare blood disorder; on the nearby mainland, only about 1 in 400 people carries it. Records show that the island was settled in the 1600s by a few dozen families. Geneticist Marta Oyarzún argues that the variant's high frequency on the island is the result of chance: one or more founding settlers happened to carry it, and it spread as their descendants intermarried, not because the variant gave carriers any advantage.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Oyarzún's argument?
choices: The blood disorder caused by the variant was first described in medical writing by physicians working on Isla Pellar in the 1880s.
Several other rare gene variants that cause no known disorders are also far more common among residents of Isla Pellar than among people on the nearby mainland.
Carriers of the variant are resistant to a parasitic infection that was widespread on Isla Pellar but rare on the mainland until the twentieth century.
Residents of Isla Pellar today have, on average, about as many children per family as do residents of the nearby mainland.

explanation.passage: A disease-causing gene variant is twenty times more common on a small island than on the mainland. 'Carrier' means a person with one copy, who does not get the disease but can pass it on. The island was founded by just a few families, so Oyarzún argues the variant became common by luck (a 'founder effect'): a founder happened to have it. She specifically rules out the idea that carriers had an advantage. To weaken her argument, look for evidence that carrying the variant did help people on the island.
choices: Incorrect. When the disorder was first written about does not tell us why the variant became common. This is true-but-irrelevant.
Incorrect. If many unrelated variants with no benefit are also unusually common on the island, that is exactly what chance and a small founding group would produce. This supports Oyarzún's argument.

Correct. If carriers resisted a parasite that was common on the island but not the mainland, carriers would have survived and had children more often there. That gives an advantage-based explanation for why the variant is common on the island specifically, which is the explanation Oyarzún rejects.
Incorrect. Similar family sizes today do not explain how the variant became common over the past centuries, and do not point to any advantage. This does not affect her argument.

passage.text: Between about 1900 and 1700 BCE, the great cities of the Indus civilization, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa in present-day Pakistan, were gradually abandoned as their inhabitants dispersed to small villages. Because this decline coincided with a weakening of the summer monsoon recorded in many parts of South Asia, historian Arjun Mehta argues that reduced monsoon rains lowered the seasonal floods that Indus farmers relied on to water their crops, leaving the cities unable to feed their populations.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Mehta's argument?
choices: Stalagmites from caves near the Indus cities record that local monsoon rainfall in the centuries of abandonment was no lower than in the cities' peak years.
Indus farmers planted wheat and barley in soil left moist by the river's seasonal floods rather than watering their fields through networks of canals.
Indus merchants traded carnelian beads, cotton cloth, and other goods with cities in Mesopotamia throughout the centuries when the Indus cities flourished.
Climate records show that rainfall also declined in Mesopotamia and Egypt at around the same time, a period when those societies too suffered crop failures and unrest.

explanation.passage: The big Indus cities emptied out between about 1900 and 1700 BCE. At about the same time, the summer monsoon (the rainy season) weakened in many parts of South Asia. Mehta connects the two: less rain meant smaller river floods, so crops failed and the cities could not be fed. His evidence is mostly timing across a broad region. To weaken his argument, find evidence that the rains did not actually weaken in the Indus cities' own area.
choices: Correct. Stalagmites (rock formations that grow in caves from dripping water) keep a record of rainfall. If the local record shows rain was no lower during the abandonment than during the cities' best years, then the local floods would not have shrunk, and the monsoon cannot explain why these particular cities emptied, even if it weakened elsewhere in South Asia.
Incorrect. Farmers depending on floods rather than canals makes them more vulnerable to weaker floods. This supports Mehta's argument.
Incorrect. Trade during the cities' good years has nothing to do with whether weaker rains caused their later abandonment. This is true-but-irrelevant.

Incorrect. Similar drying and crop failures elsewhere at the same time make a climate cause seem more plausible, so this fits Mehta's argument. It does not show that the Indus region itself stayed wet.

passage.text: At the cemetery of Huaca Sol on the coast of Peru, used between about 800 and 1100 CE, many individuals have elongated skulls produced by binding the head in infancy, a practice known as cranial modification. Bioarchaeologist Inés Calderón found that individuals with modified skulls were buried with gold ornaments and fine textiles far more often than were individuals with unmodified skulls. She argues that at Huaca Sol, cranial modification served primarily to mark membership in an elite social class.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Calderón's argument?
choices: Cranial modification of a similar kind was also practiced at several other coastal Peruvian sites during the period when Huaca Sol was in use.
Isotope analysis shows that nearly all individuals with modified skulls grew up in a highland region where head binding was practiced by rich and poor families alike.
Individuals with modified skulls at Huaca Sol show markedly fewer skeletal signs of childhood malnutrition than do individuals with unmodified skulls buried at the site.
The gold ornaments buried at Huaca Sol were made using metalworking techniques that had been practiced at the site for several centuries.

explanation.passage: At an ancient Peruvian cemetery, some people had skulls reshaped by binding their heads as babies. Those people were more often buried with gold and fine cloth, signs of wealth. Calderón argues head shaping was mainly a badge of upper-class status. But two things can appear together without one marking the other. To weaken her argument, look for another feature these people shared that could explain both their skull shape and their wealth.
choices: Incorrect. The practice existing at other sites does not tell us what it meant at Huaca Sol. This is outside the scope of the argument.

Correct. Isotope analysis can show where a person grew up. If almost everyone with a shaped skull came from a highland region where all families, rich or poor, bound their babies' heads, then skull shape marks where a person came from, not their class. Their richer burials could reflect the wealth of that migrant group, so head shaping was not mainly an elite badge.
Incorrect. Better childhood nutrition suggests these individuals were well off, which fits the idea that they were elite. This supports her argument.
Incorrect. How the gold was made says nothing about who received it or why. This is a topic match that misses the claim.

passage.text: Tree rings from across Europe show that summers around 536 CE were among the coldest of the past two thousand years. A layer of ice in a Greenland ice core dated to 536 contains a spike in sulfate, a chemical released by volcanic eruptions that, once in the upper atmosphere, can block sunlight and cool the climate. Because Greenland lies close to Iceland, glaciologist Sigrid Holm argues that the cold summers resulted from a large eruption of an Icelandic volcano.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Holm's argument?
choices: Particles of volcanic glass in the 536 ice layer have a chemical composition that matches rock from volcanoes in Central America but not rock from volcanoes in Iceland.
Ice cores drilled in Antarctica show no sulfate spike in the layers dating to 536, though they do show clear spikes for several other large eruptions of that era.
Records indicate that several Icelandic volcanoes erupted repeatedly during the centuries before 536, sometimes producing large amounts of ash.
The sulfate spike in the Greenland ice layer dating to 536 is larger than any other sulfate spike recorded anywhere in that ice core for the entire first millennium CE.

explanation.passage: In 536 CE, Europe had extremely cold summers. A Greenland ice core shows a burst of sulfate, a chemical from volcanoes, in that same year. Sulfate high in the sky blocks sunlight, so a volcano is a good suspect. Holm goes one step further and names the volcano's location, Iceland, mostly because Iceland is near Greenland. The question asks you to weaken that specific step, the claim about where the eruption happened.
choices: Correct. Volcanic glass carries the chemical fingerprint of the volcano that produced it. If the glass in the 536 layer matches Central American volcanoes and not Icelandic ones, the eruption most likely happened in Central America. That directly contradicts Holm's claim that an Icelandic volcano was responsible.

Incorrect. A spike in Greenland but none in Antarctica suggests the eruption was in the far north, since big eruptions near the equator tend to leave sulfate at both poles. That fits an Icelandic eruption, so this supports Holm.
Incorrect. Icelandic volcanoes being active before 536 makes an Icelandic eruption in 536 seem possible, if anything. It does not weaken her argument.
Incorrect. A very large spike shows the eruption was big enough to cool the climate, but it says nothing about where the volcano was. It does not challenge her claim about the location.

passage.text: In 2015, a microfinance organization began offering small loans to aspiring business owners in 40 villages in northern Ghana. Three years later, economist Kwame Asante found that average household income in those villages was 18 percent higher than in 40 nearby villages where the loans had not been offered. He concludes that access to the loans caused the higher household income.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Asante's conclusion?
choices: Most borrowers in the 40 villages used their loans to start or expand small shops selling food, clothing, and household goods.
Borrowers in the 40 villages repaid more than 95 percent of their loans on schedule during the three years after the program began.
The organization selected the 40 villages because, before 2015, household incomes there were already rising faster than in surrounding villages.
Household incomes also rose between 2015 and 2018 in the 40 nearby villages where loans were not offered, though by a noticeably smaller amount.

explanation.passage: Villages that got small business loans had higher incomes three years later than villages that did not. Asante concludes the loans caused the difference. This kind of comparison only works if the two groups of villages were alike to begin with. If the loan villages were already different, the gap might have existed or grown without the loans. To weaken his conclusion, look for evidence that the two groups were not alike from the start.
choices: Incorrect. Knowing what borrowers spent the loans on does not tell us whether the loans caused the income gap. It is consistent with Asante's conclusion.
Incorrect. High repayment rates show the program ran smoothly, but they do not show whether something other than the loans explains the income difference.

Correct. If the loan villages were picked because their incomes were already growing faster, they would likely have pulled ahead even without loans. The 18 percent gap could reflect that head start rather than the effect of the loans, which undercuts Asante's causal conclusion.
Incorrect. Incomes rising in both groups, but more in the loan villages, is consistent with the loans adding extra growth. This does not weaken the conclusion.

passage.text: Karahan Tepe, a site in southeastern Turkey, features massive carved stone pillars erected around 11,000 years ago. Excavators have recovered thousands of charred cereal grains from the site, but all of them have the slender shape and brittle stalk attachment typical of wild cereals, rather than the plump shape and tough attachment typical of domesticated cereals. Archaeologist Deniz Aksoy concludes that the people who built Karahan Tepe gathered wild plants and did not yet cultivate crops.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Aksoy's conclusion?
choices: Animal bones recovered at Karahan Tepe come overwhelmingly from wild species such as gazelle, wild boar, and red deer rather than from domesticated herd animals.
The carvings on the stone pillars at Karahan Tepe depict wild animals such as foxes, snakes, and vultures but no crops.
Most cereal grains recovered at other sites in the region dating to about 9,000 years ago are of the domesticated type.
In experiments, wild cereals planted and harvested by people for many generations kept their wild-type grain shape and stalk attachment for centuries.

explanation.passage: At an 11,000-year-old site with giant carved pillars, every cereal grain found looks wild: thin, with a stalk that breaks easily. Domesticated grain looks different: plump, with a tough stalk. Aksoy concludes the builders gathered wild plants and did not farm. Her reasoning assumes that if people were farming, their grain would already look domesticated. To weaken her conclusion, look for evidence that people could farm cereals while the grains still looked wild.
choices: Incorrect. Wild animal bones show the people hunted, which fits the picture of foragers. This does not weaken the conclusion about plants, and it leans toward supporting it.
Incorrect. What the carvings show is a topic match, but carvings are art, not evidence of what people planted. This does not weaken the argument.

Incorrect. Domesticated grain appearing 2,000 years later at other sites does not tell us whether Karahan Tepe's builders were cultivating crops. It is consistent with Aksoy's view that farming came later.

Correct. If cereals grown by people kept their wild shape for centuries, then 'wild-looking grain' does not prove the grain was gathered wild. The builders could have been planting and harvesting crops that had not yet changed shape, so Aksoy's evidence fits early farming just as well as foraging.

passage.text: During a 2019 marine heat wave around the island of Ofu in American Samoa, most colonies of the coral *Acropora hyacinthus* in deeper reef zones bleached, expelling the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and supply them with food, and many colonies died. On the shallow reef flat, however, most colonies of the same species survived without bleaching. Marine biologist Talia Faleolo found that the reef-flat colonies mostly hosted a type of algae known to tolerate heat, and she concludes that hosting this algae is what protected them.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Faleolo's conclusion?
choices: The heat-tolerant algae supply their coral hosts with somewhat less food than other types of algae supply under normal conditions.
Reef-flat colonies endure large daily temperature swings at low tide, and colonies exposed to such swings in experiments resist bleaching whatever algae they host.
Reef-flat colonies that hosted the heat-tolerant algae were considerably more likely to survive the 2019 heat wave than were reef-flat colonies hosting other types of algae.
Coral bleaching events in the waters around Ofu have become considerably more frequent since the 1990s than they were in earlier decades.

explanation.passage: Corals have tiny algae living inside them that feed them. In a heat wave, stressed corals 'bleach,' meaning they push out the algae and often die. On one reef, deep corals bleached but shallow reef-flat corals did not. The shallow corals mostly had a heat-tolerant type of algae, so Faleolo concludes the algae protected them. But the reef flat differs from deep water in other ways too. To weaken her conclusion, look for another difference that could explain the shallow corals' survival.
choices: Incorrect. This describes a downside of the heat-tolerant algae under normal conditions. It does not say anything about whether the algae protected the corals during the heat wave.

Correct. If reef-flat corals are used to big daily temperature swings, and corals exposed to such swings resist bleaching no matter which algae they carry, then the reef flat's conditions alone could explain why those corals survived. The algae may not be what protected them, which undercuts Faleolo's conclusion.
Incorrect. If reef-flat corals with the heat-tolerant algae survived better than reef-flat corals without it, that points to the algae as protective. This supports her conclusion.
Incorrect. More frequent bleaching around Ofu is background information about the area. It does not explain why reef-flat corals survived in 2019.

passage.text: The woolly mammoths of Wrangel Island, off the coast of northeastern Siberia, survived until about 4,000 years ago, thousands of years after mainland mammoths had died out. A common explanation for their disappearance is that humans, who arrived on the island at around that time, hunted them to extinction. Paleogeneticist Hendrik Lund and colleagues, however, reject that explanation.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Lund and colleagues reject the common explanation presented in the text?
choices: The Wrangel Island mammoths had very low genetic diversity, a condition that has made some small modern animal populations more vulnerable to hunting.
The earliest human inhabitants of Wrangel Island made many of their tools and weapons from walrus ivory and driftwood.
Radiocarbon dates show that the most recent mammoth remains on Wrangel Island are several centuries older than the earliest evidence of humans there.
Mammoths on the Siberian mainland disappeared at roughly the same time that humans began occupying the regions where they lived.

explanation.passage: Mammoths lived on Wrangel Island long after they disappeared elsewhere. The usual story is that people arrived on the island and hunted the last ones. Lund and colleagues do not accept that story. The question asks what finding would give them a good reason to reject it. For humans to have hunted the mammoths to extinction, humans and mammoths must have been on the island at the same time.
choices: Incorrect. This says the mammoths' low genetic diversity could have made them easier to wipe out by hunting. That makes the hunting explanation more believable, not less, so it is no reason to reject it.
Incorrect. What the first islanders used for tools has nothing to do with whether they killed the mammoths. This is true-but-irrelevant.

Correct. If the youngest mammoth remains are centuries older than the first signs of people, the mammoths were already gone when humans arrived. People cannot hunt to extinction animals that had already disappeared, so this directly explains why Lund and colleagues reject the hunting explanation.
Incorrect. Mammoths vanishing on the mainland just as humans arrived there is a pattern that supports the idea that humans hunted mammoths. It gives no reason to reject the common explanation.

passage.text: Historians have long credited the spread of the printing press in fifteenth-century Europe with dramatically increasing the number of books in circulation. Economic historian Clara Weiss agrees that print vastly expanded book production, but she argues that its effect on ordinary people's literacy was far slower and more uneven than is commonly assumed. Weiss concedes, however, that in certain cities literacy may have risen quickly once print shops opened there.

question: Which finding, if true, would provide the best evidence that Weiss was right to make the concession described in the text?
choices: In several German cities, the share of guild members able to sign their names rose sharply within a decade of the first local print shop opening.
Printed books in the fifteenth century cost only a fraction of what comparable handwritten manuscripts had cost a century earlier.
In rural areas far from any print shop, literacy changed little for more than a century after the printing press was introduced.
Most books printed in the fifteenth century were written in Latin, a language that few ordinary Europeans of the period could read or understand.

explanation.passage: The passage is about the printing press. Weiss agrees it produced many more books, but she argues it did not quickly make ordinary people literate. Then she 'concedes' (admits a point that goes partly against her own view): in some cities, literacy may have jumped quickly after print shops opened. The question asks for evidence that this admission was justified. So you need a finding showing a fast rise in literacy in a city soon after printing arrived, not evidence for her main argument.
choices: Correct. A sharp rise in people able to sign their names within ten years of a local print shop opening is exactly a quick rise in literacy in certain cities after printing arrived. That is what Weiss conceded, so this shows she was right to concede it.
Incorrect. Cheaper books support the point Weiss already agrees with, that print expanded book production. It says nothing about whether literacy rose quickly in any city.
Incorrect. Slow change in rural areas supports Weiss's main argument that print's effect on literacy was slow and uneven. It does not support the concession about fast change in certain cities.
Incorrect. Books being mostly in Latin would help explain why literacy rose slowly, which supports Weiss's main argument, not her concession.

passage.text: The number of barn swallows breeding in parts of Britain has fallen sharply since the 1970s. The most common explanation is that modern farm buildings, with sealed metal walls and closed doors, have replaced the open timber barns where swallows attach their mud nests, leaving the birds with too few places to breed. Ornithologists Fiona Rait and Daniel Achterberg, however, reject this explanation.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Rait and Achterberg reject the common explanation presented in the text?
choices: Agricultural surveys show that many British farms have replaced their traditional timber barns with steel-framed buildings since the 1970s.
Where swallows have declined, most old barns remain intact and open, yet the nest sites in them that swallows used in past decades now go unused.
Barn swallows rarely nest anywhere other than inside buildings, where they attach their mud nests to the beams and walls beneath a roof.
National bird surveys show that the number of barn swallows breeding in Britain has varied considerably from one year to the next since the 1970s.

explanation.passage: Fewer barn swallows breed in Britain than in the 1970s. The usual explanation is a housing shortage: open wooden barns, where swallows build nests, have been replaced by sealed modern buildings. Two ornithologists (bird scientists) reject that explanation. You need a finding that would show the housing-shortage idea is wrong, meaning that places to nest are not actually what is missing.
choices: Incorrect. Old barns being replaced by sealed buildings is exactly what the common explanation says happened. This supports the explanation instead of giving a reason to reject it.

Correct. If the old barns are still standing and open, but the nest sites in them sit empty, then swallows are not short of places to breed. Something else must be reducing their numbers, which is a strong reason to reject the nest-site explanation.
Incorrect. If swallows nest almost only in buildings, losing open barns would hurt them badly. This makes the common explanation more convincing, not less.
Incorrect. Year-to-year ups and downs do not tell us what caused the long-term decline. This is true-but-irrelevant.

passage.text: On Racetrack Playa, a dry lakebed in Death Valley, California, rocks weighing up to 300 kilograms leave long trails in the cracked mud, showing that they have somehow slid across the surface. A common explanation was that powerful winds alone pushed the rocks across the slick mud after rare rains. Geologists Rhea Calloway and Ben Okafor, however, reject this explanation, arguing that thin sheets of floating ice must also be involved.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Calloway and Okafor reject the common explanation presented in the text?
choices: Rain falls on Racetrack Playa only a few times each year, and most of that rain falls during the winter months.
Winds measured at the playa over a decade never approached the speeds that experiments show are needed to push the heaviest rocks across wet mud.
Most of the rocks on Racetrack Playa have broken off a dolomite hillside at the southern end of the lakebed.
Strong gusts of wind are common on Racetrack Playa during the winter months, when the surface of the lakebed is most likely to be wet, soft, and slick.

explanation.passage: Heavy rocks on a dry lakebed in California leave trails, so they must move somehow. The old explanation said strong wind alone pushes them across wet, slippery mud. Calloway and Okafor reject that and say ice must also help. The question asks for a finding that would explain their rejection, meaning a reason to think wind alone is not enough.
choices: Incorrect. Knowing when it rains tells us when the mud is slick, but it does not show that wind is too weak to move the rocks. It does not explain the rejection.

Correct. If ten years of measurements show the wind never gets close to the speed needed to push the heaviest rocks, then wind alone cannot explain how those rocks move. Something else, such as ice, must be helping, which is exactly why the geologists reject the common explanation.
Incorrect. Where the rocks came from does not tell us how they slide. This is true-but-irrelevant.
Incorrect. Strong winds happening when the mud is wet would make the wind explanation seem more likely. This supports the common explanation.

passage.text: The giraffe's neck, which can exceed two meters in length, is often said to have evolved because it allowed giraffes to reach leaves too high for competing browsers such as antelope, giving long-necked individuals an advantage when food was scarce. Zoologists Naomi Fischer and Peter Mwangi, however, reject this common explanation.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain why Fischer and Mwangi reject the common explanation presented in the text?
choices: Giraffes can reach leaves more than five meters above the ground, far higher than any other browsing animal in the African savanna can reach.
The giraffe's long neck contains seven vertebrae, the same number found in the necks of nearly all other mammals.
During the dry season, when food is scarcest, giraffes feed mostly on shrubs at shoulder height or lower rather than on high branches.
Antelope living in the same habitats as giraffes feed mainly on grasses and on shrubs less than a meter tall.

explanation.passage: The common explanation for the giraffe's long neck has two parts: the neck lets giraffes reach high leaves other animals cannot, and that matters most when food is scarce. Fischer and Mwangi reject this. The question asks what would justify rejecting it. Look for a finding that shows giraffes do not actually depend on high leaves at the very time the explanation says the neck matters most.
choices: Incorrect. This shows giraffes can reach much higher than other animals, which supports the idea that the neck gives them access to food others cannot get. It is no reason to reject the explanation.
Incorrect. The number of neck bones is an interesting fact, but it does not tell us why the neck became long. This is true-but-irrelevant.

Correct. The common explanation says the neck helps most when food is scarce, by letting giraffes eat high leaves. If, in the scarcest season, giraffes mostly eat low shrubs instead, the neck is not giving them that advantage when it supposedly matters most. That undercuts the explanation.
Incorrect. Antelope eating low plants means giraffes avoid competition by eating high, which fits the common explanation. This supports it rather than giving a reason to reject it.

passage.text: Many of the great cities of the Classic Maya lowlands were abandoned between about 800 and 950 CE.
