"The barnacle volumes earned Darwin the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1853 and secured his reputation as a careful, systematic naturalist, a standing that would later lend weight to his far more controversial book among scientists who had never read the barnacle work."
"Among the barnacles Darwin found tiny 'complemental males' living inside the shells of much larger hermaphrodites, a discovery he regarded as among the strangest of his career."

"Again and again he found that specimens he had placed in a single species differed in nearly every part he measured; by 1854 he no longer doubted that variation was everywhere and abundant, a conviction that runs through the opening chapters of the Origin."

explanation.passage: The passage contrasts the 'detour' view with the student's view. The student's claim links three things: (1) the barnacle work, (2) Darwin's new belief that variation within a species is widespread, and (3) the importance of that belief in the *Origin*. The best quotation ties the barnacle work to the variation idea and ideally to the *Origin*. Choices that describe other results of the barnacle years do not help.
choices: Incorrect. This shows that the work was boring and hard on Darwin. If anything, it fits the 'detour' view, and it says nothing about variation.
Incorrect. This is true but irrelevant. Winning a medal and gaining a reputation is a real benefit of the work, but the claim is about what Darwin learned regarding variation, not about his career.

Incorrect. This describes a striking discovery from the barnacle work, so it is a topic match. But odd reproductive arrangements are not the same as variation among members of one species, and nothing links this to the *Origin*.

Correct. Specimens of "a single species" differing "in nearly every part" is the evidence of variation within species (parts 1 and 2). "He no longer doubted that variation was everywhere and abundant" shows the change in his belief, and the reference to the *Origin*'s opening chapters covers part 3.

passage.text: The name "Silk Road" can suggest caravans carrying goods all the way from China to the Mediterranean. A student writing about this trade network argues that, in fact, very few goods or merchants traveled its entire length; instead, goods typically passed through many hands, moving in a series of short stages between regional markets.

question: Which quotation from a work by a historian would most directly support the student's claim?
choices: "Silk found in Egyptian tombs of the first millennium BCE shows that Chinese textiles reached the Mediterranean world remarkably early."

"The documents from the oasis towns record merchants whose journeys seldom exceeded a few hundred miles; a bolt of silk that reached Samarkand had most likely changed owners at every market between there and Dunhuang."
"Marco Polo's account of his travels to the court of Kublai Khan was read across Europe as a guide to the riches of the East."

"Caravans crossing the Taklamakan Desert depended on Bactrian camels, which could carry several hundred pounds and go for days without water, and on the wells maintained at oases along the desert's northern and southern rims."

explanation.passage: The student's claim corrects a common image. It says (1) few goods or merchants made the whole trip, and (2) goods moved in short stages, changing hands at regional markets. The right quotation should show short journeys and repeated changes of owner. Be careful with choices that show goods traveling far, since that alone does not tell you how they traveled.
choices: Incorrect. This shows that Chinese silk did reach the Mediterranean early. But it says nothing about how it got there, in one long trip or many short ones, so it does not support the claim.

Correct. Merchants whose journeys "seldom exceeded a few hundred miles" shows that few traveled the whole way (part 1), and silk that "changed owners at every market" shows goods passing through many hands in stages (part 2).

Incorrect. Marco Polo is famous for traveling the whole route, so this example, if anything, suggests a long journey, which works against the claim. It is also about a book's popularity, not about how goods moved.
Incorrect. This describes how caravans crossed a desert. It is about the means of transport, not about whether goods traveled the whole route or in short stages.

passage.text: When Samuel Johnson began work on his *Dictionary of the English Language* (1755), many of his supporters hoped the book would fix the language in a permanent, correct form. A student claims that by the time Johnson finished, he had abandoned that hope and had come to regard change in a living language as impossible to stop.

question: Which quotation from the preface to Johnson's *Dictionary* would most directly support the student's claim?
choices: "I have, notwithstanding this discouragement, attempted a dictionary of the English language, which, while it was employed in the cultivation of every species of literature, has itself been hitherto neglected."

"Every language has its anomalies, which, though inconvenient, and in themselves once unnecessary, must be tolerated among the imperfections of human things, and which require only to be registered, that they may not be increased, and ascertained, that they may not be confounded."

"Those who think well of my design require that it should fix our language. With this hope I confess I flattered myself for a while; but now begin to fear that I have indulged expectation which neither reason nor experience can justify. To enchain syllables, and to lash the wind, are equally the undertakings of pride."
"I am not yet so lost in lexicography as to forget that words are the daughters of earth, and that things are the sons of heaven."

explanation.passage: The student claims a change of mind: Johnson once hoped his dictionary could freeze English in place, but by the end he gave up that hope and saw language change as unstoppable. So the right quotation must show (1) the earlier hope and (2) its abandonment because change cannot be stopped. One choice talks about accepting flaws in language, which is close but different.
choices: Incorrect. Johnson explains why he took on the project (English had no proper dictionary). It describes his purpose, not a change in his views about fixing the language.

Incorrect. This is the near-synonym trap. Johnson accepts that languages have irregularities ("anomalies") that must be "tolerated." Putting up with oddities is not the same as believing change cannot be stopped, and there is no sign of a hope he gave up.

Correct. Johnson admits he once "flattered" himself that the dictionary could "fix our language" (the earlier hope), but now fears that hope cannot be justified (the abandonment). Comparing the effort to trying to "enchain syllables" or "lash the wind" shows he now sees language change as impossible to control.
Incorrect. This famous line says words are less important than the real things they name. It is a reflection on words versus reality, not on whether language can be kept from changing.

passage.text: People who take a 50-minute walk in a park often perform better afterward on tests of directed attention, such as repeating strings of digits in reverse order, than they did before the walk. Psychologist Mira Castellanos and colleagues hypothesize that this benefit comes specifically from looking at natural scenery, which holds attention effortlessly and lets the mental resources used for concentration recover, not merely from the exercise and the break from work that a walk in a park also provides.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Castellanos and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: Participants who walked in a park for 50 minutes improved on attention tests more than participants who spent the same 50 minutes working at their desks.
Participants who walked in a park rated the experience as more pleasant and less tiring than did participants who walked on an indoor treadmill for the same time.
Participants who walked on an indoor treadmill for 50 minutes improved on attention tests about as much as participants who walked in a park for 50 minutes.
Participants who sat indoors viewing photographs of natural scenes improved on attention tests more than those who sat viewing photographs of city streets.

explanation.passage: After a walk in a park, people do better on tests that require focus. But a park walk bundles several things together: seeing nature, getting exercise, and taking a break. The researchers' hypothesis picks out ONE of these: seeing nature is what helps, not the exercise or the break. To support it, you need a comparison that keeps exercise and the break the same (or removes them) and changes only whether people see nature.
choices: Incorrect. The walkers got nature, exercise, and a break, while the desk workers got none of these. The improvement could come from any of the three, so this does not isolate nature.
Incorrect. How pleasant the walk felt is not the same as how well people did on attention tests. This is true-but-irrelevant to the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. If an indoor treadmill walk, with no natural scenery, helped just as much, then exercise and the break explain the benefit, which weakens the hypothesis.

Correct. Both groups sat (no exercise) and both took the same kind of break from work. The only difference was whether the pictures showed nature or city streets. The nature group improving more points to natural scenery itself as the cause.

passage.text: Patients with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, vary widely in how they respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that release a "brake" on the immune system so that it can attack tumors. A team led by Teodor Lindqvist observed that patients who responded well tended to have higher levels of the gut bacterium *Bifidobacterium longum* than patients who did not. The team hypothesizes that the bacterium itself strengthens the drug's effect, rather than simply being a marker of some other trait that good responders happen to share.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
choices: Patients with high levels of *B. longum* also tended to eat diets richer in fiber than other patients did, and high-fiber diets are known to change the numbers of many kinds of gut bacteria.
Levels of *B. longum* in good responders' guts did not change over the course of their treatment.
Patients who did not respond to the drug showed no improvement even when they had high levels of gut bacteria other than *B. longum*.
Mice with tumors that received gut bacteria from good responders responded better to the drug than identical mice that received the same bacteria with *B. longum* removed.

explanation.passage: The team noticed a link: good responders had more of a certain gut bacterium. But a link alone does not show cause, because the bacterium could just travel along with some other trait (like diet) that is really responsible. The team's hypothesis is that the bacterium itself causes the better response. The best support would be a test where only the bacterium changes and the result changes with it.
choices: Incorrect. This points to a possible other cause: diet. If high-fiber diets are the real reason, the bacterium might just be a marker, so this finding weakens the hypothesis rather than supporting it.
Incorrect. Knowing that bacteria levels stayed steady does not tell you whether the bacterium caused the better response. It is neutral.
Incorrect. This is about other bacteria, not *B. longum*. It does not show that *B. longum* itself does anything.

Correct. The two groups of mice were identical and got the same bacteria except for *B. longum*. Only the mice with *B. longum* responded better, so the bacterium itself made the difference. This is the cause-and-effect test the hypothesis needs.

passage.text: In the coastal town of Port Asher, younger residents increasingly pronounce the vowel in words like "boat" farther forward in the mouth than older residents do. Sociolinguist Inès Moreau hypothesizes that this change is spreading mainly through close personal contact, with speakers picking up the new pronunciation from people they talk with regularly, rather than through exposure to television and other broadcast media, in which the fronted vowel is also common.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moreau's hypothesis?
choices: The fronted vowel is much more common among Port Asher residents under thirty than among residents over sixty.
Among residents of the same age who watch similar amounts of television, those whose closest friends use the fronted vowel use it far more often than those whose closest friends do not.
The fronted vowel is heard frequently in nationally broadcast television programs that are popular with young viewers in Port Asher, and it is rarely heard in programs aimed at older audiences.
Older Port Asher residents who use the fronted vowel report that they began using it only as adults.

explanation.passage: A sound change is happening in Port Asher: younger people say the vowel in "boat" differently. There are two possible routes for the change: personal contact (friends and family) or media (TV). Moreau says personal contact is the main route. The passage notes the new vowel is ALSO common on TV, so a supporting finding must show that personal contact matters even when TV exposure is the same.
choices: Incorrect. This only confirms that the change is happening among young people, which the passage already says. It does not show HOW the change spreads, so it fits both routes equally.

Correct. By comparing people of the same age who watch the same amount of TV, this finding holds media exposure constant. The difference in use then lines up with whether close friends use the vowel, which points to personal contact as the route.
Incorrect. This supports the media route, the alternative Moreau rejects. It is a reversal trap: it shows young people hear the vowel on TV, which would make media a likely source.
Incorrect. This tells us when some older speakers started using the vowel, but not where they picked it up. It is true-sounding but irrelevant to the contact-versus-media question.

passage.text: Over several months, the star VX Corvi dimmed to less than half its usual brightness before recovering. Astronomer Rafael Quintero hypothesizes that the dimming was caused by a cloud of dust that passed between the star and Earth, rather than by a temporary drop in the amount of light the star itself gave off. Dust grains of the kind found around such stars block short-wavelength (blue) light much more effectively than long-wavelength (infrared) light, whereas a drop in a star's own output would reduce its brightness by similar proportions at all wavelengths.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Quintero's hypothesis?
choices: VX Corvi dimmed by about the same proportion at visible wavelengths as it did at infrared wavelengths.
Several other stars similar in size and age to VX Corvi have dimmed by comparable amounts over similar periods of several months.
During the dimming, VX Corvi's brightness fell by about 60 percent in blue light but by less than 10 percent in infrared light.
VX Corvi has dimmed by smaller amounts at irregular intervals throughout the century in which it has been observed.

explanation.passage: The star got dimmer, and there are two possible explanations: dust blocking its light (Quintero's view) or the star itself giving off less light. The last sentence gives you the test: dust blocks blue light much more than infrared light, while a real drop in the star's output dims all colors by about the same share. So support for the dust idea would be dimming that is much stronger in blue than in infrared.
choices: Incorrect. Equal dimming across wavelengths is exactly what the passage says would happen if the star's own output dropped. This is a reversal trap: it supports the explanation Quintero rejects.
Incorrect. Other stars dimming similarly says nothing about the cause of VX Corvi's dimming. It is irrelevant to dust versus a drop in output.
Correct. A 60 percent drop in blue light but under 10 percent in infrared is the uneven, blue-heavy pattern the passage says dust produces. This matches the test for the dust hypothesis.
Incorrect. This shows the star has a history of small dimming events but gives no information about what caused this event. It fits either explanation.

passage.text: The mushroom *Neonothopanus gardneri*, which grows at the base of palm trees in northeastern Brazil, gives off a green glow that is brightest at night, a rhythm controlled by an internal daily clock. Biologist Renata Alves and colleagues hypothesize that the glow attracts night-active insects, which then carry the fungus's spores to new sites, helping the fungus spread across a forest floor where little wind reaches the ground to carry its spores.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
choices: The fungus's glow begins to brighten each evening at the usual time even when the mushrooms are grown in a laboratory and kept in constant darkness for several days.
Several other species of glowing fungi have been found growing on dead wood and leaf litter in forests in Japan, Australia, and North America.
Night-active beetles and flies are strongly drawn to a scent that the mushrooms release, and these insects visit the mushrooms most often on humid nights.
Plastic model mushrooms lit to match the glow drew far more insects at night than unlit models did, and insects on real mushrooms carried the fungus's spores.

explanation.passage: This mushroom glows, especially at night. The team thinks the glow has a job: it draws in insects that are active at night, and those insects carry the fungus's spores (its 'seeds') to new places, which matters because there is little wind on the forest floor. A finding that supports this must show two things: the glow itself attracts insects, and the insects actually carry spores.
choices: Incorrect. This confirms that the glow is controlled by an internal clock, which the passage already states. It says nothing about insects or spores, so it does not support the hypothesis about why the fungus glows.
Incorrect. Other glowing fungi existing elsewhere is outside the scope of the hypothesis. It does not show that the glow attracts insects or spreads spores.

Incorrect. This is a topic match that misses the claim. It shows insects are drawn to the mushrooms, but by a scent, not the glow. That points to a different explanation and does not support the idea that the glow is what attracts them.

Correct. The plastic models had no scent or living tissue, only light, so their attracting more insects shows the glow by itself draws insects. Finding spores on insects visiting real mushrooms shows the second part: insects carry the spores. Both parts of the hypothesis are supported.

passage.text: When maize (corn) is grown in alternating rows with soybeans, the maize plants often produce more grain than maize grown alone. Soybeans host bacteria in their roots that "fix" nitrogen, converting nitrogen gas from the air into a form plants can use. Agronomist Lúcia Ferraz hypothesizes that the maize benefits because some of this fixed nitrogen moves through the soil from the soybeans to the neighboring maize plants.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferraz's hypothesis?
choices: Soybeans grown alongside maize produced fewer beans per plant than soybeans grown alone.
When the soybeans were supplied with nitrogen gas containing a rare, traceable form of nitrogen, that form of nitrogen was later detected in the leaves of nearby maize plants.
Maize grown alongside sorghum, a crop that does not fix nitrogen, also produced more grain per plant than maize grown alone in the same fields.
Fields planted with maize and soybeans together had fewer weeds than fields planted with maize alone, so the maize in those fields faced less competition for water and light.

explanation.passage: The passage reports that maize grows better next to soybeans. Soybeans (through bacteria in their roots) turn nitrogen from the air into plant food. Ferraz says the maize benefits because that nitrogen travels from the soybeans to the maize. The best support would show nitrogen actually moving from soybean to maize.
choices: Incorrect. This is about the soybeans' yield, not the maize's. It does not show nitrogen moving to the maize.
Correct. The traceable nitrogen was given to the soybeans, and it later turned up in maize leaves. That directly shows nitrogen fixed by the soybeans moving to the maize, which is the hypothesis.
Incorrect. If maize also grows better next to a crop that cannot fix nitrogen, the benefit may have nothing to do with nitrogen. This weakens the hypothesis.
Incorrect. Fewer weeds is a different possible reason the maize grows better. It offers an alternative explanation instead of supporting Ferraz's.

passage.text: Sociologists distinguish strong ties (close friends and immediate collaborators) from weak ties (acquaintances with whom one interacts only occasionally). Studying a large company that shifted to fully remote work, sociologist Dana Whitcombe hypothesizes that remote work erodes weak ties while leaving strong ties largely intact, because weak ties are sustained mostly by chance encounters in shared physical spaces such as hallways and break rooms.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitcombe's hypothesis?
choices: After the shift to remote work, employees sent more electronic messages overall than they had before.

After the shift to remote work, employees communicated less often both with their closest collaborators and with colleagues in other departments, and they reported feeling more isolated from the company as a whole.
Employees who reported having many acquaintances at work before the shift also reported higher job satisfaction.

After the shift to remote work, communication between employees who had previously interacted only occasionally fell by nearly half, while communication within close working groups stayed near its previous level.

explanation.passage: The first sentence defines two kinds of work relationships: strong ties (close collaborators) and weak ties (occasional acquaintances). Whitcombe's hypothesis has two halves: remote work (1) weakens weak ties but (2) leaves strong ties mostly unchanged. A supporting finding must show both: a drop in weak-tie contact AND little change in strong-tie contact.
choices: Incorrect. More messages overall tells you nothing about which ties grew or shrank. It is irrelevant to the difference between weak and strong ties.

Incorrect. This is half right. Less contact with colleagues in other departments fits the first half, but less contact with closest collaborators contradicts the second half (strong ties staying intact).
Incorrect. This links acquaintances to job satisfaction before the shift. It may be interesting, but it says nothing about what remote work did to either kind of tie.
Correct. Contact between occasional acquaintances (weak ties) fell by nearly half, while contact within close working groups (strong ties) held steady. Both halves of the hypothesis are matched.

passage.text: In a well-known study, shoppers offered 24 varieties of jam were less likely to buy any jam than shoppers offered 6 varieties. Later studies, however, often failed to find this "choice overload" effect. Psychologist Mireille Okonkwo-Barr hypothesizes that large assortments discourage people from choosing only when the options are hard to compare, as when they differ on many features at once, and not when the options can easily be ranked along a single dimension.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okonkwo-Barr's hypothesis?
choices: Shoppers presented with 24 varieties of a product spent more time examining the options than did shoppers presented with 6 varieties.

Shoppers were less likely to buy from a large assortment than from a small one, regardless of whether the options differed on one feature or on several, and the size of this drop was similar in both cases.

When pens differed only in price, shoppers bought as often from 30 options as from 5; when pens varied in price, ink color, grip, and tip width, shoppers bought far less often from 30 options than from 5.
Shoppers who said they enjoyed shopping were less affected by the size of an assortment than were shoppers who said they did not.

explanation.passage: "Choice overload" means that having too many options makes people less likely to choose at all. Because later studies sometimes found it and sometimes did not, Okonkwo-Barr proposes a condition: overload happens only when options are hard to compare (many features), not when they can be ranked on one feature. A supporting finding should show overload in the many-features case but not in the one-feature case.
choices: Incorrect. Time spent looking is not the same as whether people buy. This finding does not address when overload occurs.
Incorrect. This says overload happened no matter how many features the options had. That contradicts the hypothesis, which says it should NOT happen when options differ on just one feature.

Correct. With pens differing only in price (easy to rank), 30 options did not reduce buying. With pens differing on four features (hard to compare), 30 options did reduce buying. This is exactly the contrast the hypothesis predicts.
Incorrect. This brings in a different factor, how much a shopper enjoys shopping. It is outside the scope of the hypothesis, which is about how easy the options are to compare.

passage.text: In temperate regions, influenza cases peak in winter. One common explanation is that people crowd together indoors in cold weather, making it easier for the virus to spread. Epidemiologist Kwame Asante hypothesizes instead that the main driver is low absolute humidity (the actual amount of water vapor in the air, which falls sharply in cold weather), because the influenza virus survives longer and spreads more easily in dry air.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Asante's hypothesis?
choices: In laboratory trials, guinea pigs passed influenza to one another far more readily at low humidity than at high humidity, even though the animals were kept equally close together and at the same temperature in every trial.
In temperate cities, influenza cases rose most sharply in the weeks after schools reopened following the winter holidays, and they rose less sharply in years when schools reopened later than usual.
In temperate regions, influenza peaks occur in the same months in which average temperatures are lowest.
Influenza virus particles were detected more often on indoor surfaces than on outdoor surfaces.

explanation.passage: There are two competing explanations for winter flu: crowding indoors (the common view) and dry air (Asante's view). The tricky part is that in real winters, cold, dry air and indoor crowding happen at the same time, so a seasonal pattern alone cannot tell them apart. Good support for Asante must show humidity mattering while crowding (and temperature) are held constant.
choices: Correct. The animals were kept equally close together (same crowding) and at the same temperature; only the humidity changed. The virus spread far more at low humidity, so dryness alone made the difference, which supports Asante.
Incorrect. Schools reopening brings children together, so this finding supports the crowding explanation, not Asante's. It is a reversal of what the question asks.
Incorrect. Cold months are both drier and more crowded indoors, so this pattern fits both explanations equally. It cannot support one over the other.
Incorrect. Finding more virus indoors is consistent with people spending time indoors (crowding) and does not involve humidity at all. It is irrelevant to Asante's specific claim.

passage.text: In German, every noun has a grammatical gender (masculine, feminine, or neuter) that determines which word for "the" comes before it: *der*, *die*, or *das*. Gender is only partly predictable from a noun's meaning (for example, nouns for male animals are usually masculine), but it is often predictable from the noun's sound: most nouns ending in "-e," for instance, are feminine. Linguist Anja Brenner hypothesizes that young German-speaking children assign gender to unfamiliar nouns mainly on the basis of such sound patterns rather than meaning.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brenner's hypothesis?
choices: Four-year-olds used the correct gender for familiar nouns more than 90 percent of the time.
When shown a picture of an unfamiliar male animal labeled with an invented word ending in "-e," most four-year-olds used *die* (the feminine form) rather than *der* (the masculine form).
When given invented words for unfamiliar objects, four-year-olds often used different genders for the same word on different occasions.
When shown a picture of an unfamiliar male animal labeled with an invented word that did not end in "-e," most four-year-olds used *der* (the masculine form), as adult German speakers also did.

explanation.passage: German nouns have genders shown by *der* (masculine), *die* (feminine), or *das* (neuter). Children could guess a new noun's gender from its meaning (male animal suggests masculine) or from its sound (ending in "-e" suggests feminine). Brenner says sound wins. The strongest test puts sound and meaning in conflict and sees which one children follow.
choices: Incorrect. Familiar nouns may simply be memorized, so this tells us nothing about how children handle unfamiliar ones. It is true-sounding but irrelevant.

Correct. Here meaning (a male animal) points to *der*, while sound (ending in "-e") points to *die*. Most children chose *die*, following the sound cue over the meaning cue, which is exactly what Brenner predicts.
Incorrect. Inconsistent answers show that children are unsure, not which cue they rely on. This does not support either side.

Incorrect. This is the subtle trap. For a male animal whose name lacks the "-e" ending, meaning points to *der* and no sound cue points to *die*, so choosing *der* fits the meaning explanation just as well as the sound explanation. It cannot show that sound is the main cue.

passage.text: Hot Jupiters are giant planets that orbit extremely close to their stars. Because such planets probably cannot form so close in, astronomers think they migrated inward from farther out. One proposal holds that they spiraled inward early, while still surrounded by the disk of gas from which they formed, which disappears within a few million years of a star's birth. Astronomer Yuki Tanabe instead hypothesizes that most hot Jupiters arrived late: they were flung onto stretched-out orbits by gravitational encounters with other planets, a process that typically takes hundreds of millions of years, and then gradually settled into close, circular orbits.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanabe's hypothesis?
choices: Hot Jupiters are found around stars only a few million years old at roughly the same rate as around much older stars.
Most known hot Jupiters have orbits that are nearly circular.
Giant planets orbiting far from their stars are more common than hot Jupiters are.
Hot Jupiters are found far less often around stars younger than about 100 million years than around older stars.

explanation.passage: Hot Jupiters are huge planets very close to their stars, and they must have moved inward. The two proposals differ mainly in TIMING: early migration happens within a few million years (while the gas disk exists), while Tanabe's late migration takes hundreds of millions of years. So the key prediction of Tanabe's idea is that very young stars should rarely have hot Jupiters yet, because there has not been time for them to arrive.
choices: Incorrect. If even very young stars have hot Jupiters as often as old stars, the planets must arrive early. This supports the early-migration proposal, the reverse of Tanabe's hypothesis.

Incorrect. The passage says that under Tanabe's idea the planets end up in circular orbits, but nothing suggests early migration would produce anything different. Since both proposals fit circular orbits, this cannot support one over the other.
Incorrect. How common far-out giant planets are is outside the question of when hot Jupiters arrive. It is irrelevant.

Correct. Fewer hot Jupiters around stars younger than about 100 million years means many hot Jupiters have not yet arrived around young stars, which is what a slow process lasting hundreds of millions of years predicts.

passage.text: Some high-strength steels become brittle and crack unexpectedly after months in service. Metallurgist Oren Halvorsen hypothesizes that this embrittlement is caused by hydrogen atoms, absorbed from moisture during use, that collect along grain boundaries (the borders between the tiny crystals that make up the metal) and weaken the bonds there.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Halvorsen's hypothesis?
choices: Cracks in embrittled parts ran along grain boundaries, but the parts contained no more hydrogen than parts of the same steel that had been in service just as long without cracking, and no hydrogen could be detected at their grain boundaries.
Steels of lower strength rarely became brittle, even after years in service.

In embrittled samples, cracks ran almost entirely along grain boundaries, and hydrogen concentrations at those boundaries were many times higher than inside the grains; samples kept free of hydrogen showed neither feature.
Embrittlement occurred more quickly in parts that were loaded and unloaded repeatedly than in parts kept under constant load.

explanation.passage: Grain boundaries are the borders between the tiny crystals inside a metal. Halvorsen's hypothesis has two connected parts: (1) hydrogen causes the brittleness, and (2) it does so by collecting at grain boundaries and weakening them. A strong supporting finding should show hydrogen concentrated at the boundaries, cracks along the boundaries, and no such problem when hydrogen is absent.
choices: Incorrect. This is half right but then fails. Cracks along grain boundaries fit the second part, but if cracked parts had no more hydrogen than uncracked ones, hydrogen is unlikely to be the cause. That weakens the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This compares steels of different strength. It is true that the passage is about high-strength steel, but this finding says nothing about hydrogen or grain boundaries.

Correct. Cracks follow the grain boundaries, hydrogen is concentrated at those boundaries, and hydrogen-free samples show neither feature. This supports both the cause (hydrogen) and the location (grain boundaries) in the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This points to repeated loading as a factor, which is outside the hypothesis. It does not involve hydrogen at all.

passage.text: Farmers sometimes plant cover crops such as rye in the months between cash-crop seasons, instead of leaving fields bare. Soil scientist Amara Diallo hypothesizes that cover crops improve soil's ability to hold water mainly by increasing the soil's organic matter (decomposed plant material), which absorbs water like a sponge.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Diallo's hypothesis?
choices: Fields planted with cover crops lost less soil to erosion during heavy rains than fields left bare.
Across many fields, the more a cover crop raised a soil's organic matter, the more extra water the soil held after rain; where organic matter did not rise, water holding did not improve.
Fields planted with cover crops held more water than bare fields, although their organic matter content was no higher, because the cover crops' roots left channels that let rain soak deeper.
Rye cover crops produced more plant material per acre than clover cover crops did.

explanation.passage: Cover crops are plants grown between main crops to protect the soil. Diallo's hypothesis has two parts: (1) cover crops help soil hold water, and (2) they do this mainly by adding organic matter. So the best support shows that the water benefit tracks the organic matter: more organic matter, more water held; no organic matter gain, no water gain.
choices: Incorrect. Less erosion is a different benefit of cover crops. It does not show better water holding, and it says nothing about organic matter.

Correct. Water holding rose in step with organic matter, and fields without an organic matter gain held no extra water. This ties the water benefit directly to organic matter, matching both parts of the hypothesis.

Incorrect. This is half right. It shows cover crops help soil hold water, but it says organic matter did NOT increase, so the benefit must come from something else. That undercuts the 'mainly by organic matter' part.
Incorrect. This compares two types of cover crop by how much plant material they produce. It does not measure water holding at all.

passage.text: After a community garden opened on a formerly vacant lot in the Eastbrook neighborhood, residents' reported trust in their neighbors rose. Sociologist Marcus Ellery hypothesizes that the increase resulted from residents repeatedly working alongside one another in the garden, rather than from the improved appearance of the lot.

question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ellery's hypothesis?
choices: Residents who regularly worked in the garden reported much larger increases in trust than residents who lived equally close to the garden and passed it daily but did not work in it.
In a nearby neighborhood where a vacant lot was cleaned and landscaped but not opened for gardening, residents' reported trust in their neighbors rose by a similar amount over the same period.
Most residents who worked in the garden said they had joined to grow vegetables rather than to meet their neighbors.
Reported trust in Eastbrook rose most during the months when the garden was in full bloom.

explanation.passage: Trust went up after the garden opened, and there are two possible reasons: working together in the garden (Ellery's view) or the lot simply looking nicer. To support Ellery, a finding should separate the two: compare people who see the improved lot equally but differ in whether they work in the garden.
choices: Correct. Both groups lived equally close and saw the garden daily, so they got the same benefit from its appearance. Only the gardeners showed big trust gains, so working together, not appearance, explains the increase.
Incorrect. Here the lot was only beautified, with no gardening, and trust still rose just as much. That supports the appearance explanation and weakens Ellery's.
Incorrect. Why people joined does not matter to the hypothesis. Even if they joined for vegetables, working side by side could still build trust, so this neither supports nor weakens it.

Incorrect. When the garden is in bloom it looks best, but it is also when people are likely working in it most. Because both explanations predict this pattern, it cannot support Ellery over the alternative.

passage.text: During a 2019 marine heat wave in Hawaii, marine biologist Keoni Akana and colleagues tracked bleaching (the loss of the symbiotic algae that supply corals with most of their food) in two reef-building corals, Porites lobata and Montipora capitata. Heat stress peaked in October and had subsided by early November. Because M. capitata can compensate for the loss of its algae by capturing plankton, Akana hypothesized that, although M. capitata might bleach more severely than P. lobata at the height of the heat wave, it would recover more quickly once water temperatures returned to normal.

figure.title: Percentage of Coral Colonies Bleached, 2019-2020

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Akana's hypothesis?
choices: In August, before heat stress peaked, a slightly larger percentage of M. capitata colonies than of P. lobata colonies was already bleached.
Both species reached their highest percentage of bleached colonies in October, the month in which heat stress was greatest.
The percentage of M. capitata colonies bleached fell from 70% in October to 4% in February, a much steeper drop than P. lobata's fall from 48% to 14%.
The percentage of P. lobata colonies bleached declined in every month after October, falling from 48% to 14% by February.

explanation.passage: Bleaching means a coral has lost the tiny algae that feed it, so a bleached coral is starving. The passage says heat stress peaked in October and was over by November, so the months after October show recovery. Akana's hypothesis has a key part: M. capitata may bleach worse at the peak, but it should recover faster afterward because it can eat plankton. So you need data that compare how fast the two species recovered after October, not just what happened at the peak.
choices: Incorrect. This is true (8% vs. 5%), but it describes August, before the heat wave peaked. The hypothesis is about recovery after the heat wave, so this is true but irrelevant.
Incorrect. Both species did peak in October (48% and 70%), but this only shows that both responded to heat. It says nothing about which species recovered faster, which is the heart of the hypothesis.

Correct. After heat stress ended, M. capitata dropped 66 percentage points (70 to 4) while P. lobata dropped only 34 points (48 to 14), and by February far fewer M. capitata colonies were still bleached. That is faster recovery despite worse peak bleaching, exactly what Akana predicted.
Incorrect. This is accurate for P. lobata, but it describes only one species. Without comparing it with M. capitata, it cannot show that M. capitata recovered more quickly.

passage.text: After corn is harvested in the fall, leftover nitrogen fertilizer can wash out of the soil as nitrate, polluting streams. Cover crops planted over the winter absorb some of this nitrogen. Agronomist Rosa Delgado compared winter nitrate leaching in Iowa cornfields left bare with fields planted with cereal rye, crimson clover (a legume, a plant that adds nitrogen to the soil through bacteria in its roots), or a rye-clover mix. In Delgado's trials, every cover crop reduced nitrate leaching relative to bare soil, but the legume alone was the least effective: ______

figure.title: Winter Nitrate Leaching by Field Treatment

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: fields planted with crimson clover leached 27 kilograms of nitrate per hectare, compared with 38 kilograms per hectare for fields with no cover crop.
fields planted with crimson clover leached 27 kilograms of nitrate per hectare, more than the 14 kilograms under cereal rye and the 18 kilograms under the rye-clover mix.
fields planted with cereal rye leached 14 kilograms of nitrate per hectare, less than half of the 38 kilograms per hectare leached from fields with no cover crop.
fields planted with the rye-clover mix leached 18 kilograms of nitrate per hectare, more than the 14 kilograms per hectare that fields planted with cereal rye alone leached.

explanation.passage: The passage explains that cover crops soak up leftover nitrogen so it doesn't wash into streams. Crimson clover is a legume, meaning it actually adds nitrogen to soil. The sentence to complete makes a specific claim: the clover by itself was the least effective of the cover crops. So the right data must show clover leaching more nitrate than each of the other cover-crop treatments.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares clover with bare soil. It shows clover helped, which is the first half of the sentence, not that clover was the least effective cover crop.
Correct. Clover fields leached 27 kg/ha, more than both rye (14) and the mix (18). Since those are the only other cover crops, this shows clover was the least effective one.
Incorrect. This is accurate (14 is less than half of 38), but it is about rye, not clover. It shows rye worked well, which does not establish that clover was the worst cover crop.
Incorrect. This compares the mix with rye. It is true, but it leaves clover out entirely, so it cannot show that clover was the least effective.

passage.text: White-nose syndrome, caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans, has killed millions of hibernating bats in North America since 2006. The fungus thrives in cold, humid caves, but within the range of temperatures found in hibernacula (the sites where bats hibernate), it grows more slowly the closer conditions are to freezing. Ecologist Kate Langwig and colleagues therefore hypothesized that little brown bat colonies hibernating in the coldest caves would suffer the smallest proportional declines after the fungus arrived. To test this, they compared colony sizes in 2008, before the fungus reached the study region, with sizes in 2013.

figure.title: Average Little Brown Bat Colony Size by Cave Temperature
figure.yLabel: Average number of bats per colony

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Langwig and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: In 2008, before the fungus arrived, colonies in 5-7°C caves were smaller on average than colonies in either the coldest caves or the warmest caves.
Colonies in 2-4°C caves fell from an average of 1,200 to 840 bats, a 30% decline, whereas colonies in 8-10°C caves fell from 1,400 to 210 bats, an 85% decline.
Colonies in every temperature group were smaller on average in 2013 than in 2008, with colonies in 5-7°C caves falling from 950 to an average of 380 bats.
In 2013, colonies in 2-4°C caves averaged 840 bats, whereas colonies in 8-10°C caves averaged 1,400 bats, the largest value for any temperature group in that year.

explanation.passage: The passage explains that the fungus grows more slowly near freezing, so bats in colder caves might be better protected. The hypothesis is about proportional decline: what share of each colony was lost between 2008 (before the fungus) and 2013 (after). So you have to compare before and after for each temperature group and see whether the coldest caves lost the smallest share. Notice the colonies started at different sizes, which is why the hypothesis talks about proportions rather than raw numbers.
choices: Incorrect. This is true (950 is less than 1,200 and 1,400), but it describes only 2008, before the fungus arrived. It says nothing about declines, so it is true but irrelevant.
Correct. The coldest colonies lost 360 of 1,200 bats (30%), while the warmest lost 1,190 of 1,400 (85%). The coldest caves had the smallest proportional decline, exactly as hypothesized.
Incorrect. Every group did shrink, but this only shows the fungus hurt all colonies. It does not compare the size of the declines across temperatures, which is what the hypothesis is about.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph: 1,400 is the 2008 value for 8-10°C caves. In 2013, those colonies averaged only 210 bats.

passage.text: Perovskite solar cells, named for the crystal structure of their light-absorbing layer, are inexpensive to manufacture but break down rapidly when exposed to moisture. Materials scientist Hyun-Jin Park and colleagues added an ultrathin two-dimensional capping layer to the surface of perovskite cells and tracked the efficiency (the percentage of incoming sunlight converted to electricity) of capped and uncoated cells over 1,000 hours at 85% humidity. A student reviewing the study claims that adding the capping layer made the cells more efficient than uncoated cells at every point in the test.

figure.title: Efficiency of Perovskite Solar Cells at 85% Humidity

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: The claim is supported, because capped cells still had 18.7% efficiency after 1,000 hours, whereas the efficiency of uncoated cells had fallen to 7.5%.
The claim is not supported, because the efficiency of capped cells declined over the course of the test, falling from 21.3% to 18.7%.
The claim is only partly supported: capped cells were more efficient than uncoated cells from 200 hours onward, but at 0 hours they were slightly less efficient.
The claim is not supported, because uncoated cells were more efficient than capped cells both at the start of the test and after 200 hours.

explanation.passage: Perovskite solar cells are cheap but fall apart in humid air. Park's team added a protective capping layer and measured efficiency (how much sunlight becomes electricity) over 1,000 hours. The student's claim is very broad: capped cells were more efficient at every point. To test an 'every point' claim, you must check every time on the graph, including the very first one.
choices: Incorrect. These numbers are correct, but they cover only the final point. The claim says 'every point,' and at 0 hours capped cells (21.3%) were below uncoated cells (22.1%), so the claim is not fully supported.
Incorrect. Capped cells did lose some efficiency, but the claim is a comparison with uncoated cells, not a claim that capped cells never declined. This addresses the wrong question.

Correct. At 200, 400, 600, 800, and 1,000 hours the capped cells were higher (for example, 20.9% vs. 19.4% at 200 hours). But at 0 hours they were lower, 21.3% vs. 22.1%. So the claim holds at most points but not at every point.
Incorrect. This misreads the 200-hour values: capped cells were at 20.9%, higher than uncoated cells at 19.4%. Only at 0 hours were uncoated cells ahead.

passage.text: M dwarfs, the most common stars in the galaxy, host many rocky planets, but they also produce superflares, sudden bursts of radiation powerful enough to strip away a planet's atmosphere. Astronomer Ekaterina Ilin and colleagues used data from the TESS space telescope to measure how often M dwarfs and Sun-like G dwarfs of different ages produce superflares. Based on atmospheric models, the team estimates that an Earth-like atmosphere can withstand, over billions of years, at most about 4 superflares per decade from its host star.

figure.title: Superflare Frequency by Stellar Type and Age

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Ilin and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Among M dwarfs, only those older than 5 billion years produce superflares at a rate that an Earth-like atmosphere could withstand over long periods.
M dwarfs of every age produce superflares too frequently for an Earth-like atmosphere to survive over long periods on a planet orbiting them.
G dwarfs of every age produce superflares at a rate low enough that an Earth-like atmosphere could withstand them over long periods.
M dwarfs aged 2-5 billion years produce superflares less frequently than G dwarfs of any age do, despite being far more common stars.

explanation.passage: Superflares are huge blasts of radiation that can strip a planet's air away. The text gives you a key number that the graph does not: an Earth-like atmosphere can survive at most about 4 superflares per decade. So the real task is to compare each bar with 4. Bars above 4 mean an atmosphere is in danger; bars below 4 mean it could survive.
choices: Correct. M dwarfs younger than 5 billion years flare 42, 18, and 6 times per decade, all above 4. Only the oldest M dwarfs, at 3.5, fall below the 4-superflare limit.
Incorrect. This is too strong. M dwarfs older than 5 billion years produce 3.5 superflares per decade, which is below the limit of about 4.
Incorrect. The youngest G dwarfs (under 0.5 billion years) produce 8 superflares per decade, double the limit. So this is not true at every age.
Incorrect. M dwarfs aged 2-5 billion years produce 6 per decade, which is more than G dwarfs aged 0.5-2 billion years (2.1) and older. Only the youngest G dwarfs (8) flare more often.

passage.text: Pteropods, or sea butterflies, are tiny swimming snails whose shells are made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate. Chemists describe seawater with an aragonite saturation state (Ω) below 1 as corrosive, meaning that aragonite will dissolve in it. Oceanographer Nina Bednaršek, however, hypothesized that pteropod shells begin to suffer damage even before seawater becomes corrosive in this strict chemical sense. Her team kept pteropods in seawater at three saturation states and measured the share of each shell's surface showing signs of dissolution.

figure.title: Pteropod Shell Dissolution at Three Saturation States

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Bednaršek's hypothesis?
choices: At Ω = 0.8, the share of shell surface showing dissolution rose from 2% to 52% over 12 days, the largest increase in any of the three treatments.
At Ω = 1.4, the share of shell surface showing dissolution never rose above 4% at any point during the 12 days of exposure.
At Ω = 1.1, the share of shell surface showing dissolution was lower than the share at Ω = 0.8 on every day after day 0.
At Ω = 1.1, the share of shell surface showing dissolution rose from 2% to 19%, whereas at Ω = 1.4 it rose only from 2% to 4%.

explanation.passage: The passage defines a key term: seawater is officially 'corrosive' only when Ω is below 1. Bednaršek's hypothesis is that shells get damaged even before that point, meaning at Ω values of 1 or higher. Of the three lines, only Ω = 0.8 is corrosive; Ω = 1.1 is just above the boundary, so it is not corrosive. So the evidence you need is damage at Ω = 1.1, compared with a healthy baseline.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but Ω = 0.8 is below 1, so that water is already corrosive. Damage there is expected and says nothing about damage before water becomes corrosive. Right topic, wrong claim.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it shows only that shells stayed healthy at Ω = 1.4. On its own it shows no damage in non-corrosive water, which does not support the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This is true, but it only shows that corrosive water causes more damage than boundary water. It doesn't show that boundary water causes meaningful damage at all.

Correct. Water at Ω = 1.1 is not below 1, so it is not corrosive by the chemists' definition, yet dissolution climbed from 2% to 19%, far more than the 2% to 4% in the Ω = 1.4 water. That is damage before the corrosive threshold.

passage.text: Cities are often several degrees hotter than surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. To measure how much street trees help, environmental scientist Ariane Middel and colleagues recorded afternoon ground-surface temperatures across Phoenix, Arizona, grouping neighborhoods by tree canopy cover (the share of ground shaded by tree crowns). Canopy cover lowered surface temperatures, but each additional increment of canopy delivered a smaller benefit than the one before: ______

figure.title: Average Afternoon Surface Temperature by Tree Canopy Cover

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: temperatures dropped 6.3°C from the 0-10% group to the 10-20% group, 3.1°C from the 10-20% group to the 20-30% group, and 1.2°C from the 20-30% group to the 30-40% group.
neighborhoods with 30-40% canopy cover were on average 10.6°C cooler than neighborhoods with 0-10% canopy cover, the largest difference between any two of the four canopy groups.
temperatures dropped 6.3°C from the 0-10% group to the 10-20% group but only 3.1°C from the 20-30% group to the 30-40% group, roughly half as large a drop as the first one.
neighborhoods with 0-10% canopy cover averaged 52.4°C, the highest surface temperature of any group and more than 10°C hotter than the most heavily shaded neighborhoods.

explanation.passage: The passage is about how much trees cool city streets. The sentence to complete makes a specific claim: more trees always helped, but each extra 10% of canopy helped less than the previous 10%. This is called diminishing returns. To show it, you need the size of each step down in temperature, and those steps must get smaller.
choices: Correct. The steps are 52.4 - 46.1 = 6.3, 46.1 - 43.0 = 3.1, and 43.0 - 41.8 = 1.2. Each drop is smaller than the one before, which is exactly what 'each additional increment delivered a smaller benefit' means.
Incorrect. This is true (52.4 - 41.8 = 10.6), but it shows only the total cooling from the least to the most shaded neighborhoods. It does not show that each step gave a smaller benefit.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. The drop from 20-30% to 30-40% is 43.0 - 41.8 = 1.2°C, not 3.1°C. (3.1°C is the drop from 10-20% to 20-30%.)
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes the hottest group and the total difference. It does not show how the benefit changes from step to step.

passage.text: Neonicotinoids are insecticides that are absorbed into a plant's tissues, including its pollen and nectar. Ecologist Maj Rundlöf and colleagues placed bumblebee colonies beside oilseed rape fields in Sweden, half of which had been grown from seeds treated with the neonicotinoid clothianidin, and counted the workers, males, and new queens each colony produced. Because only new queens can found colonies the following year, the researchers hypothesized that exposure to the insecticide would disproportionately reduce the production of queens compared with the production of other bees.

figure.title: Average Number of Bees Produced per Colony

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Colonies beside treated fields produced fewer workers, fewer males, and fewer queens on average than colonies beside untreated fields did.
Colonies beside treated fields produced 48 fewer workers on average than colonies beside untreated fields, the largest difference for any type of bee.
Colonies beside untreated fields produced more workers than males and more males than queens, and the same was true of colonies beside treated fields.
Colonies beside treated fields produced about 15% fewer workers and males than colonies beside untreated fields, but about 86% fewer queens.

explanation.passage: Neonicotinoids are pesticides that get inside the plant, so bees eat them in pollen and nectar. The key word in the hypothesis is 'disproportionately': the pesticide should cut queen production by a much larger share than it cuts the production of workers or males. Because colonies make hundreds of workers but only a handful of queens, you have to compare percentages, not raw numbers.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it only shows that all three numbers went down. It does not show that queens dropped by a larger share, so it matches only half the hypothesis.

Incorrect. The difference of 48 (310 - 262) is the largest raw difference, but that is only because colonies make so many workers. As a share it is just about 15%, so this actually points away from the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This ordering is true in both groups, but it compares bee types within each group rather than measuring how much the insecticide reduced each type.

Correct. Workers fell from 310 to 262 (about 15%), males from 48 to 41 (about 15%), but queens from 14 to 2 (12 of 14, about 86%). Queens were hit far harder, which is what 'disproportionately' means.

passage.text: Microbiologist Thomas Berendonk and colleagues measured the percentage of E. coli bacteria carrying the antibiotic resistance gene blaCTX-M at five points along a German wastewater system: a river upstream of a treatment plant, hospital effluent (wastewater leaving a hospital), the plant's inflow, the plant's outflow, and the river downstream. The plant removes more than 99% of E. coli cells. A colleague argued that, because the plant eliminates nearly all of these bacteria, it cannot be contributing to antibiotic resistance among bacteria in the river.

figure.title: E. coli Carrying a Resistance Gene, by Sampling Site

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken the colleague's argument?
choices: The percentage of E. coli carrying the gene was higher in plant outflow (9.7%) than in plant inflow (6.8%) and higher in the downstream river (3.9%) than upstream (1.2%).
The percentage of E. coli carrying the gene was higher in hospital effluent, at 24.5%, than at any of the other four sampling sites along the wastewater system.
The percentage of E. coli carrying the gene was lower in plant inflow (6.8%) than in hospital effluent (24.5%), as hospital wastewater mixed with other sewage.
The percentage of E. coli carrying the gene was lower in the downstream river (3.9%) than in plant outflow (9.7%), the site just before the water entered the river.

explanation.passage: The study tracks what percentage of E. coli carry a resistance gene as wastewater moves from hospitals, through a treatment plant, and into a river. The colleague's reasoning is: the plant kills over 99% of the bacteria, so it can't be making river bacteria more resistant. To weaken this, you need evidence that the plant still shifts the river toward resistance, for example if the bacteria that survive treatment are more often resistant and the river below the plant has more resistance than the river above it.
choices: Correct. The resistant share went up during treatment (6.8% to 9.7%), meaning resistant bacteria survived treatment better than others, and the river had over three times the resistant share downstream (3.9%) as upstream (1.2%). Killing most cells did not stop the plant from raising resistance in the river.
Incorrect. This is true, but it is about the hospital, not about whether the treatment plant affects the river. True but irrelevant.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes what happens before the plant does anything. It tells us nothing about the plant's effect on the river.
Incorrect. This is true, but it shows the river diluting the outflow. On its own it does not suggest the plant adds to resistance, so it doesn't weaken the argument.

passage.text: As Arctic permafrost (ground that has stayed frozen for at least two years) thaws, microbes decompose long-frozen organic matter and release methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Most climate models assume thaw proceeds gradually, a few centimeters at a time. Ecologist Merritt Turetsky and colleagues note, however, that ice-rich ground can thaw abruptly, collapsing into waterlogged pits called thermokarst. To compare the two processes, they measured methane emissions at sites of known thaw age in Alaska.

figure.title: Methane Emissions After Permafrost Thaw
figure.yLabel: Methane emitted (mg per m² per day)

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Turetsky and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: By 30 years after thaw began, methane emissions at abrupt-thaw sites had fallen below the emissions measured at gradual-thaw sites.
Models that assume gradual thaw would underestimate methane emissions from abruptly thawing permafrost throughout the first 30 years after thaw.
Methane emissions at both abrupt-thaw and gradual-thaw sites rose steadily throughout the 30 years after thaw began.
Abrupt thaw releases more total carbon than gradual thaw does once both methane and carbon dioxide emissions are taken into account.

explanation.passage: When permafrost thaws, microbes eat the old frozen plant matter and give off methane. The text tells you that most climate models assume gradual thaw, but some ground thaws suddenly. The graph compares methane from the two kinds of sites over 30 years. So the question is really: if a model uses the gradual-thaw numbers, how wrong would it be for abrupt-thaw ground?
choices: Incorrect. At 30 years, abrupt-thaw sites emitted 70 and gradual-thaw sites 57, so abrupt sites were still higher. The gap is shrinking, but the lines have not crossed.

Correct. Abrupt-thaw emissions were higher than gradual-thaw emissions at every point (12 vs. 10, 85 vs. 18, 140 vs. 27, and so on to 70 vs. 57). A model that assumes gradual thaw would therefore predict too little methane for abrupt-thaw ground across the whole period.
Incorrect. Gradual-thaw emissions rose steadily, but abrupt-thaw emissions peaked at 140 in year 10 and then fell to 70. Only half of this statement is true.
Incorrect. The study measured only methane. Nothing in the text or graph gives carbon dioxide data, so this goes outside the scope of the evidence.

passage.text: Seagrass meadows trap organic carbon in the sediment beneath them, storing it for centuries; this stored carbon is often called blue carbon. Along Virginia's coast, conservationists have replanted eelgrass in bays where it had disappeared, and marine ecologist Jonathan Lefcheck and colleagues measured sediment carbon in two of those bays. Citing the study, a student claims that ten years of restoration is enough for a replanted meadow to store about as much carbon as a natural meadow does.

figure.title: Sediment Organic Carbon in Two Virginia Bays

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: The claim is supported, because in both bays meadows restored for 10 years stored more carbon than bare sediment and more than meadows restored for 4 years.
The claim is not supported, because in both bays meadows restored for 10 years stored less than half as much carbon as natural meadows did.
The claim is supported for South Bay, where 10-year meadows stored 52 metric tons per hectare versus 55 in natural meadows, but not for Hog Island Bay, where they stored 33 versus 58.
The claim is supported for Hog Island Bay but not for South Bay, because carbon storage rose more between years 4 and 10 of restoration in Hog Island Bay than in South Bay.

explanation.passage: Seagrass stores carbon in the mud below it. Some Virginia bays had their seagrass replanted, and the graph shows carbon at bare sites, young restored meadows, 10-year restored meadows, and natural meadows in two bays. The student's claim compares just two bars in each bay: 'Restored 10 years' versus 'Natural meadow.' If they are about equal, the claim holds for that bay.
choices: Incorrect. This is true in both bays, but it shows only that restoration increases carbon over time. The claim is that 10-year meadows match natural meadows, which this does not address.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph in both bays. In South Bay, 10-year meadows stored 52 versus 55, nearly equal. Even in Hog Island Bay, 33 is more than half of 58 (which would be 29).
Correct. In South Bay, 52 is close to 55, so the claim holds there. In Hog Island Bay, 33 is far below 58, so it does not. The data support the claim in one bay but not the other.
Incorrect. This reverses the bays. Carbon rose 22 tons (30 to 52) in South Bay but only 9 tons (24 to 33) in Hog Island Bay, and Hog Island Bay's 10-year meadows are far below its natural meadows.

passage.text: Birds often collide with wind turbine blades, possibly because the moving blades blur together and are hard to see. At the Smøla wind farm in Norway, ecologist Roel May and colleagues painted one of the three blades black on four turbines, leaving four nearby turbines unpainted as controls, and counted bird carcasses found beneath each turbine before and after the painting. The researchers concluded that the black blade, not some other change at the site, accounted for the reduction in collisions: ______

figure.title: Bird Carcasses Found per Turbine per Year at Smøla

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: carcass counts at the painted turbines fell from 11.0 to 3.3 per turbine per year after the painting, a decline of about 70% from their earlier level.
before the painting, the turbines that would later be painted had slightly more carcasses per year (11.0) than the control turbines had (10.4).
carcass counts at the control turbines were about three times as high after the painting as they had been before the painting.
carcass counts at the painted turbines fell from 11.0 to 3.3 per year after painting, while counts at the control turbines stayed nearly the same.

explanation.passage: The researchers painted one blade black on some turbines to make the blades easier for birds to see. The sentence to complete says the black blade, 'not some other change at the site,' caused fewer collisions. That phrase is the key: to rule out other site-wide changes (weather, bird numbers), you need the control turbines, which were not painted, to show no similar drop.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it only shows that painted turbines killed fewer birds. Without the control turbines, a site-wide change could explain the drop. It matches only half the claim.
Incorrect. This is true but describes only the period before painting. It does not show any effect of the black blade.

Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Control turbines went from 10.4 to 10.0, nearly unchanged. 'About three times' is the after-painting comparison between control and painted turbines (10.0 vs. 3.3).
Correct. Painted turbines dropped sharply while unpainted control turbines in the same place and years barely changed (10.4 to 10.0). That rules out a site-wide change and points to the paint.

passage.text: Plant breeders have developed drought-tolerant (DT) maize varieties for sub-Saharan Africa, where rainfall is increasingly erratic. Many farmers, however, are reluctant to adopt them, fearing that a variety bred for dry conditions will yield less in good years. Agricultural economist Kindie Tesfaye compared the yields of a DT variety and a widely planted conventional variety on farms in Ethiopia and Kenya. Tesfaye claims that the DT variety's advantage increases as drought becomes more severe and that the DT variety never yields less than the conventional variety.

figure.title: Maize Yield Under Three Rainfall Conditions

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Tesfaye's claim?
choices: Under severe drought, the DT variety yielded 1.9 metric tons per hectare, compared with 1.2 metric tons per hectare for the conventional variety.
Under normal rainfall, the conventional variety yielded 4.7 metric tons per hectare, slightly more than the 4.6 metric tons yielded by the DT variety.
Both varieties yielded more under normal rainfall than under either moderate or severe drought, with the largest yields for each variety in normal years.
The DT variety's advantage was smaller under moderate drought (0.5 metric tons per hectare) than under severe drought (0.7 metric tons per hectare).

explanation.passage: The passage is about maize bred to survive drought and farmers' worry that it does worse in normal years. Tesfaye's claim has two parts: (1) the DT variety's lead gets bigger as drought gets worse, and (2) the DT variety never yields less than the conventional one. To weaken the claim, you need data that break one of those parts.
choices: Incorrect. This shows the DT variety winning under severe drought, which agrees with Tesfaye. It supports the claim rather than weakening it.
Correct. 'Never yields less' is broken by a single counterexample, and here it is: in normal years the conventional variety (4.7) beat the DT variety (4.6). This also confirms the farmers' fear.
Incorrect. This is true, but it compares rainfall conditions within each variety. It doesn't say anything about which variety did better, so it neither supports nor weakens the claim.
Incorrect. These numbers are right (3.1 - 2.6 = 0.5; 1.9 - 1.2 = 0.7), but they show the advantage growing as drought gets more severe, which supports the first part of the claim.

passage.text: As mountain glaciers shrink, the meltwater they release at first increases, because a warming climate melts more ice each year. Eventually, though, the glaciers become too small to sustain this output, and annual runoff begins to fall. Hydrologist Matthias Huss and colleagues call the turning point peak water and note that communities relying on glacial meltwater for irrigation face growing shortages once a basin has passed it. The team modeled runoff for two Himalayan river basins, one fed by large glaciers and one fed by small glaciers.

figure.title: Modeled Annual Glacial Runoff in Two River Basins

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Huss and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Communities in the small-glacier basin are likely to face growing meltwater shortages several decades sooner than communities in the large-glacier basin.
By 2100, runoff in the large-glacier basin is projected to fall to less than half of its 2000 level, as runoff in the small-glacier basin is projected to do.
The two basins are projected to reach peak water in the same decade, although the large-glacier basin will release far more water at its peak.
The large-glacier basin will pass peak water first because its glaciers, being larger, lose more ice each year than the small glaciers do.

explanation.passage: 'Peak water' is the year when a glacier's runoff stops rising and starts falling. The text tells you that once a basin passes peak water, communities face growing shortages. So you need to find the peak year for each line and compare them: the small-glacier basin peaks at 4.6 in 2020, while the large-glacier basin keeps rising until 13.4 in 2060.
choices: Correct. The small-glacier basin peaks around 2020 and the large-glacier basin around 2060, about four decades later. Since shortages begin after peak water, communities in the small-glacier basin will face them much sooner.
Incorrect. The small-glacier basin does fall below half (4.1 to 0.9), but the large-glacier basin goes from 10.2 to 9.6, only a small drop. This is half right.
Incorrect. The peaks are about 40 years apart (2020 vs. 2060), not in the same decade.
Incorrect. This reverses the order. The small-glacier basin peaks first (2020). The reason given also is not stated anywhere in the text.

passage.text: Bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill bacteria, are being studied as an alternative to antibiotics, but bacteria can quickly evolve resistance to them. Microbiologist Paul Turner and colleagues tested whether pairing a phage with an antibiotic could solve this problem, reasoning that bacteria which evolve phage resistance often become more vulnerable to antibiotics in the process. The team hypothesized that the combination would prevent the rebound in bacterial numbers that occurs when phage-resistant bacteria emerge. They tracked cultures of Pseudomonas aeruginosa under three treatments. (Bacterial density is shown on a logarithmic scale, so a drop of 1 unit means a tenfold decrease.)

figure.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Density Under Three Treatments

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Turner and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: With phage alone, bacterial density fell to 2.8 at 12 hours, lower than the density with the antibiotic alone at that same time, which was 4.6.
With the antibiotic alone, bacterial density declined only modestly over the 30 hours, from 6.0 at the start to 4.6 at the end of the experiment.
With phage alone, bacterial density rose from 2.8 at 12 hours to 7.0 at 30 hours, whereas with phage and antibiotic combined it kept falling, to 0.5.
With phage and antibiotic combined, bacterial density at 6 hours was 2.9, lower than the density with either the phage alone or the antibiotic alone.

explanation.passage: Phages are viruses that kill bacteria, but bacteria can evolve to resist them, so the bacteria come back. The researchers hoped that adding an antibiotic would stop that comeback, called a rebound. So the evidence you need has two parts: the rebound happens with phage alone, and it does not happen when the antibiotic is added.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that phage worked well early on. It says nothing about the later rebound or whether the combination prevents it.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but the antibiotic-alone line has no phage, so it can't show anything about phage resistance or a rebound.

Correct. With phage alone, bacteria rebounded from 2.8 to 7.0, higher than where they started, which is the rebound the hypothesis describes. With the combination, density kept dropping to 0.5, so no rebound occurred.
Incorrect. This is true (2.9 vs. 3.1 and 5.2), but it describes only the first 6 hours, before any rebound. It doesn't address whether the rebound was prevented.

passage.text: Concrete inevitably cracks, letting in water that corrodes the steel inside. Microbiologist Henk Jonkers developed a self-healing concrete containing dormant bacteria that, when water seeps into a crack, wake up and produce limestone that can seal it. Ordinary concrete can also partly seal very fine cracks on its own, as minerals in the cement react with water. Jonkers found that his concrete outperformed ordinary concrete at every crack width tested, but the healing agent was no cure-all for wide cracks: ______

figure.title: Crack Closure After 28 Days in Water

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: ordinary concrete closed only 2% of 0.8 mm cracks, compared with the 34% of those cracks that bacterial concrete closed.
bacterial concrete closed 92% of 0.4 mm cracks, nearly three times the 31% of those cracks that ordinary concrete closed.
bacterial concrete closed only 61% of 0.8 mm cracks, compared with 100% of the narrowest cracks, which were 0.2 mm wide.
bacterial concrete closed 100% of 0.2 mm cracks but only 34% of 0.8 mm cracks, the widest cracks tested.

explanation.passage: Jonkers's concrete contains bacteria that make limestone to fill cracks. The sentence first says his concrete beat ordinary concrete at every width, then turns with 'but': it is 'no cure-all for wide cracks.' The blank must show that limitation, meaning bacterial concrete did much worse on wide cracks than on narrow ones.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows bacterial concrete beating ordinary concrete, which is the first part of the sentence. It doesn't show the weakness with wide cracks.
Incorrect. This is accurate but again shows the advantage of bacterial concrete, at a fairly narrow crack width. It doesn't illustrate the limitation.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Bacterial concrete closed 61% of 0.6 mm cracks; for 0.8 mm cracks it closed only 34%.
Correct. Bacterial concrete fully sealed the narrowest cracks but closed only about a third of the widest ones. That shows it is not a cure-all for wide cracks.

passage.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp; where otters are abundant, urchins are kept in check and kelp forests flourish. In the 1990s, killer whales in Alaska's Aleutian Islands began preying heavily on otters. Ecologist James Estes and colleagues report that otter numbers fell by more than 80% around Adak and Kiska islands but remained stable around Amchitka and Attu, where otters shelter in shallow lagoons that killer whales cannot enter. Estes hypothesized that the loss of otters, by releasing urchins from predation, caused a decline in kelp.

figure.title: Kelp Density at Four Aleutian Islands

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Estes's hypothesis?
