choices: Kelp density fell sharply at Adak and Kiska, from 8.8 and 9.5 to 2.1 and 1.7 plants per m², but changed little at Amchitka and Attu.
Kelp density at Kiska was the highest of the four islands in 1990 and then the lowest of the four islands in 2000, at 1.7 plants per m².
Kelp density at Attu rose slightly between 1990 and 2000, from 8.1 to 8.4 plants per m², while it fell slightly at Amchitka over the same decade.
In 1990, before the otter decline began, kelp density was similar at all four islands, ranging only from 8.1 to 9.5 plants per m².

explanation.passage: This is a food-chain passage: otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp. When killer whales started eating otters, otters crashed at Adak and Kiska but not at Amchitka and Attu. That gives a natural experiment. If losing otters really caused kelp loss, kelp should drop where otters dropped and hold steady where otters stayed. The text gives you which islands lost otters; the graph gives the kelp.
choices: Correct. Kelp crashed only at the two islands that lost their otters (Adak and Kiska) and stayed about the same at the two islands where otters remained (Amchitka 9.2 to 8.9, Attu 8.1 to 8.4). The pattern matches the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one island. Without comparing it with islands that kept their otters, it can't show that otter loss caused the decline.
Incorrect. This is accurate but describes only the islands where otters stayed. It shows kelp held steady there, but on its own says nothing about what happened where otters were lost.
Incorrect. This is true, but it describes conditions before the otter decline. It tells you the islands started out similar, not that losing otters reduced kelp.

passage.text: Most plants form partnerships with mycorrhizal fungi, which extend through the soil and deliver phosphorus to plant roots in exchange for sugars. Because the fungi consume sugars the plant could otherwise use for growth, ecologist Nancy Johnson has argued that the partnership is not always beneficial. Johnson hypothesized that mycorrhizal fungi boost seedling growth in phosphorus-poor soils but become a net cost to seedlings in phosphorus-rich soils, where plants can easily obtain phosphorus without help. Her team grew seedlings with and without fungi in soils with three levels of phosphorus.

figure.title: Seedling Biomass With and Without Mycorrhizal Fungi

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Johnson's hypothesis?
choices: Seedlings with fungi had more biomass in medium-phosphorus soil (4.1 g) than they had in low-phosphorus soil (2.8 g), and more still in high-phosphorus soil.
Seedlings with fungi outweighed those without fungi in low-phosphorus soil (2.8 g vs. 1.1 g) but weighed less in high-phosphorus soil (4.4 g vs. 5.0 g).
Seedlings without fungi grown in high-phosphorus soil had more biomass, at 5.0 g, than seedlings in any of the other five groups in the experiment.
Seedlings with fungi outweighed seedlings without fungi at every soil phosphorus level, though by different amounts at each of the three levels.

explanation.passage: Mycorrhizal fungi trade phosphorus to plants for sugar. Johnson's point is that this is only a good deal when the plant can't get phosphorus on its own. Her hypothesis has two halves: fungi help seedlings in low-phosphorus soil, and fungi hurt seedlings (a 'net cost') in high-phosphorus soil. You need data showing both halves, which means comparing with-fungi and without-fungi bars at each end.
choices: Incorrect. This compares soils for seedlings that all had fungi. It shows that more phosphorus helps, but it doesn't compare seedlings with and without fungi.

Correct. In low-phosphorus soil, fungi more than doubled biomass (2.8 vs. 1.1), a benefit. In high-phosphorus soil, seedlings with fungi were lighter (4.4 vs. 5.0), a net cost. Both halves of the hypothesis are matched.
Incorrect. This is true, but it only describes one group. It hints at the second half of the hypothesis but leaves out the low-phosphorus benefit, so it matches only half.
Incorrect. This is false. In high-phosphorus soil, seedlings without fungi (5.0 g) outweighed those with fungi (4.4 g).

passage.text: Lithium-ion batteries lose capacity in the cold because the liquid electrolyte that carries lithium ions between electrodes becomes thick and sluggish. Chemist Xiulin Fan and colleagues developed an electrolyte based on a fluorinated solvent that remains fluid at low temperatures and compared it with a standard electrolyte. A student summarizing the study claims that the new electrolyte kept batteries above half of their room-temperature capacity at every temperature tested, whereas the standard electrolyte fell below half capacity at every temperature below 0°C.

figure.title: Battery Capacity Retained at Low Temperatures

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: The claim is supported, because at -40°C batteries with the standard electrolyte retained only 9% of their capacity, while those with the new electrolyte retained 58%.
The claim is not supported, because batteries with the new electrolyte retained only 58% of their capacity at -40°C, much less than they retained at 25°C.
The claim is only partly supported: the new electrolyte kept batteries above half capacity at every temperature, but the standard one stayed above half capacity down to -20°C.
The claim is fully supported, because batteries with the new electrolyte retained more capacity than those with the standard electrolyte at every temperature below 25°C.

explanation.passage: Batteries weaken in the cold because the liquid inside thickens. The graph shows how much capacity two batteries keep as it gets colder. The student's claim has two parts, both about the 50% line: (1) the new electrolyte stays above 50% at every temperature, and (2) the standard one drops below 50% at every temperature below 0°C. Check each part against the numbers.
choices: Incorrect. These numbers are correct, but they come from only the coldest temperature. The second part of the claim says the standard electrolyte is below half at every temperature below 0°C, and at -10°C (71%) and -20°C (52%) it is not.
Incorrect. 58% is still above half, so this doesn't contradict the first part of the claim. Losing some capacity is not what the claim is about.
Correct. Part 1 holds: the new electrolyte's lowest value is 58%, above half. Part 2 fails: the standard electrolyte keeps 71% at -10°C and 52% at -20°C, and only drops below half at -30°C (28%).

Incorrect. This is true, but the claim isn't simply that the new electrolyte was better. It makes a specific statement about the standard electrolyte falling below half below 0°C, which is false at -10°C and -20°C.

passage.text: Near-Earth asteroids are classified by their surface composition: S-type asteroids are stony and relatively bright, while C-type asteroids are rich in carbon and among the darkest objects in the solar system. Telescopes that detect visible light find asteroids by the sunlight they reflect, so dark asteroids are harder for them to spot. Infrared telescopes, by contrast, detect the heat an asteroid gives off, which depends little on how dark its surface is. Astronomer Amy Mainzer and colleagues compared the composition of near-Earth asteroids found by the two kinds of survey.

figure.title: Composition of Near-Earth Asteroids Detected by Two Surveys

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Mainzer and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: C-type asteroids make up a larger share of near-Earth asteroids than S-type asteroids do, though visible-light surveys suggest otherwise.
Infrared surveys are biased against detecting X-type asteroids, which make up a smaller share of infrared detections than visible-light detections.
C-type asteroids are more likely than S-type asteroids to collide with Earth because their dark surfaces make them harder to track.
Estimates of the share of near-Earth asteroids that are C-type are likely to be too low if they are based only on visible-light surveys.

explanation.passage: The text explains a bias: visible-light telescopes see asteroids by reflected sunlight, so dark C-type asteroids are easy to miss, while infrared telescopes see heat and aren't fooled by darkness. The graph then shows that C-types are 15% of visible-light detections but 34% of infrared detections. Putting the two together, the infrared survey gives the fairer count, and the visible survey misses many dark asteroids.
choices: Incorrect. Even in the less biased infrared survey, S-types (41%) outnumber C-types (34%). Nothing shows C-types are the larger share.
Incorrect. X-types are 15% of infrared detections and 13% of visible-light detections, so they are actually a slightly larger share in the infrared survey, not a smaller one.
Incorrect. The text says nothing about collision chances. This goes outside the scope of the passage.

Correct. The text says visible-light surveys struggle to spot dark asteroids, and C-types, the darkest, drop from 34% in the infrared survey to 15% in the visible survey. Relying only on visible light would undercount them.

passage.text: Lionfish, native to the Indo-Pacific, have invaded Caribbean coral reefs, where native fish do not recognize them as predators. Marine ecologist Mark Hixon and colleagues removed all lionfish from several reefs in the Bahamas and left lionfish on similar nearby reefs, then counted juvenile native fish on each reef over eight weeks. The team concluded that lionfish can rapidly deplete native fish populations: ______

figure.title: Juvenile Native Fish on Bahamian Reefs

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: on reefs where lionfish remained, juvenile native fish fell from 210 to 44 per reef over eight weeks, while reefs cleared of lionfish stayed near 200.
on reefs cleared of lionfish, the number of juvenile native fish stayed at roughly 200 per reef at every survey during the eight weeks.
at the start of the study, reefs with lionfish had slightly more juvenile native fish (210 per reef) than reefs without lionfish had (205).
on reefs where lionfish remained, juvenile native fish fell from 210 to 98 per reef over the full eight weeks of the study.

explanation.passage: Lionfish are invasive predators, and native Caribbean fish don't know to avoid them. Hixon's team compared reefs with lionfish to reefs where lionfish were removed. The sentence says lionfish 'rapidly deplete' native fish, so the blank needs to show native fish dropping fast where lionfish stayed, ideally compared with reefs without lionfish to show the lionfish were the cause.
choices: Correct. With lionfish, juvenile fish fell from 210 to 44, a loss of about 80% in eight weeks. Without lionfish they held steady near 200, so the decline can be tied to the lionfish.
Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the reefs without lionfish. It never shows any depletion, so it doesn't illustrate the conclusion.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes week 0, before any effect could appear. It is true but irrelevant.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. 98 is the week 4 value; by week 8 the number had fallen to 44.

passage.text: Flooded rice paddies produce large amounts of methane because microbes in waterlogged soil, which lacks oxygen, generate the gas as they break down organic matter. In a practice called alternate wetting and drying (AWD), farmers periodically drain their fields, letting oxygen into the soil. Agronomist Bjoern Ole Sander and colleagues compared methane emissions from continuously flooded paddies and AWD paddies in the Philippines. In the AWD paddies, water was drained for the first time on day 20 after transplanting; fields were then reflooded and drained repeatedly for the rest of the season.

figure.title: Methane Emissions from Rice Paddies During One Growing Season
figure.yLabel: Methane emitted (mg per m² per hour)

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Sander and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: AWD reduced methane emissions substantially from the time of transplanting, even before the first drainage of the fields took place.
AWD had little effect on methane emissions before the first drainage but kept emissions well below those of flooded paddies for the rest of the season.
Methane emissions from AWD paddies declined steadily from day 15 through the end of the season as the fields were repeatedly drained.
Continuously flooded paddies produced their highest emissions near the end of the season, when AWD paddies produced their lowest emissions.

explanation.passage: Flooded rice fields release methane because soil microbes make it when there is no oxygen. AWD means draining the field now and then to let oxygen in. The text gives a timing detail that matters: the first drainage happened on day 20. So you should look at the graph in two parts, before day 20 (only day 0 and day 15) and after it.
choices: Incorrect. Before the first drainage, the two fields were nearly identical (2 vs. 2 at day 0, 8 vs. 7 at day 15). There was no substantial early reduction.
Correct. At day 15, before draining, AWD emitted 7 versus 8, almost the same. From day 30 on, AWD was far lower at every point (6 vs. 15, 9 vs. 22, 5 vs. 24, 8 vs. 19, 4 vs. 12, 2 vs. 6).
Incorrect. AWD emissions went up and down (7, 6, 9, 5, 8, 4, 2) rather than declining steadily, probably because the fields were reflooded between drainings.
Incorrect. Flooded paddies peaked at day 60 (24), in the middle of the season. Near the end they had fallen to 6.

passage.text: Bed nets treated with pyrethroid insecticides have prevented hundreds of millions of malaria cases, but many mosquito populations have evolved resistance, often by producing enzymes that break pyrethroids down. Newer nets add piperonyl butoxide (PBO), a compound that blocks those enzymes. Entomologist Natacha Protopopoff and colleagues tested standard and PBO nets in experimental huts in regions where mosquitoes showed different levels of resistance. Protopopoff hypothesized that the advantage of PBO nets over standard nets would be greatest where resistance was highest.

figure.title: Mosquito Mortality in Experimental Huts
figure.xLabel: Level of pyrethroid resistance in region

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Protopopoff's hypothesis?
choices: PBO nets killed 62% of mosquitoes in the high-resistance region, a smaller percentage than they killed in the low- or moderate-resistance regions.
Standard nets killed 92% of mosquitoes in the low-resistance region but only 23% of mosquitoes in the high-resistance region.
PBO nets killed 3 percentage points more mosquitoes than standard nets did in the low-resistance region but 39 points more in the high-resistance region.
PBO nets killed more mosquitoes than standard nets did in all three regions, and they killed more than 80% of mosquitoes in each region.

explanation.passage: Mosquitoes have evolved enzymes that destroy the insecticide on bed nets. PBO blocks those enzymes, so it should matter most where mosquitoes rely on them, meaning where resistance is high. The hypothesis is about the advantage of PBO nets, which is the gap between the two bars in each region. You need to show that the gap grows as resistance increases.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only PBO nets. It shows PBO nets work less well against resistant mosquitoes, not how their advantage over standard nets changes.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only standard nets. Without the PBO numbers, it can't show the size of PBO's advantage.
Correct. The gap is 95 - 92 = 3 points with low resistance and 62 - 23 = 39 points with high resistance. The advantage is much bigger where resistance is highest, as Protopopoff predicted.
Incorrect. The first part is true, but the second is false: PBO nets killed only 62% in the high-resistance region.

passage.text: Polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) are both sold as biodegradable alternatives to conventional plastics such as polyethylene. Biodegradation, however, depends on conditions: PLA breaks down readily in industrial composters heated to about 58°C, but whether it does so in cooler environments is less clear. Environmental chemist Collin Ward and colleagues submerged samples of all three plastics in seawater at 20°C and weighed them every four weeks. A student cites the study as evidence that plastics labeled biodegradable break down in the ocean much faster than conventional plastics do.

figure.title: Plastic Mass Remaining in Seawater at 20°C

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: The claim is supported, because after 24 weeks both PLA and PHA retained less of their original mass than polyethylene, which lost none of its mass.
The claim is not supported, because even PHA, the plastic that broke down most, still retained more than a quarter of its mass after 24 weeks.
The claim is supported for PLA but not for PHA, because PLA lost mass steadily throughout the experiment while PHA's losses slowed over time.
The claim is supported for PHA, which lost 73% of its mass over 24 weeks, but not for PLA, which lost only 3%, barely more than polyethylene.

explanation.passage: Both PLA and PHA are sold as biodegradable, but the text warns that PLA breaks down well only in hot industrial composters, not necessarily in cool water. The experiment put all three plastics in 20°C seawater. The student's claim covers both biodegradable plastics and uses the word 'much': they break down much faster than conventional plastic. So you must check PLA and PHA separately against polyethylene.
choices: Incorrect. Technically both retained less than 100%, but PLA lost only 3%. That is not breaking down 'much faster,' so this ignores the key word in the claim.
Incorrect. The claim compares biodegradable plastics with polyethylene; it doesn't say they disappear completely. PHA's 73% loss versus polyethylene's 0% supports the claim for PHA.
Incorrect. This reverses the two plastics. PHA lost mass quickly (100 to 27), while PLA barely changed (100 to 97). Also, PHA's losses did not slow: it lost 11 to 14 points every four weeks.

Correct. PHA fell from 100% to 27%, a 73% loss, far more than polyethylene's 0%. PLA fell only from 100% to 97%, nearly the same as polyethylene. The claim holds for one 'biodegradable' plastic but not the other.

passage.text: Each winter, eastern monarch butterflies gather in a few mountain forests in central Mexico, and the area they cover is used to estimate the population's size. Since the late 1990s, the spread of herbicide-tolerant crops has sharply reduced milkweed, the only plant monarch caterpillars eat, across the U.S. Midwest. Ecologist Orley Taylor has hypothesized that year-to-year changes in the monarch population closely track changes in Midwest milkweed abundance. The graph shows both measures as indexes, with 1999 values set to 100.

figure.title: Midwest Milkweed and Overwintering Monarchs (Index, 1999 = 100)

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Taylor's hypothesis?
choices: Between 2014 and 2017, the monarch index more than doubled, from 12 to 28, while the milkweed index stayed nearly unchanged, going from 31 to 30.
Between 1999 and 2008, both the milkweed index and the monarch index fell by more than half, dropping to 42 and 48, respectively, by the end of that period.
The milkweed index declined in every interval shown on the graph, falling from 100 in 1999 to 30 in 2017, a total drop of 70 points.
The monarch index reached its lowest value in 2014, at 12, when the milkweed index, at 31, was also close to the lowest value it reached during the period.

explanation.passage: Milkweed is the only food for monarch caterpillars, and milkweed has declined in the Midwest. Taylor's hypothesis is that the monarch population 'closely tracks' milkweed, meaning when milkweed changes, monarchs change in the same way. Indexes just show each measure as a percentage of its 1999 value. To weaken the hypothesis, look for a period when the two lines move very differently.
choices: Correct. From 2014 to 2017, monarchs jumped from 12 to 28 even though milkweed barely changed (31 to 30). If monarchs closely tracked milkweed, they should have stayed flat too.
Incorrect. This is true (100 to 42 and 100 to 48), and it shows the two lines moving together. That supports the hypothesis rather than weakening it.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes only milkweed. It says nothing about whether monarchs followed the same pattern.
Incorrect. This shows the two measures being low at the same time, which fits the hypothesis. It does not weaken it.

passage.text: The soils of the Amazon rainforest are poor in phosphorus, a nutrient essential for plant growth, and rain and flooding wash away an estimated 22 thousand metric tons of it each year. Phosphorus-rich dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara helps make up for this loss. Using satellite measurements, atmospheric scientist Hongbin Yu and colleagues found that the amount of dust reaching the Amazon depends on rainfall in the Sahel, the semiarid region on the Sahara's southern edge: after a wet rainy season, new vegetation holds soil in place and less dust is lifted.

figure.title: Dust-Borne Phosphorus Reaching the Amazon
figure.xLabel: Preceding rainy season in the Sahel
figure.yLabel: Phosphorus deposited (thousand metric tons per year)

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Yu and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Dust from the Sahara deposits enough phosphorus to offset the Amazon's annual phosphorus losses regardless of rainfall conditions in the Sahel.
In years following a wet rainy season in the Sahel, dust-borne phosphorus is likely insufficient to replace the phosphorus the Amazon loses.
The Amazon loses the most phosphorus to rain and flooding in years following a dry rainy season in the Sahel, when more dust arrives.
Dust-borne phosphorus deposited after an average rainy season in the Sahel is roughly half the amount deposited after a dry rainy season.

explanation.passage: The Amazon's soil is low in phosphorus and loses about 22 thousand tons a year to rain and floods. Saharan dust brings some back. The amount of dust depends on rain in the Sahel: a wet season means more plants, which hold the soil, so less dust blows away. The text's number, 22, is the key: compare each bar with 22 to see whether the dust replaces what is lost.
choices: Incorrect. After a wet Sahel season, only 15 thousand tons arrive, less than the 22 thousand lost. So the dust does not offset losses in every case.
Correct. After a wet season, dust delivers 15 thousand tons, which is 7 thousand short of the 22 thousand lost each year. The dust would not fully replace the losses in those years.
Incorrect. The text gives the Amazon's losses as a single yearly estimate and never says they change with Sahel rainfall. This goes outside the scope of the passage.
Incorrect. After an average season the dust delivers 23, and after a dry season 31. Half of 31 would be about 15.5, so 23 is far more than half.

passage.text: A diverse community of gut microbes is associated with lower inflammation and better health. Microbiologists Erica and Justin Sonnenburg assigned adults to one of two ten-week diets: a high-fiber diet rich in beans, whole grains, and vegetables, or a diet rich in fermented foods such as yogurt, kimchi, and kombucha. The researchers expected the fiber, which feeds gut microbes, to have the bigger effect. Instead, it was the fermented-food diet that substantially increased microbial diversity: ______

figure.title: Gut Microbial Diversity Before and After Ten-Week Diets

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: at the start of the study, participants assigned to the high-fiber diet had more microbial species on average (142) than those assigned to the fermented-food diet (139).
participants on the fermented-food diet had an average of 171 microbial species at week 10, more than the 139 they had on average at baseline.
participants on the fermented-food diet went from 139 to 171 microbial species on average, whereas those on the high-fiber diet went from 142 to only 145.
participants on the high-fiber diet went from 142 to 171 microbial species on average, whereas those on the fermented-food diet went from 139 to 145.

explanation.passage: The study compared two diets to see which one made gut bacteria more diverse (more kinds of species). The researchers expected fiber to win, but the sentence says fermented foods 'substantially' raised diversity 'instead.' That word 'instead' means you need a contrast: fermented foods raised diversity a lot, and fiber did not.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the starting point, before either diet had any effect. It is true but irrelevant.

Incorrect. This is accurate, but it shows only the fermented-food result. The sentence says it was the fermented-food diet and not the fiber diet, so you also need the fiber comparison. This is half right.
Correct. The fermented-food group gained 32 species (139 to 171), while the fiber group gained only 3 (142 to 145). That shows fermented foods, not fiber, made the big difference.
Incorrect. This swaps the two diets. In the graph, 171 belongs to the fermented-food group and 145 to the high-fiber group.

passage.text: Hydrogen fuel can be made by using electricity to split water, but the reaction requires a catalyst, and the best catalyst, platinum, is scarce and expensive. Catalysts are compared by their overpotential, the extra voltage beyond the theoretical minimum needed to drive the reaction; a lower overpotential means a more efficient catalyst. Chemist Thomas Jaramillo and colleagues measured the overpotential of platinum and three platinum-free catalysts in acidic and alkaline electrolytes. Jaramillo claims that at least one platinum-free catalyst can outperform platinum, but only in alkaline conditions.

figure.title: Overpotential of Four Catalysts in Two Electrolytes

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Jaramillo's claim?
choices: Cobalt phosphide had a lower overpotential in the acidic electrolyte (85 millivolts) than in the alkaline electrolyte (120 millivolts), unlike nickel-molybdenum.
Nickel-molybdenum had a lower overpotential than platinum did in both the acidic electrolyte and the alkaline electrolyte, making it the best catalyst overall.
Iron sulfide had the highest overpotential of any catalyst in both electrolytes, at 210 millivolts in the acidic electrolyte and 190 in the alkaline one.
In alkaline electrolyte, nickel-molybdenum's overpotential was below platinum's (45 vs. 70 millivolts), but in acidic electrolyte platinum's was the lowest of all four.

explanation.passage: To make hydrogen from water you need a catalyst, and platinum is the best but very expensive. The passage defines overpotential as wasted extra voltage, so lower is better; this is the trap, because on this graph shorter bars mean better catalysts. Jaramillo's claim has two parts: (1) some platinum-free catalyst beats platinum in alkaline conditions, and (2) none does in acidic conditions.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares one catalyst with itself in two electrolytes. It doesn't compare anything with platinum.

Incorrect. In the acidic electrolyte, nickel-molybdenum needed 140 mV while platinum needed only 30 mV, so nickel-molybdenum was worse there. This also contradicts the 'only in alkaline' part of the claim.
Incorrect. This is accurate (210 and 190 are the highest values), but it is about the worst catalyst. It doesn't show any platinum-free catalyst beating platinum.

Correct. In alkaline conditions, nickel-molybdenum's 45 mV beats platinum's 70 mV (lower is better). In acidic conditions, all three platinum-free catalysts (140, 85, 210) are worse than platinum's 30 mV. Both parts of the claim are matched.

passage.text: Deep-sea hydrothermal vents release mineral-rich fluid that feeds chemosynthetic bacteria (microbes that make food from chemicals rather than sunlight), which in turn support dense communities of animals such as giant tubeworms. When a vent stops flowing, these animals die off. Deep-sea ecologist Lauren Mullineaux and colleagues surveyed the East Pacific Rise and hypothesized that long-inactive vents do not simply revert to the condition of the surrounding seafloor but instead support a distinct community, because their hard mineral chimneys offer surfaces that suspension feeders, such as sponges and corals, can attach to.

figure.title: Animal Density at Four Types of Deep-Sea Site

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Mullineaux and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: Suspension feeders were densest at vents inactive for more than 20 years, at 48 per m², far denser than at active vents (6) or on non-vent seafloor (4).
Tubeworm density fell from 310 per m² at active vents to 42 at recently inactive vents and to 0 at vents that had been inactive for more than 20 years.
At vents inactive for less than five years, neither tubeworms (42 per m²) nor suspension feeders (15 per m²) reached a density of 50 per m².
Vents inactive for more than 20 years and the non-vent seafloor both had no tubeworms at all, so the two types of site had identical tubeworm densities.

explanation.passage: Hydrothermal vents are hot springs on the sea floor that feed huge animal communities. When the vents shut off, those animals die. The hypothesis is that old, dead vents don't just turn back into ordinary seafloor: they get a new, different community of animals like sponges that cling to the leftover rock chimneys. So you need data showing that long-inactive vents differ from both active vents and plain seafloor.
choices: Correct. At vents dead for over 20 years, suspension feeders reached 48 per m², eight times the density at active vents and twelve times that of plain seafloor. That is a community unlike either, as hypothesized.
Incorrect. This is true, but it only shows the old vent community disappearing. The hypothesis is about a new, distinct community appearing, which this doesn't show.
Incorrect. This is accurate (42 and 15 are both under 50), but it describes recently inactive vents, not long-inactive ones. It doesn't address the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This is true, but it points out a similarity between old vents and plain seafloor, which works against the idea that old vents are distinct.

passage.text: After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, elk began avoiding areas where wolves hunted most often. Ecologists William Ripple and Robert Beschta argued that this change allowed willows, which elk eat, to recover along streams. To test the idea, they measured willow height at sites with high and low levels of wolf activity. Willow recovery, they found, was concentrated where wolves were most active: ______

figure.title: Average Willow Height in Yellowstone

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: willows at sites with both high and low wolf activity were taller on average in 2013 than they had been in 1995.
willows at high-activity sites grew from 85 cm in 1995 to 210 cm in 2013, while willows at low-activity sites grew only from 80 cm to 104 cm.
willows at high-activity sites were already slightly taller on average than willows at low-activity sites in 1995, at 85 cm versus 80 cm.
willows at low-activity sites grew from an average of 80 cm in 1995 to an average of 210 cm in 2013.

explanation.passage: Wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, and elk started avoiding places where wolves hunt. Fewer elk means less munching on willows. The sentence says willow recovery was 'concentrated' where wolves were most active. So the blank must compare the two kinds of sites and show much more growth at the high-wolf sites.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows growth at both kinds of site without comparing how much. It doesn't show recovery was concentrated in high-wolf areas.
Correct. High-wolf sites gained 125 cm (85 to 210), while low-wolf sites gained only 24 cm (80 to 104). Most of the recovery happened where wolves were active.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes 1995, the year wolves returned, before recovery could happen. It is true but irrelevant.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. 210 cm is the 2013 height at high-activity sites; low-activity sites reached only 104 cm.

passage.text: As a comet nears the Sun, its ices turn directly into gas, and astronomers can track this activity by measuring how many water molecules the comet releases each second. If water production depended only on the comet's distance from the Sun, it would be symmetrical around perihelion (the point of closest approach): equal on matching days before and after. Planetary scientist Dennis Bodewits and colleagues, however, hypothesized that comet C/2021 K4 exhibits thermal lag, in which heat penetrates the nucleus slowly, so that activity peaks some time after perihelion and stays elevated as the comet recedes.

figure.title: Water Production of Comet C/2021 K4

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Bodewits and colleagues' hypothesis?
choices: Water production rose steadily from 60 days before perihelion to perihelion itself, increasing from 1.2 to 6.3 × 10^27 molecules per second.
Water production 40 days after perihelion (4.9 × 10^27 molecules per second) was slightly lower than production 20 days before perihelion (5.1).
Water production peaked 20 days after perihelion at 8.4 × 10^27 molecules per second, well above the 5.1 recorded 20 days before perihelion.
Water production at perihelion, 6.3 × 10^27 molecules per second, was the highest value recorded during the 120 days of observation.

explanation.passage: Comets release water as the Sun heats their ice. Perihelion is the moment the comet is closest to the Sun, so you might expect the most water then, with matching amounts on matching days before and after. Thermal lag is the idea that heat soaks in slowly, like a pizza stone that keeps getting hotter after you turn the oven down, so the peak comes after perihelion. You need data showing a peak after day 0 and an imbalance between matching days.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but rising activity as the comet approaches the Sun is expected with or without thermal lag. It doesn't show a delayed peak.
Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but day +40 and day -20 are not matching days, so comparing them says nothing about symmetry. It is true but irrelevant.

Correct. The highest value, 8.4, came 20 days after perihelion, not at perihelion. And on the matching day before perihelion (-20), production was only 5.1. That delayed, lopsided peak is what thermal lag predicts.
Incorrect. This is false. The highest value was 8.4, recorded 20 days after perihelion, not 6.3 at perihelion.

passage.text: Wildfire smoke contains fine particles, measured as PM2.5 (particulate matter under 2.5 micrometers across), that scatter and absorb sunlight before it reaches solar panels. During the 2020 California wildfires, energy researchers led by Marc Perez compared actual solar output with the output expected under clear skies at the same time of year. An engineer advising grid operators has claimed that smoke reduces solar output only once PM2.5 concentrations exceed 55 micrograms per cubic meter, so that operators can safely ignore light smoke when forecasting supply.

figure.title: Solar Output During the 2020 California Wildfires
figure.xLabel: Air quality (PM2.5, micrograms per cubic meter)

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken the engineer's claim?
choices: Under heavy smoke, rooftop systems produced only 52% of their expected output, the lowest percentage for any type of system under any condition.
Rooftop systems produced a smaller percentage of their expected output than utility-scale plants did under every one of the four air-quality conditions.
Under moderate smoke, utility-scale plants produced 78% of their expected output, 20 percentage points less than they produced under clear skies.
Under light smoke, utility-scale plants produced 91% and rooftop systems 89% of expected output, compared with 98% and 97% under clear skies.

explanation.passage: Smoke particles block some sunlight from reaching solar panels. The engineer claims smoke only matters once PM2.5 goes above 55, so 'light smoke' (12-55) can be ignored. To weaken that claim, you need evidence that light smoke, below 55, already reduces output. Data about heavier smoke won't help, because the engineer already agrees that heavy smoke lowers output.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but heavy smoke is above 55, where the engineer agrees smoke reduces output. It is consistent with the claim.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but it compares two kinds of systems. It doesn't address whether light smoke reduces output.
Incorrect. This is true (98 - 78 = 20), but moderate smoke (56-150) is above 55, so this fits the engineer's claim rather than weakening it.

Correct. Light smoke is below the engineer's 55 threshold, yet output fell about 7 to 8 percentage points for both kinds of systems. Smoke reduced output before PM2.5 passed 55, so light smoke cannot safely be ignored.

passage.text: Most vaccines must be kept between 2°C and 8°C from factory to clinic, and breaks in this cold chain spoil millions of doses each year, especially in hot regions with unreliable electricity. Biomedical engineer Fiorenzo Omenetto and colleagues embedded a measles vaccine in a film of silk fibroin, a protein that can shield delicate molecules from heat, and stored standard and silk-stabilized doses at 37°C. Under World Health Organization guidelines, a dose is considered usable if it retains at least 80% of its original potency.

figure.title: Measles Vaccine Potency During Storage at 37°C

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Omenetto and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Silk-stabilized doses could be stored at 37°C for at least 8 weeks and remain usable, whereas standard doses would become unusable within the first week.
Silk-stabilized doses would remain usable throughout 12 weeks of storage at 37°C, while standard doses would lose all of their potency in that time.
Silk stabilization eliminates the need to refrigerate measles vaccine doses, even during long periods of storage in hot regions.
Standard doses would remain usable for about two weeks at 37°C, about one quarter as long as silk-stabilized doses would remain usable.

explanation.passage: Vaccines usually need refrigeration, and keeping them cold is hard in hot places. The researchers wrapped a vaccine in silk protein and stored it at body temperature, 37°C. The text gives the rule you need: a dose is usable only if it keeps at least 80% of its potency. So compare each line with 80 to find when each kind of dose stops being usable.
choices: Correct. Silk-stabilized doses were at 84% at week 8, still above 80%. Standard doses had already fallen to 61% by week 1, below 80%, so they became unusable within the first week.
Incorrect. The second half is true (standard doses reached 0%), but the first half is false: silk-stabilized doses fell to 78% by week 12, below the 80% usable line. Half right.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The study tested only 12 weeks, and potency was still falling, dipping below 80% by week 12. Nothing shows refrigeration is never needed.
Incorrect. Standard doses were at 38% at week 2 and only 61% at week 1, both below 80%, so they were not usable for two weeks.

passage.text: Wastewater treatment plants capture most microplastics, but the outflow still carries many synthetic fibers shed by laundry, and most such fibers are denser than water and sink. Aquatic ecologist Chelsea Rochman and colleagues counted microplastic particles in the guts of fish caught upstream and downstream of treatment plants on tributaries of Lake Ontario, grouping the fish by where in the water they feed. The team hypothesized that fish feeding near the bottom are the most exposed to microplastics released by the plants.

figure.title: Microplastic Particles in Fish Guts

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' hypothesis?
choices: Fish in all three feeding groups contained more microplastic particles on average downstream of the plants than upstream of the plants.
Downstream of the plants, bottom feeders averaged 8.7 more particles than upstream, while mid-water and surface feeders averaged only 1.6 and 1.2 more.
Upstream of the plants, bottom feeders contained more microplastic particles on average (3.1) than either mid-water feeders (2.4) or surface feeders (2.0).
Surface feeders caught downstream of the plants contained fewer microplastic particles on average than bottom feeders caught upstream of the plants.

explanation.passage: Treatment plants release laundry fibers, and most of these fibers sink. The researchers compared fish above and below the plants, grouped by where they feed. The hypothesis is specific: bottom feeders are the most exposed to plastic coming from the plants. The upstream fish show the background level, so the plant's effect is the jump from upstream to downstream. You need to show that the jump is biggest for bottom feeders.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it only shows the plants add plastic for every group. It doesn't show bottom feeders are the most exposed, so it is half right.

Correct. The jumps are 11.8 - 3.1 = 8.7 for bottom feeders, 4.0 - 2.4 = 1.6 for mid-water feeders, and 3.2 - 2.0 = 1.2 for surface feeders. Bottom feeders picked up far more plastic from the plants than any other group.
Incorrect. This is accurate, but upstream fish are above the plants, so their plastic didn't come from the plants. It doesn't address exposure to plant releases.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Downstream surface feeders averaged 3.2 particles, slightly more than upstream bottom feeders at 3.1, not fewer.

passage.text: Salt marshes can survive rising seas only if their surfaces build up, through trapped sediment and accumulating roots, at least as fast as sea level rises; otherwise they gradually drown and become open water. Coastal geologist Matthew Kirwan and colleagues tracked cumulative changes in sea level and marsh surface elevation since 2000 at two Chesapeake Bay marshes: Site A, which receives abundant sediment from a nearby river, and Site B, which is cut off from riverborne sediment.

figure.title: Cumulative Change in Sea Level and Marsh Elevation Since 2000

question: Based on the information in the text and the graph, Kirwan and colleagues could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Both marshes gained elevation more slowly than sea level rose from 2000 to 2020, though Site B lagged further behind than Site A did.
Site B's elevation gain slowed after 2012 because the rate of sea-level rise at the site accelerated during the same period.
Site A kept pace with sea-level rise from 2000 to 2020, whereas Site B fell increasingly behind it, putting Site B at risk of drowning.
Site A will continue to build elevation at least as fast as sea level rises through the end of the twenty-first century.

explanation.passage: A salt marsh survives rising seas only if its ground builds up at least as fast as the water rises. The graph shows how much sea level and each marsh's surface rose since 2000. Site A gets plenty of river mud; Site B does not. To judge each marsh, compare its line with the sea-level line: if the marsh line stays at or above sea level, it is keeping up.
choices: Incorrect. Site A was above sea level at every point (for example, 89 vs. 86 in 2020), so it did not gain elevation more slowly. Only Site B fell behind.

Incorrect. The graph shows the two trends happening at the same time, but nothing shows one caused the other. Site B's gains were already shrinking before 2012 (10, 9, 8 mm per period). This claims a cause the data can't establish.

Correct. Site A's elevation stayed above sea level throughout (18 vs. 14, 35 vs. 30, and so on). Site B's shortfall grew from 4 mm to 11, 20, 32, and 45 mm, and the text says a marsh that falls behind will drown.
Incorrect. The data stop in 2020, and Site A's margin over sea level is small (3 mm in 2020). Predicting 80 more years goes beyond the evidence.

passage.text: Biochar, a charcoal-like material made by heating crop waste without oxygen, is often promoted as a way to raise crop yields while locking carbon in the soil. Because biochar is alkaline, it can neutralize acidic soils that would otherwise limit plant growth. Soil scientist Simon Jeffery and colleagues analyzed results from hundreds of field trials and found that biochar's benefit was concentrated in acidic soils and could even disappear in alkaline ones: ______

figure.title: Average Change in Crop Yield After Adding Biochar
figure.note: Lower pH values indicate more acidic soil; values above 7.0 indicate alkaline soil.

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: biochar raised yields by an average of 14% in soils with a pH between 5.0 and 6.0, which are moderately acidic.
biochar raised yields in every soil-pH group, though by an average of only 3% in soils with a pH between 6.0 and 7.0.
biochar raised yields by an average of 28% in soils with a pH above 7.0 but lowered them by 2% in soils with a pH below 5.0.
biochar raised yields by an average of 28% in soils with a pH below 5.0 but lowered them by 2% in soils with a pH above 7.0.

explanation.passage: Biochar is charcoal added to soil. It is alkaline (the opposite of acidic), so it can fix soils that are too acidic. The pH scale measures this: lower numbers are more acidic, and above 7 is alkaline. The sentence makes two points: the benefit is biggest in acidic soils, and it can disappear in alkaline soils. The blank must show both.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate, but one middle group can't show that the benefit is concentrated in acidic soils or that it disappears in alkaline ones.
Incorrect. This is false. In soils above pH 7.0, yields went down by 2%, so biochar did not raise yields in every group.
Incorrect. This swaps the soil groups. The 28% gain was in the most acidic soils (below 5.0), and the 2% loss was in alkaline soils (above 7.0).
Correct. The biggest gain, 28%, came in the most acidic soils, and in alkaline soils yields actually fell by 2%. That shows both halves of the sentence.

passage.text: The chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis has driven dozens of frog species to extinction. In Panama, frog populations in cool highland streams, which average about 16°C, crashed after the fungus arrived, while populations in warm lowland streams, which average about 28°C, largely persisted. Herpetologist Ana Longo attributes this difference to temperature. A colleague proposes a different explanation: that the strain of the fungus found in lowland streams is simply a slower-growing strain than the highland strain at all temperatures. Longo's team grew both strains in the laboratory across a range of temperatures.

figure.title: Laboratory Growth of Two Chytrid Strains

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken the colleague's explanation?
choices: At 20°C and 24°C, the lowland strain grew faster than the highland strain, producing 6.9 and 6.4 thousand zoospores per mL compared with 5.8 and 3.0.
At 12°C and 16°C, the highland strain grew faster than the lowland strain, producing 3.2 and 6.1 thousand zoospores per mL compared with 1.8 and 4.6.
At 32°C, both strains produced fewer zoospores than they did at any other temperature tested, with the highland strain producing only 0.1 thousand per mL.
The highland strain reached its fastest growth at a lower temperature (16°C) than the temperature at which the lowland strain grew fastest (20°C).

explanation.passage: A fungus has wiped out highland frogs in Panama, while lowland frogs survived. Longo thinks temperature is the reason. Her colleague instead says the lowland fungus strain is just slower-growing 'at all temperatures.' A claim about all temperatures can be knocked down by a single temperature where the lowland strain grows faster than the highland strain.
choices: Correct. At 20°C (6.9 vs. 5.8) and 24°C (6.4 vs. 3.0), the lowland strain out-grew the highland strain. So the lowland strain is not slower at all temperatures, which directly contradicts the colleague.
Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but they show the lowland strain growing more slowly, which fits the colleague's explanation instead of weakening it.
Incorrect. This is true, but it shows both strains doing poorly in the heat. It doesn't compare the strains in a way that challenges the colleague.
Incorrect. This is true, but it is about where each strain peaks, not about which strain grows faster at a given temperature. It doesn't contradict the 'slower at all temperatures' claim.

passage.text: Spider dragline silk is stronger by weight than steel, but spiders cannot be farmed, so researchers have engineered bacteria to produce silk proteins instead. Early bacterial silks were disappointingly weak, and some scientists blamed the bacteria themselves. Materials scientist Fuzhong Zhang and colleagues hypothesized instead that the weakness came from the short protein chains bacteria had been making, not from any inherent flaw in bacterial production. They engineered bacteria to make silk proteins of increasing length, measured in repeating units, and tested the strength of fibers spun from them. Supporting the team's hypothesis, ______

figure.title: Tensile Strength of Silk Fibers

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: natural dragline silk, at 1,100 megapascals, was stronger than every one of the fibers spun from proteins that the engineered bacteria produced.
fibers from 192-unit proteins reached 1,030 megapascals, nearly matching natural silk's 1,100, while fibers from 96-unit proteins reached only 520.
fibers from 128-unit proteins reached 760 megapascals, roughly 70% of the strength of natural dragline silk, at 1,100 megapascals.
fibers from 192-unit proteins were nearly twice as strong as fibers from 128-unit proteins, reaching 1,030 megapascals versus 760 megapascals.

explanation.passage: Spider silk is incredibly strong, so scientists use bacteria to make silk proteins. Early bacterial silk was weak. Zhang's team argued the problem was short protein chains, not the bacteria. Their hypothesis has two parts: (1) longer chains make stronger silk, and (2) bacteria can make silk nearly as good as real spider silk once the chains are long enough. The best data would show strength rising with length and approaching natural silk.
choices: Incorrect. This is true, but it only shows that natural silk is stronger. It doesn't show that chain length matters, and on its own it could even suggest bacteria are the problem.

Correct. Fiber strength doubled from 520 to 1,030 as the chains got longer, so length matters. And at 1,030, the longest-chain fiber nearly matched natural silk's 1,100, showing bacteria can make strong silk. Both parts of the hypothesis are supported.
Incorrect. The math is right (760 is about 69% of 1,100), but this describes a single fiber. It doesn't show that longer chains make stronger silk.
Incorrect. This misstates the data. 1,030 divided by 760 is about 1.36, so the 192-unit fibers were about one-third stronger, not nearly twice as strong.

passage.text: When people estimate an unfamiliar quantity, they are often swayed by an arbitrary number they encountered just beforehand, a bias known as anchoring. Some researchers have argued that anchoring disappears once people recognize that the number carries no information. To test this view, psychologists Tomasz Wierzbicki and Helen Achebe showed participants a photograph of an unfamiliar antique clock and then a number—either $20 or $900—before asking them to estimate the clock's price. Half the participants were told that the number had been generated at random; the other half were told that it was the sale price of a similar clock. Wierzbicki and Achebe hypothesized that anchoring persists even when people know an anchor is random, although it is weaker than when the anchor seems informative.

figure.title: Mean Price Estimates for an Antique Clock
rows: Anchor was a similar clock's price
Anchor was a similar clock's price

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Wierzbicki and Achebe's hypothesis?
choices: Among participants told the anchor was random, mean estimates were $170 higher after the $900 anchor than after the $20 anchor, whereas among participants told the anchor was a similar clock's price, the difference was $425.

Participants told the anchor was a similar clock's price gave a mean estimate of $520 after the $900 anchor, which was considerably higher than the mean estimate of $310 given by participants who had been told that the same anchor was random.
Participants who saw no anchor gave a mean estimate of $210, which was higher than the mean estimate of either group of participants who saw the $20 anchor.

Among participants told the anchor was random, the mean estimates after the $20 and $900 anchors differed from each other by less than either one differed from the control group's mean estimate of $210.

explanation.passage: Anchoring means a random number you just saw pulls your guess toward it. Some researchers think this stops happening once you know the number is meaningless. Wierzbicki and Achebe disagree, and their hypothesis has two parts: (1) anchoring still happens when people know the anchor is random, and (2) it is weaker than when the anchor seems informative. The best way to measure the pull of an anchor is the gap between the low-anchor and high-anchor estimates within a group. So you need a choice that shows a real gap for the 'random' group AND a bigger gap for the 'similar clock' group.
choices: Correct. For the 'random' group, $310 - $140 = $170, so the anchor still moved guesses a lot (part 1: anchoring persists). For the 'similar clock' group, $520 - $95 = $425, a much larger gap (part 2: anchoring is weaker when the anchor is known to be random). This is the only choice that supports both halves of the hypothesis.

Incorrect. Half right: this comparison suggests the random anchor had less pull than the informative one, but it never shows that the random anchor had any pull at all. Without comparing the random group's $900 result to its $20 result (or to the control), it doesn't show that anchoring persists.

Incorrect. Half right: this is accurate ($140 and $95 are both below $210), but it lumps the two kinds of anchors together and says nothing about whether the random anchor was weaker than the informative one.

Incorrect. This misreads the table. The random group's two estimates differ by $170, while they differ from the control's $210 by only $70 ($210 - $140) and $100 ($310 - $210). So the statement is false.

passage.text: In 2023, three middle schools in the Pell River school district installed water bottle refill stations in their hallways, while three demographically similar schools in the district did not. Public health researcher Amara Okonkwo surveyed students at all six schools about their weekly beverage consumption both in 2022, before the installations, and in 2024. Okonkwo concluded that installing the refill stations caused students to replace sugary drinks with water, a finding she argues should encourage other districts to adopt the stations.

figure.title: Average Weekly Beverage Consumption per Student

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Okonkwo's conclusion?
choices: Students at schools with refill stations drank 4.5 bottles of water per week in 2024, more than twice as many as they drank in 2022.
In 2022, students at comparison schools drank slightly more bottles of water per week than students at schools that later installed refill stations did.
Sugary drink consumption fell by 1.6 drinks per week at comparison schools, nearly the same as the decline of 1.7 drinks per week at schools with refill stations.
Water consumption at comparison schools rose from 2022 to 2024 by about as much as water consumption at schools with refill stations did over the same two-year period.

explanation.passage: Six similar schools were compared: three got water refill stations in 2023 and three did not. Okonkwo surveyed students before (2022) and after (2024). Her conclusion is specific: the stations CAUSED students to REPLACE sugary drinks with water. To weaken a cause-and-effect claim, look at the comparison schools, which did not get stations. If something changed there just as much, the stations probably weren't the cause of that change.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate (2.0 to 4.5 is more than double), but it supports Okonkwo rather than weakening her. It shows the stations may have increased water drinking.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: 2.1 vs. 2.0 is a tiny starting difference and says nothing about whether the stations caused a change.

Correct. Comparison schools went from 4.6 to 3.0 sugary drinks (a drop of 1.6), and station schools went from 4.8 to 3.1 (a drop of 1.7). Since sugary drinking fell almost equally at schools without stations, the decline was probably caused by something else, so the stations did not cause students to swap sugary drinks for water.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Comparison schools rose only from 2.1 to 2.3 (0.2 more), while station schools rose from 2.0 to 4.5 (2.5 more).

passage.text: Japanese vocabulary is commonly divided into three layers: wago, native Japanese words; kango, words borrowed from Chinese many centuries ago; and gairaigo, more recent loanwords, most of them from English. Commentators frequently complain that the spread of gairaigo is crowding out native Japanese vocabulary. Linguist Kenji Oda tested this complaint by classifying every word in large samples of newspaper articles from four years. Although gairaigo are often blamed for displacing native words, Oda's data show that ______

figure.title: Share of Words in Japanese Newspaper Articles by Origin (%)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the share of gairaigo nearly quadrupled between 1960 and 2020, increasing faster than the share of any other type of word.
as the share of gairaigo rose from 4% to 15% between 1960 and 2020, the share of wago fell by only 2 percentage points while the share of kango fell by 8 points.
the share of wago declined more steeply than the share of kango did as gairaigo became more common between 1960 and 2020.
the combined share of wago and kango remained essentially unchanged between 1960 and 2020, even as gairaigo became steadily more common in Japanese newspaper articles.

explanation.passage: The passage explains three kinds of Japanese words: native words (wago), old Chinese borrowings (kango), and newer mostly English loanwords (gairaigo). People complain that gairaigo are pushing out NATIVE words, meaning wago. The blank comes after 'Although gairaigo are often blamed for displacing native words,' so it must say something that pushes back on that complaint. You need data showing that wago barely shrank while something else absorbed most of the loss.
choices: Incorrect. True but irrelevant: 4% to 15% is close to quadrupling, but this only describes gairaigo's growth. It doesn't say what was displaced, so it can't push back on the complaint the 'Although' sets up.

Correct. Wago went from 37% to 35% (down 2 points), while kango went from 52% to 44% (down 8 points). So the loanwords mostly replaced old Chinese-derived words, not native ones, which is exactly the contrast the 'Although' sentence needs.
Incorrect. Reversal: wago fell only 2 points, while kango fell 8 points, so kango declined more steeply, not wago.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: wago plus kango was 89% in 1960 (37 + 52) but only 79% in 2020 (35 + 44), a drop of 10 points.

passage.text: In March 2024, the city of Halvorsen began charging a fee to private cars entering its downtown zone on weekdays; taxis, ride-hail vehicles, and buses were exempt. To evaluate the policy, the city's transportation office compared average weekday vehicle counts recorded at downtown entry points in April 2023 and April 2024. Citing the roughly 20 percent drop in private cars shown in the table, council member Dana Reyes argues that the congestion charge reduced private car traffic downtown by about one-fifth.

figure.title: Average Weekday Vehicles Entering Downtown Halvorsen (thousands)

question: Which consideration, if true, should make Reyes most hesitant to rely on what the table suggests is the effect of the congestion charge on private car traffic?
choices: Taxis and ride-hail vehicles, which were exempt from the charge, entered downtown more often in April 2024 than in April 2023.
Congestion charges introduced in several other cities have reduced private car traffic in those cities' central zones by between 15 and 25 percent.
Delivery trucks entering downtown Halvorsen are charged a higher fee than private cars are.
A new commuter rail line connecting Halvorsen's suburbs to downtown opened in February 2024, a month before the charge took effect.

explanation.passage: Halvorsen started charging private cars to enter downtown in March 2024. The table compares April 2023 (before) with April 2024 (after). Private cars fell 20%, and Reyes says the charge caused that whole drop. The question asks what should make her hesitant, which means you are looking for another reason private car traffic could have fallen between those two Aprils. That would make the 20% figure an unreliable measure of the charge's effect.
choices: Incorrect. This just restates the table (18 to 21 thousand). Some drivers switching to exempt ride-hail trips is consistent with the charge working; it gives no other reason private cars dropped.
Incorrect. This would make Reyes more confident, not less, because a 20% drop fits what happened in other cities.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: the fee trucks pay doesn't explain the change in private car traffic, which is what Reyes is talking about.

Correct. A new commuter rail line opened between the two Aprils being compared. Some suburban drivers may have switched to the train whether or not there was a charge, so part of the 20% drop may be due to the rail line, not the charge.

passage.text: At the Neolithic settlement of Tell Qaran, grain was at first stored in clay-lined pits dug into the floors of individual houses. In later occupation phases, residents also built large communal storehouses. Archaeologist Leila Haddad measured the total storage capacity of both kinds of features in each of the site's three occupation phases. Haddad notes that the number of houses at Tell Qaran remained roughly constant, at about 40, across all three phases.

figure.title: Grain Storage Capacity at Tell Qaran by Occupation Phase

question: Based on the text and the graph, Haddad could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: By Phase III, the households at Tell Qaran had stopped storing grain inside their own houses and relied entirely on communal storehouses.
Total storage capacity at Tell Qaran declined from Phase I to Phase II as households began moving their grain into communal storehouses.
The rise in communal storage from Phase I to Phase III was not merely a transfer of grain out of household pits, since total capacity nearly doubled while the number of houses stayed about the same.

The population of Tell Qaran grew sharply between Phase II and Phase III, which forced residents to build large communal storehouses to hold the additional grain that the growing number of households needed.

explanation.passage: Tell Qaran is an ancient farming village. Early on, each house stored its own grain in a pit; later, people also built shared storehouses. The graph shows how much grain each kind of storage could hold in three phases. The key extra fact is in the text: the number of houses stayed about 40 the whole time. To answer, add the two bars for each phase to get total capacity, then think about what that means given a steady number of houses.
choices: Incorrect. Too strong: household pits still held 4 cubic meters in Phase III, so households had not stopped storing grain at home entirely.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Total capacity was 18 in Phase I (18 + 0) and 20 in Phase II (11 + 9), so it rose slightly rather than declining.

Correct. Total capacity went from 18 (Phase I) to 35 (Phase III, 4 + 31), almost double. If grain had simply been moved from pits to storehouses, the total would have stayed about the same. Since the number of houses didn't change, the extra capacity can't be explained by more households, so the storehouses added real new capacity.
Incorrect. This contradicts the text, which says the number of houses stayed about 40 in all three phases. Nothing in the passage indicates sharp population growth.

passage.text: Economists disagree about whether raising the minimum wage reduces employment among teenagers, who are disproportionately likely to hold minimum-wage jobs. Economist Rafael Moreno compiled data on four neighboring counties with similar economies: Ashby and Corvin raised their minimum wage in 2021, while Dellwood and Easton did not. Reviewing Moreno's data, a student claims that the 2021 increase reduced teen employment in Ashby and Corvin.

figure.title: Teen Employment Rate in Four Counties (%)

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the table?
choices: It is weakly supported, because although teen employment fell in both counties that raised the minimum wage, it fell by a similar amount in both counties that did not.
It is strongly supported, because the teen employment rate was lower in 2022 than in 2020 in both Ashby and Corvin.
It is not supported, because teen employment rose between 2020 and 2022 in both counties that raised the minimum wage.
It is weakly supported, because only one of the two counties that raised the minimum wage had a lower teen employment rate in 2022 than it had in 2020, before the increase.

explanation.passage: The question is whether raising the minimum wage cost teenagers jobs. Moreno picked four similar counties: two raised the wage (Ashby, Corvin) and two didn't (Dellwood, Easton). The two that didn't are a comparison group: they show what would probably have happened anyway. The student claims the wage increase caused teen employment to fall. To judge that, compute each county's change from 2020 to 2022 and compare the 'Yes' counties to the 'No' counties.
choices: Correct. Ashby fell 0.8 points (31.2 to 30.4) and Corvin fell 0.8 (28.7 to 27.9), but Dellwood fell 0.9 (30.1 to 29.2) and Easton fell 0.7 (27.5 to 26.8). Since teen employment dropped about the same amount where the wage didn't change, the data give little reason to blame the wage increase.

Incorrect. Half right: both counties did decline, but this ignores the comparison counties, which declined just as much. A drop that happens everywhere can't be credited to a policy only two counties adopted.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: teen employment fell, not rose, in both Ashby and Corvin.
Incorrect. The verdict 'weakly supported' sounds right, but the reason is false: both Ashby and Corvin had lower rates in 2022 than in 2020.

passage.text: Historians often estimate literacy in early America by counting how many people signed their wills with their names rather than with a mark such as an X. Using wills from Middlesex County, Massachusetts, historian Abigail Thorne calculated the signature rates shown in the table. Thorne cautions, however, that signature rates likely overstate reading ability among men and understate it among women: in this period, girls were commonly taught to read but not to write, while boys who learned to write their names usually also learned to read. If Thorne's caution is correct, the table suggests that ______

figure.title: Middlesex County Will-Makers Who Signed Their Names (%)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: fewer than half of the women who made wills in Middlesex County in any of the four periods were able to read.
men's ability to read increased more slowly between 1660 and 1799 than their ability to sign their names did, so the rise in men's signature rates overstates their progress.
by 1780-1799, at least 90 percent of the men who made wills in Middlesex County could both read and write.
in each period, the gap between men's and women's reading ability was likely smaller than the gap in signature rates, which ranged from 30 to 42 percentage points.

explanation.passage: Historians use signatures on wills as a rough measure of literacy. Thorne's table shows that men signed far more often than women. But she warns that signatures are a distorted measure: they make men look like better readers than they were, and women look like worse readers than they were, because girls were often taught reading without writing. The blank asks what the table suggests IF that warning is true. So you have to adjust the numbers in the direction she describes: men's true reading rates are lower or equal, and women's are higher.
choices: Incorrect. This treats signature rates as reading rates, ignoring the caution. Thorne says signatures understate women's reading, so women's true reading rates were probably higher than 31-48%; the table can't show that fewer than half could read.

Incorrect. Outside the scope: Thorne's caution is about the gap between signing and reading at any given time, not about how either changed over time. Nothing supports a claim about relative rates of increase.
Incorrect. Too strong, and backward: 90% of men signed, but Thorne says signatures may overstate men's reading, so the share who could read could be lower than 90%, not 'at least' 90%.

Correct. The signature gaps are 30 (61 - 31), 32, 39, and 42 points. If men's reading is lower than their signature rate and women's is higher, the true reading gap must be smaller than each signature gap.

passage.text: Advocates of the four-day workweek argue that employees who work fewer hours for the same pay become more productive in each hour they work. Management researcher Priya Natarajan tracked four firms that cut their schedules from 40 hours to 32 hours per week without reducing pay. She measured each firm's weekly output and output per hour in the year after the change, using the year before the change as a baseline of 100. Natarajan hypothesized that the gain in output per hour under a four-day week can be large enough that a firm's total weekly output does not fall.

figure.title: Productivity at Four Firms After Adopting a Four-Day Week

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Natarajan's hypothesis?
choices: At Corrigan, output per hour rose to 121, the smallest increase in output per hour among the four firms.
At Delmar, output per hour rose to 130, and total weekly output rose to 104.
At Fenwick, output per hour rose to 124, while total weekly output was 99.
At every firm, output per hour rose by more than 20 points after the change to a four-day week.

explanation.passage: Four firms cut the workweek from 40 to 32 hours without cutting pay. The graph sets the year before as 100, so any number above 100 means an increase. Natarajan's hypothesis has two linked parts: output per hour rises, AND it rises enough that total weekly output does NOT fall (stays at 100 or above). Notice that two firms, Corrigan (97) and Fenwick (99), did see weekly output fall, so you have to pick a firm that meets both conditions.
choices: Incorrect. True but unhelpful: Corrigan's total weekly output fell to 97, below the baseline of 100, so Corrigan is an example that goes against the hypothesis.

Correct. Delmar's output per hour rose to 130, and its total weekly output rose to 104, above 100. That shows the hourly gain was large enough to make up for the lost hours, which is exactly what the hypothesis says can happen.
Incorrect. Fenwick's total weekly output was 99, slightly below 100, so its weekly output did fall. This weakens rather than supports the hypothesis.

Incorrect. Half right: every firm's output per hour did rise above 120, but this says nothing about total weekly output, which is the key second part of the hypothesis. Two firms' total output actually fell.

passage.text: Many students prepare for exams by rereading their notes, partly because rereading makes material feel familiar and therefore well learned. Educational psychologists Elena Vasquez and Tom Brennan had high school students read a passage about how volcanoes form and then spend ten minutes either rereading the passage, taking a practice quiz on it, or drawing a concept map of its ideas. Some students were tested right away; others were tested one week later. The results suggest that the feeling of familiarity can be misleading, since rereading produced ______

figure.title: Average Test Scores by Study Method (%)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: higher average scores than the practice quiz did on both the immediate test and the test taken one week later.
the highest average score on the immediate test but the lowest average score on the test taken one week later.
the smallest drop in average score between the immediate test and the test taken one week later.
a lower average score than concept mapping did on the immediate test but a higher average score on the test taken one week later.

explanation.passage: Students often reread because the material starts to feel familiar, which feels like learning. Vasquez and Brennan compared three ways of studying and tested students either right away or a week later. The sentence says familiarity 'can be misleading,' so the blank needs to show rereading looking good at first but turning out badly. Look for rereading doing well on the immediate test and poorly on the delayed test.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: rereading beat the quiz immediately (78 vs. 71), but not a week later (49 vs. 64).

Correct. Rereading had the top immediate score (78, above 71 and 74) but the bottom one-week score (49, below 64 and 55). That pattern is exactly what 'misleading familiarity' predicts: it felt learned at first but was forgotten.
Incorrect. Reversal: rereading had the biggest drop, 29 points (78 to 49), compared with 7 points for the quiz and 19 for the concept map.
Incorrect. This reverses both comparisons: rereading scored higher than concept mapping immediately (78 vs. 74) and lower one week later (49 vs. 55).

passage.text: Beginning with the 2020 election, the state of Marenta automatically mailed a ballot to every registered voter in a set of pilot counties; in the state's other counties, voters still had to request a mail ballot. Political scientist Owen Fairbanks compared turnout among registered voters in the two sets of counties in 2016 and 2020. Fairbanks cautions that turnout rose throughout Marenta in 2020, largely because that year's statewide races were unusually competitive.

figure.title: Turnout Among Registered Voters in Marenta (%)

question: Based on the text and the table, Fairbanks could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: The entire increase in turnout in the pilot counties between 2016 and 2020 can be attributed to the automatic mailing of ballots, since turnout rose in those counties in every age group shown in the table.
Turnout among voters aged 65 and older rose more in the pilot counties than turnout among voters aged 18-29 did.
The competitiveness of the 2020 statewide races raised turnout more among older voters than among younger voters.
Automatically mailing ballots appears to have increased turnout most among voters aged 18-29, whose turnout rose about 6 percentage points more in the pilot counties than in the other counties.

explanation.passage: Marenta mailed ballots to everyone in some 'pilot' counties starting in 2020; other counties didn't. The table shows turnout by age in 2016 and 2020 for both groups. The text adds an important warning: turnout rose everywhere in 2020 because the races were exciting. So the rise in the OTHER counties shows how much turnout would have risen anyway. The effect of mailed ballots is the extra rise in pilot counties beyond the rise in other counties.
choices: Incorrect. Too strong, and it ignores Fairbanks's caution. Turnout also rose in counties without automatic ballots (for example, 37% to 44% for ages 18-29), so part of the pilot counties' increase came from the competitive races.
Incorrect. Reversal: in the pilot counties, turnout among those 65 and older rose 3 points (72 to 75), while turnout among those aged 18-29 rose 13 points (38 to 51).

Incorrect. Reversal: the other counties show the effect of competitiveness alone, and there turnout rose 7 points for ages 18-29 (37 to 44) but only 2 points for ages 65 and older (73 to 75). So competitiveness raised young voters' turnout more.

Correct. Among 18-29-year-olds, pilot turnout rose 13 points (38 to 51) and other-county turnout rose 7 points (37 to 44), a 6-point difference. The differences for the older groups are smaller: 4 points (8 vs. 4), 2 points (5 vs. 3), and 1 point (3 vs. 2).

passage.text: When adults address infants, they often speak at a markedly higher pitch than usual, a style known as infant-directed speech. Some researchers have claimed that this exaggerated pitch is a universal feature of human caregiving. Linguist Sofia Lindqvist noted, however, that in tonal languages such as Mandarin and Yoruba, changes in pitch distinguish one word from another, so a large overall rise in pitch might make words harder for an infant to recognize. Lindqvist recorded mothers in four language communities speaking first to an adult and then to their infant, and her findings were consistent with her expectation: ______

figure.title: Mothers' Average Speaking Pitch by Language and Listener
figure.note: English and Spanish are not tonal languages; Mandarin and Yoruba are tonal languages.

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: mothers speaking Mandarin and Yoruba raised their pitch by 30 Hz and 32 Hz, respectively, when addressing their infants, compared with increases of 80 Hz and 70 Hz among mothers speaking English and Spanish.
mothers in all four language communities spoke at a higher average pitch when addressing their infants than when addressing an adult.
mothers speaking Mandarin used a higher average pitch when addressing an adult than mothers in any of the other three language communities did.
