mothers speaking Mandarin and Yoruba used a lower average pitch when addressing their infants than mothers speaking English and Spanish used when addressing an adult, even though tonal languages depend on pitch.

explanation.passage: Adults usually raise their pitch (how high the voice sounds, measured in hertz, Hz) when talking to babies. Lindqvist points out a problem for tonal languages, where pitch changes the meaning of a word: a big pitch rise could blur words. So her expectation is that mothers who speak tonal languages raise their pitch LESS. The blank must show a smaller rise for Mandarin and Yoruba than for English and Spanish. To find the rise, subtract the adult bar from the infant bar for each language.
choices: Correct. Mandarin: 245 - 215 = 30 Hz. Yoruba: 232 - 200 = 32 Hz. English: 285 - 205 = 80 Hz. Spanish: 280 - 210 = 70 Hz. The tonal-language mothers raised their pitch far less, exactly matching Lindqvist's expectation.

Incorrect. Topic match, claim miss: this is true, but it treats all four languages the same and says nothing about tonal languages showing a smaller rise. If anything, it fits the 'universal' view Lindqvist questions.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: Mandarin mothers' adult pitch (215 Hz) was the highest, but Lindqvist's expectation is about how much pitch rises for infants, not about starting levels.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph. Mandarin (245) and Yoruba (232) infant-directed pitches are higher than English (205) and Spanish (210) adult-directed pitches.

passage.text: To increase flu vaccination rates, a regional clinic network randomly assigned its patients to receive no reminder, a generic text message ("Flu shots are now available"), or a personalized text message stating that a flu shot had been reserved in the patient's name. Health researcher Ines Carvalho, who analyzed the results, claims that personalized reminders raised vaccination rates more than generic reminders did in every age group the network serves.

figure.title: Patients Vaccinated Against Flu by Reminder Type (%)

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which Carvalho's claim is supported by data from the table?
choices: It is strongly supported, because in every age group, patients who received a personalized text message were vaccinated at a higher rate than patients in the same age group who received no reminder at all.
It is not supported, because patients aged 65 and older who received a personalized text were vaccinated at a lower rate than those who received a generic text.
It is only partly supported, because personalized texts beat generic texts by 5 percentage points among patients aged 18-49 but did not beat generic texts at all among patients aged 65 and older.
It is only partly supported, because personalized texts outperformed generic texts among patients aged 50 and older but not among younger patients.

explanation.passage: A clinic network tested three options: no text, a generic 'flu shots are available' text, and a personalized 'we reserved one for you' text. Carvalho's claim is specific: personalized texts beat GENERIC texts in EVERY age group. So the comparison that matters is the 'Personalized text' column versus the 'Generic text' column, row by row. Watch for choices that compare against the wrong column ('No reminder').
choices: Incorrect. Wrong comparison: this compares personalized texts to no reminder, but Carvalho's claim is about personalized versus generic texts.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: for patients 65 and older, both types of texts produced 66%, so personalized was equal, not lower.

Correct. For 18-34, 30 vs. 25 (5 points); for 35-49, 38 vs. 33 (5 points). But for 65 and older, both were 66%, so personalized texts did not beat generic ones there. The claim holds for some age groups but fails the 'every age group' part.
Incorrect. Reversal: personalized texts did best compared with generic texts among younger patients (5-point gaps) and had little or no edge among older ones (1 point for 50-64, 0 for 65 and older).

passage.text: Psychologists Grace Mbeki and Lars Hoffmann studied how sleep loss affects eyewitnesses. Participants watched a video of a staged theft and then slept a full night, slept only four hours, or stayed awake all night (the sleep-deprived group) before viewing a photo lineup. In half the lineups the thief was present; in the other half the thief was absent, so any person chosen was innocent. Critics of earlier sleep studies had argued that sleep-deprived witnesses are not worse at remembering faces but are simply more reluctant to pick anyone from a lineup. Mbeki and Hoffmann's data, however, are difficult to reconcile with that view, since sleep-deprived participants ______

figure.title: Lineup Decisions by Rested and Sleep-Deprived Participants (%)
columns: Thief absent: chose an innocent person

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: correctly chose the thief from lineups in which the thief was present less often than rested participants did (47% versus 62%).
declined to choose anyone from lineups in which the thief was present more often than rested participants did.

chose an innocent person from lineups in which the thief was absent more often than they correctly chose the thief from lineups in which the thief was present, a pattern not seen among rested participants.
chose an innocent person from lineups in which the thief was absent far more often than rested participants did (41% versus 24%) and declined to choose anyone slightly less often (18% versus 21%).

explanation.passage: Participants either slept or stayed up all night, then looked at a lineup. Sometimes the real thief was in it; sometimes only innocent people were. Critics say tired witnesses aren't worse at memory, just more cautious about picking anyone. Think about what that view predicts: cautious witnesses would say 'no one' MORE often and pick innocent people LESS often. The blank needs data showing the opposite pattern, which would be hard to square with the 'just reluctant' explanation.
choices: Incorrect. True but it doesn't settle the debate: fewer correct picks (47% vs. 62%) is what you'd expect whether tired witnesses have worse memory or are simply more reluctant to pick. So it can't make the critics' view hard to reconcile.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: sleep-deprived participants chose no one 18% of the time, less often than rested participants (21%).
Incorrect. This misreads the table: sleep-deprived participants chose an innocent person 41% of the time, which is less than the 47% of the time they correctly chose the thief.

Correct. Reluctant witnesses would pick innocent people less and decline more, but tired participants did the reverse: they wrongly picked innocent people much more (41% vs. 24%) and declined slightly less (18% vs. 21%). That pattern points to impaired memory, not caution.

passage.text: Street trees cool cities in two ways: their canopies shade the ground directly beneath them, and through evapotranspiration—the release of water vapor from leaves—they cool the surrounding air across a wider area. Urban ecologist Marisol Duarte measured midday summer surface temperatures on sidewalks in four neighborhoods of Caldera City that differ in their overall tree canopy cover. In each neighborhood she measured sidewalks directly under trees and sunlit sidewalks on the same blocks. Duarte hypothesized that, on Caldera City's sidewalks, trees' cooling effect comes mainly from shade rather than from evapotranspiration.

figure.title: Midday Sidewalk Surface Temperatures in Four Neighborhoods

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Duarte's hypothesis?
choices: Sidewalks under trees in the neighborhood with 45% canopy cover had a temperature of 39°C, the lowest temperature recorded in any of the four neighborhoods.
In every neighborhood, sidewalks under trees were 17°C cooler than sunlit sidewalks, but sunlit sidewalks were only 2°C cooler in the 45% canopy neighborhood than in the 5% canopy neighborhood.
Sunlit sidewalks in the neighborhood with 45% canopy cover were much cooler than sunlit sidewalks in the neighborhood with 5% canopy cover, even though both were measured at the same time of day.
Sidewalks under trees in the neighborhood with 5% canopy cover were warmer than sunlit sidewalks in the neighborhood with 45% canopy cover.

explanation.passage: Trees cool in two ways: shade (only right underneath) and evapotranspiration (water from leaves cooling the air over a wide area). Duarte thinks shade does most of the work. Here's how to test that with the graph: shade's effect is the gap between shaded and sunlit sidewalks on the same block. Evapotranspiration's effect would show up as sunlit sidewalks getting cooler in leafier neighborhoods, since more trees would cool the whole area. Her hypothesis predicts a big shade gap and only a small neighborhood-wide difference.
choices: Incorrect. True but irrelevant: 39°C is the lowest value, but a single number can't tell you whether the cooling came from shade or from evapotranspiration.

Correct. Shaded sidewalks were 17°C cooler in every neighborhood (58 - 41, 57 - 40, 57 - 40, 56 - 39), a large shade effect. But going from 5% to 45% canopy cooled sunlit sidewalks by only 2°C (58 to 56), so the area-wide evapotranspiration effect was small. Both parts point to shade as the main cause.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph (58°C vs. 56°C is only a 2°C difference), and a large difference here would actually suggest a strong evapotranspiration effect, weakening the hypothesis.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph: shaded sidewalks in the 5% neighborhood were 41°C, much cooler than the 56°C sunlit sidewalks in the 45% neighborhood.

passage.text: Coin hoards—collections of coins that were deliberately buried and never recovered—are often interpreted as signs of insecurity, since people tended to bury valuables when threatened and might never return for them if they were killed or forced to flee. Archaeologist Marco Pellegrini catalogued coin hoards found in Roman Britain, dating each hoard by its most recent coin. Historical sources describe the decades between 260 and 289 CE as a time of invasions and civil war in the region.

figure.title: Coin Hoards from Roman Britain by Date
columns: Median number of coins per hoard

question: Based on the text and the table, Pellegrini could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: The data are consistent with the view that hoards reflect insecurity, since about four times as many hoards date to 260-289 CE as to the preceding thirty years.
Insecurity in Roman Britain led people to bury fewer coins in each hoard than they did in calmer times, since the median number of coins per hoard was smallest in 260-289 CE.
Roman Britain was more secure in 290-319 CE than in any other period shown, since that period produced the fewest hoards.
Every hoard dating to 260-289 CE was buried by someone who was fleeing invasion or civil war.

explanation.passage: A coin hoard is a stash of coins someone buried and never came back for. Archaeologists often think hoards mean dangerous times: people hid money when threatened, and if they died or fled, the coins stayed buried. The text tells you 260-289 CE was a violent period. So the question is whether the table lines up with that: are there more hoards in 260-289?
choices: Correct. There are 211 hoards from 260-289 versus 52 from 230-259, about four times as many (211 ÷ 52 ≈ 4.1). A spike during the documented period of invasions fits the idea that hoards reflect insecurity. Note the cautious wording 'consistent with,' which the data can support.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: the median hoard size in 260-289 was 640 coins, the largest of any period, not the smallest.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: 290-319 had 61 hoards, but 200-229 had only 34, so 290-319 did not have the fewest.
Incorrect. Too strong: the data show a pattern, not the reason behind each individual hoard. Some hoards could have been buried for other reasons.

passage.text: In many rural regions, households receive remittances—money sent home by relatives working abroad. Economist Lucía Ferreira surveyed households in four municipalities of the highland region of Alta Serrana and recorded how much each spent per child on schooling, including fees, uniforms, and books. Noting that remittance-receiving households in every municipality spent about 60 percent more per child, a policy analyst concludes that remittances themselves cause families to invest more in their children's education.

figure.title: Average Annual Education Spending per Child in Alta Serrana (US dollars)

question: Which consideration, if true, should make the policy analyst most hesitant to rely on what the table suggests is the effect of remittances on education spending?
choices: In all four municipalities, households receiving remittances spent more per child on education than households not receiving remittances did.
Remittances to households in Alta Serrana are usually sent monthly rather than in a single annual payment.
In Alta Serrana, the households that receive remittances are mostly those whose adult members already had higher incomes and more years of schooling before any relative went abroad.
School fees in Tamarindo are higher than school fees in the other three municipalities, which helps explain why spending per child there was the highest for both types of households surveyed.

explanation.passage: Remittances are money that family members working in other countries send home. Ferreira's table shows that, in all four towns, families receiving remittances spent much more per child on school. The analyst jumps from that pattern to a cause: the remittances MADE families spend more. The question asks what should make the analyst hesitant, so look for a reason the two groups of families might differ in education spending even without the remittances.
choices: Incorrect. This simply restates the table. It is the pattern the analyst is relying on, not a reason to doubt it.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: how often the money arrives doesn't change whether remittances, or something else, explain the higher spending.

Correct. If remittance families were already richer and more educated before anyone migrated, they likely would have spent more on schooling anyway. Then the gap in the table could come from those prior differences, not from the remittances.

Incorrect. This might explain why Tamarindo's numbers ($342 and $215) are higher than other towns', but it affects both groups of families in that town equally, so it doesn't explain the gap between them.

passage.text: Online retailers generally assume that higher customer ratings lead to higher sales. Marketing researchers Daniel Osei and Hana Kimura questioned this assumption after studying an online store's kitchen products. They hypothesized that products with near-perfect average ratings (4.9 to 5.0 stars) sell fewer units than products rated 4.5 to 4.8 stars, because shoppers suspect that flawless ratings are fake. To check, they grouped products by average rating and by how many reviews each product had received.

figure.title: Average Weekly Sales of Kitchen Products by Star Rating

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken Osei and Kimura's hypothesis?
choices: Among products with fewer than 50 reviews, those rated 4.9-5.0 stars sold an average of 20 units per week, fewer than the 27 units sold by those rated 4.5-4.8 stars.
In every rating group, products with 50 or more reviews sold more units per week, on average, than products with fewer than 50 reviews did.
Among products with 50 or more reviews, those rated 4.9-5.0 stars sold an average of 71 units per week, more than the 66 units sold by those rated 4.5-4.8 stars.
Among products with fewer than 50 reviews, those rated 3.5-3.9 stars sold fewer units per week, on average, than those rated 4.9-5.0 stars did.

explanation.passage: Most stores assume more stars means more sales. Osei and Kimura predict an exception: products with almost perfect ratings (4.9-5.0) should sell LESS than products rated 4.5-4.8, because shoppers think perfect ratings look fake. So the only comparison that tests the hypothesis is the 4.5-4.8 bar versus the 4.9-5.0 bar. To weaken it, you need a case where the 4.9-5.0 products sold MORE.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it supports the hypothesis: for products with few reviews, near-perfect ratings did sell less (20 vs. 27).
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: it compares products with many reviews to products with few reviews, which isn't what the hypothesis is about.

Correct. For products with 50 or more reviews, the 4.9-5.0 group sold 71 units a week versus 66 for the 4.5-4.8 group. Here near-perfect ratings were linked to higher sales, the opposite of what the hypothesis predicts.
Incorrect. Topic match, claim miss: 12 vs. 20 is accurate, but the hypothesis compares near-perfect ratings with 4.5-4.8 ratings, not with 3.5-3.9 ratings.

passage.text: Medieval Paris levied a tax called the taille on its residents, and the surviving tax rolls list each taxpayer's trade. Historian Claire Dumont used the rolls of 1292 and 1313 to study women's work in the city's crafts. Reviewing her data for four trades, a student claims that women's participation in Parisian crafts declined between 1292 and 1313 in every trade, measured by the share of each trade's taxpayers who were women.

figure.title: Taxpayers in Four Parisian Trades, 1292 and 1313

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the student's claim is supported by data from the table?
choices: It is mostly but not fully supported, because the share of taxpayers who were women fell in silk working, brewing, and baking but rose in tailoring.
It is fully supported, because the number of women taxpayers was lower in 1313 than in 1292 in every trade shown.
It is not supported, because women made up most of the taxpayers in silk working in both 1292 and 1313.
It is mostly but not fully supported, because the number of women taxpayers was lower in 1313 than in 1292 in every one of the trades shown except baking, where it rose.

explanation.passage: Dumont used medieval tax lists, which record each person's trade. The student says women's SHARE of each trade fell from 1292 to 1313 in EVERY trade. To check, you have to divide women by all taxpayers for each trade and year, then see if each share dropped. Notice the word 'every': a single exception means the claim isn't fully supported.
choices: Correct. Silk: 84/112 = 75% fell to 71/104 ≈ 68%. Brewing: 22/58 ≈ 38% fell to 15/61 ≈ 25%. Baking: 9/74 ≈ 12% fell to 6/70 ≈ 9%. But tailoring: 19/96 ≈ 20% rose to 23/90 ≈ 26%. Three of four trades fit; one doesn't.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: the number of women in tailoring rose from 19 to 23, so it did not fall in every trade.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: women were most of the silk workers in both years, but the claim is about whether women's share went down, and it did go down in silk working.
Incorrect. The verdict sounds right, but the exception is wrong: women in baking fell from 9 to 6. The trade where women's numbers and share rose was tailoring.

passage.text: Sociologists have long observed that people who stay in one place tend to build stronger local ties. Sociologist Harriet Kwan surveyed residents of a mid-sized city about how many of their neighbors they knew by name, sorting respondents by how long they had lived in their neighborhood and by their type of housing. Kwan hypothesized that the number of neighbors a resident knows by name increases steadily with years of residence, regardless of housing type.

figure.title: Average Number of Neighbors Known by Name

question: Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken Kwan's hypothesis?
choices: Homeowners who had lived in their neighborhood more than 10 years knew 12.5 neighbors by name, on average, about four times as many as homeowners who had lived there fewer than 2 years.
In every group based on years of residence, homeowners knew more neighbors by name, on average, than renters in apartment buildings did.
In every group based on years of residence, renters in single-family houses knew more neighbors by name, on average, than homeowners did.
Renters in apartment buildings knew about two neighbors by name, on average, whether they had lived in their neighborhood fewer than 2 years or more than 10 years.

explanation.passage: Kwan expects that the longer you live somewhere, the more neighbors you know, and she adds 'regardless of housing type,' meaning this should be true for homeowners, house renters, AND apartment renters. To weaken a claim that says 'regardless,' you only need one housing type where the pattern doesn't hold. So scan each column from top to bottom and see whether the numbers climb.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate (12.5 is about four times 3.1), but it supports the hypothesis by showing the predicted increase for homeowners.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: comparing homeowners to apartment renters at the same length of residence doesn't test whether ties grow over time.
Incorrect. Reversal: homeowners knew more neighbors than single-family renters in every row (for example, 12.5 vs. 11.2).
Correct. Apartment renters' numbers stay flat at about 2 (1.9, 2.2, 2.0, 2.3) no matter how long they had lived there. That breaks the 'regardless of housing type' part of the hypothesis.

passage.text: In dual-language immersion programs, students receive about half of their instruction in English and half in another language, such as Spanish. Some parents worry that this arrangement slows students' development as English readers. Education researcher Andrea Solís compared the average English reading scores of students in one district's dual-language program with those of students in its English-only program. At a school board meeting, a board member who opposes the program claimed that dual-language students never catch up to English-only students in English reading.

figure.title: Average English Reading Scores by Program and Grade

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the board member's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: It is supported, because students in the dual-language program scored 8 points lower in English reading than students in the English-only program did in grade 2.
It is not supported, because although dual-language students scored lower than English-only students in grade 2, they scored slightly higher in grades 5 and 8.
It is not supported, because dual-language students scored higher in English reading than English-only students did in every grade shown.
It is partly supported, because dual-language students scored lower than English-only students in grades 2 and 5 but scored higher in grade 8.

explanation.passage: In a dual-language program, kids learn in two languages. The worry is that they fall behind in English reading. The board member makes a strong claim: they NEVER catch up. 'Never catch up' would mean dual-language students are behind in every grade, including the later ones. So compare the two bars in each grade, especially grades 5 and 8.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: dual-language students were behind in grade 2 (182 vs. 190), but being behind early doesn't show they never catch up; they were ahead in later grades.

Correct. In grade 2 they trailed (182 vs. 190), but in grade 5 they were slightly ahead (214 vs. 213) and in grade 8 ahead by more (236 vs. 231). So they did catch up, which contradicts 'never catch up.'
Incorrect. Too strong: in grade 2, dual-language students scored lower (182 vs. 190).
Incorrect. This misreads grade 5: dual-language students scored 214, which is higher than English-only students' 213, not lower.

passage.text: In 2022, the city of Brennard began requiring chain restaurants to display a salt-shaker warning icon next to any menu item containing more than 2,300 milligrams of sodium, the recommended daily limit for adults. Public health researcher Ji-woo Park compared the orders placed at the city's chain restaurants in 2021 and in 2023. Park found that diners who avoided the labeled items did not simply switch to items falling just below the labeling threshold: ______

figure.title: Share of Orders at Brennard Chain Restaurants by Sodium Content

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the share of orders for labeled items fell from 18% to 12%, while the share for items under 1,500 mg rose from 48% to 53% and the share for items of 1,500-2,300 mg barely changed.
the share of orders for items with more than 2,300 mg of sodium fell by more than half between 2021 and 2023, the period during which the warning icons were introduced at chain restaurants.
items with more than 2,300 mg of sodium accounted for a smaller share of orders than items with less than 1,500 mg did in both 2021 and 2023.
the share of orders for items with 1,500-2,300 mg of sodium rose by more than the share of orders for items with less than 1,500 mg did.

explanation.passage: Brennard made chain restaurants put a warning icon on very salty items (over 2,300 mg). Park compared what people ordered before and after. The sentence says diners who stopped ordering the labeled items did NOT just move to the items right under the cutoff (1,500-2,300 mg). So the blank must show that labeled items dropped, the just-under-the-line items barely moved, and the lowest-sodium items picked up the difference.
choices: Correct. Labeled items fell 6 points (18% to 12%), the 1,500-2,300 mg items rose only 1 point (34% to 35%), and the lowest-sodium items rose 5 points (48% to 53%). That shows most of the shift went to the lowest-sodium items, not to items just below the threshold.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: going from 18% to 12% is a drop of one-third, not more than half. It also says nothing about where diners switched.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: 18% < 48% and 12% < 53%, but this doesn't say anything about where diners went after avoiding labeled items.
Incorrect. Reversal: the 1,500-2,300 mg share rose only 1 point, while the under-1,500 mg share rose 5 points.

passage.text: Many speakers of American English pronounce the vowels in words such as cot and caught identically, a pattern linguists call the cot-caught merger. Linguist Rachel Odom recorded speakers from four generations in a western Pennsylvania town where the merger was once rare. Because people who move away often pick up features of other dialects, Odom also noted whether each speaker had ever lived outside the region for at least a year.

figure.title: Speakers Who Merge the Vowels in Cot and Caught (%)

question: Based on the text and the table, Odom could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Having lived outside the region for at least a year is the main reason that speakers born in 2000-2009 adopted the cot-caught merger at a much higher rate than any of the earlier generations did.
In every generation, speakers who had never lived outside the region were more likely to merge the vowels than speakers who had lived elsewhere for a year or more, which suggests the merger is local.
Most speakers born in 1940-1959 who had lived outside the region merged the vowels in cot and caught.
Living outside the region was linked to much more merging among older speakers, but the merger appears to have spread among younger speakers largely regardless of whether they had lived elsewhere.

explanation.passage: The 'cot-caught merger' means saying cot and caught the same way. Odom studied four generations in a town where this used to be rare. She also checked whether people had lived somewhere else, because moving away might teach you the merger from other dialects. So for each generation, compare the two columns: how much difference does having lived elsewhere make, and does that difference change over time?
choices: Incorrect. This contradicts the table: among the youngest speakers, 81% of those who never left merged, almost the same as the 83% who had lived elsewhere. Moving away can't be the main reason.
Incorrect. Reversal: in every generation, those who had lived outside the region merged more often (for example, 31% vs. 12%).
Incorrect. This misreads the table: only 31% of these speakers merged the vowels, which is less than half.

Correct. For the two older generations, the gap is large: 19 points (31 vs. 12) and 17 points (44 vs. 27). For the younger ones, it shrinks to 5 (63 vs. 58) and 2 (83 vs. 81). So among younger people, the merger spread whether or not they had lived elsewhere.

passage.text: Psychologist Daniela Ruiz surveyed 2,400 first-year and fourth-year students at a large university, asking each how many hours per day they spent on social media and having each complete a standard questionnaire that measures loneliness on a scale from 0 to 60. Because average loneliness scores rose steadily with daily social media use in both groups of students, Ruiz suggests that spending more time on social media makes college students lonelier.

figure.title: Average Loneliness Score by Daily Social Media Use

question: Which consideration, if true, should make Ruiz most hesitant to rely on what the graph suggests about the effect of social media use on loneliness?
choices: Average loneliness scores rose with daily social media use among both first-year students and fourth-year students.
First-year students had slightly higher average loneliness scores than fourth-year students did at every level of daily social media use, from less than 1 hour a day to more than 4 hours a day.
In a follow-up survey, students who were already lonely at the start of the school year were more likely than other students to increase their social media use over the following months.
The loneliness questionnaire Ruiz used has been shown to give consistent results when the same people complete it twice a few weeks apart.

explanation.passage: Ruiz found that students who use social media more tend to be lonelier. She then claims a direction of cause: social media use CAUSES loneliness. But a link between two things can run the other way. The question asks what should make her hesitant, so look for evidence that something other than her proposed cause could produce the same pattern in the graph.
choices: Incorrect. This restates the pattern in the graph (22 to 38 and 20 to 35). It's the evidence Ruiz is relying on, not a reason to doubt it.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: the difference between first-year and fourth-year students doesn't affect whether social media use causes loneliness.

Correct. This suggests reverse causation: loneliness may lead students to use social media more, rather than social media making them lonely. That alternative explains the same graph, so Ruiz should be hesitant to conclude social media is the cause.
Incorrect. This would make Ruiz more confident, because it shows the loneliness measure is reliable.

passage.text: Microfinance lenders often make joint-liability loans: borrowers form a group, and if any member fails to repay, the entire group loses access to future loans. Such loans are typically repaid at higher rates than individual loans are. Economist Samuel Adeyemi hypothesized that this advantage arises mainly from peer monitoring—members keeping watch over one another's businesses—and should therefore be much larger when group members live in the same village and can easily observe one another.

figure.title: Loan Repayment Rates by Loan Type and Borrowers' Residence (%)
figure.note: For individual-liability loans, the columns compare borrowers recruited from a single village with borrowers recruited from several villages.

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Adeyemi's hypothesis?
choices: Joint-liability loans to groups of 5 had the highest repayment rate shown in the table, 97%, when members lived in the same village.

Joint-liability loans to groups of 5 were repaid at a rate 9 points higher than individual loans when borrowers lived in the same village but only 2 points higher when they lived in different villages.

Individual-liability loans had nearly identical repayment rates whether borrowers had been recruited from a single village (88%) or from several different villages (87%), a difference of only 1 percentage point.
When members lived in different villages, joint-liability loans to groups of 10 were repaid at a higher rate than joint-liability loans to groups of 5.

explanation.passage: In joint-liability lending, a group shares responsibility: if one person doesn't pay, nobody in the group gets another loan. Adeyemi thinks this works because members watch each other (peer monitoring). If he's right, the boost from joint liability (compared with individual loans) should be big when members live close together and small when they live apart. So you need a choice that compares the joint-liability advantage across the two residence columns.
choices: Incorrect. True but incomplete: 97% is the highest value, but this doesn't compare it to individual loans or to borrowers in different villages, so it doesn't show the advantage depends on living close together.

Correct. Same village: 97 - 88 = 9 points better. Different villages: 89 - 87 = 2 points better. The joint-liability advantage is much larger when members can watch one another, exactly what the peer-monitoring hypothesis predicts.

Incorrect. Half right: this shows that living in the same village doesn't help individual loans by itself, which is useful background, but it never shows that joint liability's advantage is larger among neighbors.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: in different villages, groups of 10 repaid at 88%, lower than the 89% for groups of 5.

passage.text: In early 2022, the city of Westbrook removed on-street parking along Garnet Avenue, a commercial street, and replaced it with protected bike lanes. Many Garnet Avenue merchants predicted that their sales would suffer because customers could no longer park in front of their shops. Urban planner Nadia Ferro later compiled retail sales data for Garnet Avenue and three similar commercial streets nearby. Ferro argues that the bike lanes increased retail sales on Garnet Avenue.

figure.title: Annual Retail Sales on Four Westbrook Streets

question: Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken Ferro's argument?
choices: Retail sales on Garnet Avenue rose from $41.2 million in 2021 to $45.3 million in 2023.
Retail sales on Birch Street, Cedar Road, and Elm Way, none of which received bike lanes, rose by 9% to 11%, about the same as on Garnet Avenue.
Garnet Avenue had higher retail sales than any of the other three streets in both 2021 and 2023.
Retail sales on Garnet Avenue fell after the bike lanes replaced on-street parking, just as the merchants on the street had predicted when the city removed their customers' parking.

explanation.passage: Westbrook swapped parking for bike lanes on Garnet Avenue. Merchants feared lower sales; Ferro argues the opposite, that the lanes RAISED sales. The other three streets didn't get bike lanes, so they show what probably would have happened to Garnet Avenue without the lanes. To weaken Ferro, look for evidence that Garnet's growth wasn't special.
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it's the evidence Ferro would point to. By itself it supports her rather than weakening her argument.
Correct. Streets without bike lanes grew 9-11%, and Garnet grew 10%, right in the middle. If sales rose just as much without bike lanes, the lanes probably weren't what raised Garnet's sales.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: Garnet's sales were the largest in both years (41.2 and 45.3), but that says nothing about whether the bike lanes caused a change.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: Garnet Avenue's sales rose 10%, so the merchants' prediction did not come true.

passage.text: Archaeologists often identify ancient feasts from animal bones. Feasting sites tend to contain a high proportion of young animals, which yield tender meat, and a high proportion of meat-rich bones such as upper limbs. By contrast, a place where animals were merely butchered and their meat carried elsewhere would be expected to contain mostly low-meat bones such as skulls and feet. At the Bronze Age site of Kerrow Hill, archaeologist Fiona MacLeod compared bones from a large ditched enclosure with bones from ordinary houses nearby.

figure.title: Animal Bones at Kerrow Hill
categories: Pig bones from animals under 1 year old
Cattle bones from animals under 2 years old

question: Based on the text and the graph, MacLeod could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: The enclosure was used for feasts attended only by the residents of the nearby houses.
Pigs and cattle were generally slaughtered at younger ages for meals eaten in the houses than for meals eaten in the enclosure, where older animals with more meat were preferred.
The bones in the enclosure are more consistent with meat being eaten there than with animals being butchered there and their meat carried elsewhere.
Cattle made up a larger share of the meat eaten at the enclosure than pigs did.

explanation.passage: The passage gives you a key for reading bones. Feasting sites: lots of young animals and lots of meat-rich bones. Butchering-only sites: mostly low-meat bones (skulls, feet), because the good cuts were carried away. MacLeod compared a big enclosure with ordinary houses. Apply the key to the graph: which pattern does the enclosure match?
choices: Incorrect. Outside the scope: the graph says nothing about who attended. Nothing in the text identifies the guests.
Incorrect. Reversal: the enclosure had higher shares of young animals (72% and 64%) than the houses did (38% and 35%).

Correct. 81% of the enclosure's bones came from meat-rich parts. A butchering-only site would have mostly low-meat bones, so the enclosure looks like a place where meat was eaten, not one where it was prepared and sent away.

Incorrect. Outside the scope: the graph gives the percent of pig bones that were young and the percent of cattle bones that were young. It doesn't say how many pig bones vs. cattle bones there were, so you can't compare how much of each animal was eaten.

passage.text: In 1851, the United States Congress sharply reduced the postage charged for mailing newspapers to subscribers. Historian Paul Harrington examined how the circulation of different kinds of newspapers in one northeastern state changed in the years that followed. Harrington argues that the rate cut especially benefited newspapers that depended on the mail to reach their subscribers. Supporting this argument, the table shows that ______

figure.title: Newspaper Circulation in One State, 1850 and 1855

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: circulation grew by roughly half for rural and religious weeklies, which were mostly mailed, but by less than 10% for city dailies, which mostly were not.
city dailies had a larger circulation than either rural weeklies or religious weeklies in both 1850 and 1855.
religious weeklies gained more readers between 1850 and 1855 than rural weeklies did.
circulation of city dailies declined between 1850 and 1855 as readers in the state switched to cheaper weekly newspapers delivered by mail after the rate cut took effect.

explanation.passage: In 1851, mailing newspapers got much cheaper. Harrington says this helped most the papers that relied on mail delivery. The table tells you which papers depended on the mail (the second column) and how circulation changed from 1850 to 1855. To support Harrington, you need to show that the mail-dependent papers grew much faster than the others.
choices: Correct. Rural weeklies grew from 120 to 174 (about 45%), religious weeklies from 64 to 98 (about 53%), and city dailies from 210 to 228 (about 9%). The mostly mailed papers (85% and 90%) grew far faster than the mostly unmailed dailies (15%).
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: city dailies were biggest in both years, but size doesn't show which kind of paper benefited most from the rate cut.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: religious weeklies gained 34 thousand readers (64 to 98), while rural weeklies gained 54 thousand (120 to 174).
Incorrect. This misreads the table: city dailies rose from 210 to 228 thousand; they did not decline.

passage.text: In 2023, the coffee chain Harbor Bean introduced a loyalty program with two tiers, Standard and Gold, that rewards members with free drinks. A year later, the chain's marketing director, Owen Castellano, compared the purchasing behavior of members and nonmembers. Pointing out that Gold members visited more than four times as often as nonmembers did, Castellano concluded that the loyalty program had greatly increased how often members visit the chain.

figure.title: Harbor Bean Customer Purchasing, 2024

question: Which consideration, if true, should make Castellano most hesitant to rely on what the table suggests is the effect of the loyalty program on how often members visit?
choices: Gold members spent more per visit, on average, than nonmembers did.
Harbor Bean did not change the prices of any of its drinks or food items between 2022, the year before the program began, and 2024.
Most nonmembers said in a survey that they had not heard of the loyalty program.
Only customers who had made at least 20 purchases in the six months before the program launched were invited to join it.

explanation.passage: Harbor Bean started a loyalty program, and a year later members were visiting far more often than nonmembers (14.1 visits a month for Gold vs. 3.4 for nonmembers). Castellano concludes the PROGRAM caused members to visit more. The question asks what should make him hesitant, so look for another reason members might visit more, one that would exist even without the program.
choices: Incorrect. This simply restates the table ($6.40 vs. $5.80), and it's about spending per visit, not how often people visit.
Incorrect. This removes one possible complication (price changes), so it would make Castellano more confident, not less.
Incorrect. This explains why some people didn't join, but it doesn't suggest members would have visited just as often without the program.

Correct. If only already-frequent customers could join, members were heavy visitors before the program began. Their high visit counts may reflect who was let in, not what the program did, so the table can't show the program's effect.

passage.text: Between 2019 and 2022, the share of American workers who did their jobs mostly from home rose dramatically. Demographer Kofi Mensah used change-of-address records to track residents moving out of the urban cores of large metropolitan areas, classifying each move by its destination. Citing Mensah's data, a journalist claimed that the shift to remote work set off a wave of moves from big-city cores to rural counties.

figure.title: Moves Out of Large-Metro Urban Cores by Destination
categories: Suburbs of the same metro area

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the journalist's claim is supported by data from the graph?
choices: It is strongly supported, because moves from urban cores to rural counties were more common in 2022 than in 2019.
It is not supported, because moves from urban cores to rural counties were less common in 2022 than in 2019.
It is strongly supported, because moves from urban cores to every type of destination shown, including rural counties, were more common in 2022 than they had been in 2019, before remote work spread.
It is weakly supported, because although moves to rural counties rose slightly, from 0.6 to 0.8 per 1,000 core residents, most of the increase in moves out of urban cores went to nearby suburbs.

explanation.passage: Remote work grew a lot from 2019 to 2022. Mensah tracked where people moved when they left big-city centers ('urban cores'). The journalist claims a 'wave' of moves to RURAL counties specifically. So you need to focus on the rural bars, and also ask whether the rural change is big compared with the other destinations. A 'wave' implies a large shift.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: rural moves did rise (0.6 to 0.8), but an increase of 0.2 per 1,000 residents is tiny, hardly a 'wave,' so 'strongly supported' goes too far.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph: rural moves rose from 0.6 to 0.8; they didn't fall.
Incorrect. Topic match, claim miss: moves did rise to every destination, but the claim is about a wave to rural counties, and the rural increase was the smallest by far.

Correct. Moves to suburbs rose by 3.7 (5.2 to 8.9), to smaller metros by 1.3 (2.1 to 3.4), and to rural counties by only 0.2 (0.6 to 0.8). Out of the total increase of 5.2, suburbs account for 3.7, which is most of it. So the data show a small rural increase, not a wave.

passage.text: Sleep researchers have found that teenagers' internal clocks shift later during adolescence, making early-morning classes especially difficult. In 2021, the Lakemont school district moved its high school start time from 7:20 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. Education researcher Brianna Cole compared class attendance before and after the change. Cole hypothesized that the later start would improve attendance mainly in first-period classes, with much smaller effects on attendance later in the day.

figure.title: Average Class Attendance at Lakemont High Schools (%)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Cole's hypothesis?
choices: First-period attendance rose by 9 percentage points, from 81% to 90%, while attendance in each of the other periods shown rose by 3 percentage points or less.
Seventh-period attendance was lower than fourth-period attendance in both the 2020-21 and 2022-23 school years.
Attendance rose in every class period shown after the district adopted the later start time.
Attendance in second period rose by more percentage points than attendance in first period did after the Lakemont district moved its start time from 7:20 a.m. to 8:30 a.m.

explanation.passage: Teens' body clocks run late, so very early classes are hard for them. Lakemont pushed the school start time later, and Cole predicted attendance would improve MAINLY in first period, with only small changes in later periods. To support that, you need two things: a big jump in first period and small changes everywhere else.
choices: Correct. First period went from 81% to 90% (up 9 points), while second rose 3 points (89 to 92), fourth rose 1 (91 to 92), and seventh rose 1 (88 to 89). That's exactly the 'mainly first period' pattern Cole predicted.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: seventh period was below fourth in both years (88 vs. 91, 89 vs. 92), but this doesn't compare before and after the change.
Incorrect. Half right: every period did rise, but this doesn't show that first period rose much more than the others, which is the heart of Cole's hypothesis.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: second period rose 3 points, while first period rose 9.

passage.text: The bystander effect is the tendency for individuals to be less likely to help someone in need when other people are present, perhaps because each person feels less personally responsible. Psychologists Ana Petrova and Michael Tran tested whether the effect occurs online. Participants joined chat groups of different sizes, in which a user posted a request for help with a computer problem; in some groups, members' real names were displayed, while in others members were anonymous. Petrova and Tran hypothesized that the bystander effect appears online even when people can be identified by name.

figure.title: Participants Who Responded to a Request for Help (%)

question: Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken Petrova and Tran's hypothesis?
choices: When members were anonymous, the share of participants who responded fell from 64% in groups of 2 to 18% in groups of 20.
When members' names were displayed, about 70% of participants responded regardless of group size, with the share ranging only from 68% to 71%.
In every group size, participants whose names were displayed responded more often than anonymous participants did.
When members' names were displayed, the share of participants who responded fell more sharply as group size increased than it did when members were anonymous.

explanation.passage: The bystander effect means people help less when there are more people around. Petrova and Tran ran online chat groups of different sizes, sometimes with names shown and sometimes anonymous. Their hypothesis is narrow: the effect still appears even when NAMES ARE DISPLAYED. To weaken it, look at the 'names displayed' column alone and ask: does helping drop as the group gets bigger?
choices: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it's about anonymous groups, where the bystander effect clearly appears. It doesn't address the hypothesis, which is about groups with names displayed.
Correct. With names shown, helping stays basically flat (71, 69, 68, 70) whether there are 2 people or 20. No drop with group size means no bystander effect, which goes against the hypothesis.

Incorrect. True but irrelevant: named participants did help more at every size, but the hypothesis is about whether helping falls as the group grows, not about named vs. anonymous helping rates at a given size.
Incorrect. Reversal: with names shown, helping barely changed (71% to 70%), while with anonymity it fell sharply (64% to 18%).

passage.text: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5)—airborne particles less than 2.5 micrometers across—can penetrate deep into the lungs. Epidemiologist Rhea Kapoor analyzed five years of hospital records in the city of Port Calder, sorting days by their PM2.5 level and counting children's emergency room visits for asthma on each day. Because visits rose with PM2.5 levels in both summer and winter, Kapoor concluded that higher PM2.5 levels cause more children to need emergency treatment for asthma.

figure.title: Children's Asthma Emergency Visits in Port Calder by PM2.5 Level

question: Which consideration, if true, should make Kapoor most hesitant to rely on what the graph suggests about the effect of PM2.5 on children's asthma?
choices: At every PM2.5 level, children's asthma emergency visits were more frequent on winter days than on summer days.
Studies in several other cities have also found that children's asthma emergency visits increase on days when PM2.5 levels in the air are high, in both summer and winter.
In Port Calder, PM2.5 levels are highest on days with stagnant air, which also traps ground-level ozone, a gas known to trigger asthma attacks.
On summer days, children's asthma emergency visits were nearly twice as frequent at high PM2.5 levels as at low PM2.5 levels.

explanation.passage: PM2.5 means tiny particles in the air. Kapoor found that on days with more of these particles, more children went to the emergency room for asthma, in both summer and winter. She concludes the particles CAUSE the extra visits. To make her hesitant, you need something else that goes up on the same days as PM2.5 and could itself cause asthma attacks.
choices: Incorrect. True but irrelevant: winter visits were higher at every level (for example, 4.8 vs. 3.1), but that's a seasonal difference, not a reason to doubt that PM2.5 drives the rise within each season.
Incorrect. This would make Kapoor more confident, since her result matches other cities.

Correct. If high-PM2.5 days are also high-ozone days, and ozone triggers asthma, then ozone could be causing some or all of the extra visits. The graph can't separate the two, so Kapoor shouldn't rely on it to show PM2.5 is the cause.
Incorrect. This restates the graph (6.0 is nearly double 3.1). It's part of Kapoor's evidence, not a reason to doubt it.

passage.text: When a school for deaf children opened in the coastal region of Marisco in 1978, the students, who had previously had little contact with one another, began creating a new sign language; the school's hearing teachers did not use sign language at all. Linguist Hannah Weiss studied one grammatical device that emerged: spatial modulation, in which a signer moves a verb sign through space to show who did what to whom. Weiss grouped signers by when they entered the school and by their age when they first entered.

figure.title: Verbs Produced with Spatial Modulation by Marisco Signers (%)
columns: Entered school at age 10 or older

question: Based on the text and the table, Weiss could most reasonably draw which conclusion?
choices: Spatial modulation became more common with each new group of students mainly among signers who began learning the language as young children.
Signers who entered the school at age 10 or older did not use spatial modulation in any of the three groups.
In the first group, signers who entered the school before age 10 used spatial modulation more than twice as often as signers who entered later did.
Spatial modulation became more common in later groups because the school's teachers began teaching it to new students.

explanation.passage: Deaf children at a new school invented their own sign language, without help from teachers, who didn't sign. Weiss tracked one grammar feature, spatial modulation (moving a sign through space to show who did what to whom). She sorted students by which group they entered with and whether they arrived young (before 10) or older. Read the table both down (over time) and across (young vs. older) to see where the feature grew.
choices: Correct. Among students who arrived young, use jumped from 14% to 46% to 71%. Among students who arrived at 10 or older, it rose only from 12% to 18% to 22%. So the growth over time happened mainly among those who learned as young children.
Incorrect. Too strong: older entrants did use the device (12%, 18%, 22%), just much less often.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: in the first group, the rates were 14% and 12%, nearly the same, not more than double.
Incorrect. This contradicts the text, which says the school's teachers did not use sign language at all, so they could not have taught the device.

passage.text: In February 2018, the country of Valdoria imposed a 25 percent tariff—a tax on imports—on washing machines made abroad, while washing machines made in Valdoria were not taxed. Economist Mei Lin Zhou tracked average retail prices of several household appliances over the following year. A commentator who supported the tariff claimed that it raised the prices only of imported washing machines and that Valdorian manufacturers, facing no tax, kept their prices unchanged.

figure.title: Average Retail Prices of Household Appliances in Valdoria

question: Which choice best describes the extent to which the commentator's claim is supported by data from the table?
choices: It is supported, because the average price of imported washing machines, which were subject to the tariff, rose by a larger percentage than the average price of Valdorian-made washing machines did over the same year.
It is supported, because dishwashers and refrigerators, which were not subject to the tariff, also rose in price between January 2018 and January 2019.

It is not supported, because the average price of Valdorian-made washing machines rose by 15%, nearly as much as that of imported ones, while appliances not related to the tariff rose by only 1% to 2%.
It is not supported, because the average price of Valdorian-made washing machines rose by more than the average price of imported washing machines did.

explanation.passage: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Valdoria taxed foreign-made washing machines but not ones made at home. The commentator makes two claims: only imported washers got pricier, and domestic washers stayed the SAME price. Dishwashers and refrigerators act as a check: since they weren't affected by the tariff, they show how much prices rose for other reasons, like general inflation.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: imported washers did rise more (18% vs. 15%), but the commentator said domestic prices didn't change at all, and they rose 15%.
Incorrect. This doesn't support the claim. Dishwashers and refrigerators barely rose (2% and 1%), which shows that general price increases can't explain why domestic washers went up 15%.

Correct. Valdorian washers went from $610 to $701 (+15%), which contradicts 'kept their prices unchanged.' And because untaxed dishwashers and refrigerators rose only 1-2%, the jump in domestic washer prices isn't just ordinary inflation. Domestic makers apparently raised prices alongside the taxed imports.
Incorrect. Right verdict, wrong reason: Valdorian-made washers rose 15%, less than imported washers' 18%, not more.

passage.text: Food riots were frequent in eighteenth-century France, and historians have usually linked them to high grain prices. Historian Isabelle Fournier proposes a refinement: riots were driven less by how high prices were than by how suddenly they had risen, since people could adjust to prices that were high but familiar. Fournier classified the years 1750-1789 by the price of wheat and by whether that price followed a sharp rise from the previous year, and she calculated the average number of recorded food riots per year in each category.

figure.title: Average Food Riots per Year in France, 1750-1789
categories: Moderate prices after a sharp rise
High prices after a sharp rise

question: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support Fournier's proposal?
choices: In both the Paris region and the provinces, years with high prices after a sharp rise averaged more riots than any other type of year, with more than 14 riots per year in each region.
In every type of year, the provinces averaged more riots per year than the Paris region did.
In the Paris region, years with high, stable prices averaged fewer riots than years with moderate, stable prices did.
In both the Paris region and the provinces, years with moderate prices after a sharp rise averaged about three times as many riots as years with high, stable prices did.

explanation.passage: Most historians say high bread prices caused French food riots. Fournier says it's really SUDDEN price jumps that matter, not high prices themselves, because people get used to prices that stay high. The cleanest test of her idea compares a year with a lower price but a sudden jump against a year with a higher price but no jump. If the sudden-jump years have more riots, the jump matters more than the price level.
choices: Incorrect. Half right: this is true (14.1 and 17.3 are the highest), but those years had both high prices and a sharp rise, so the result fits the traditional 'high prices' view just as well. It can't show that suddenness matters more.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: the provinces did have more riots in every category, but that compares regions, not price patterns.
Incorrect. This misreads the graph: in Paris, high stable years averaged 3.2 riots, more than the 1.8 in moderate stable years.

Correct. Paris: 9.6 vs. 3.2 (3.0 times). Provinces: 11.8 vs. 4.1 (about 2.9 times). Years with LOWER prices but a sudden rise had about three times as many riots as years with HIGHER but stable prices, showing that suddenness mattered more than price level.

passage.text: According to the left-digit effect, shoppers pay disproportionate attention to the first digit of a price, so that $19.99 seems much cheaper than $20.00 even though the difference is only one cent. Marketing researcher Carla Benítez tested this idea by randomly showing visitors to an online bookstore one of four prices for the same hardcover book. Her results were consistent with the left-digit effect: ______

figure.title: Weekly Sales of a Hardcover Book at Four Prices

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: the $19.00 price produced the most copies sold per week of any price that Benítez tested.
a one-cent cut, from $20.00 to $19.99, raised weekly sales by 86 copies, whereas a further 49-cent cut, to $19.50, raised weekly sales by only 7 more copies.
weekly revenue was higher at the $19.00 price than at any of the other three prices Benítez tested.
each successive reduction in the price of the book, from $20.00 down to $19.00, increased weekly sales by roughly the same number of copies as the reduction before it.

explanation.passage: The left-digit effect says we focus on the first digit of a price. To shoppers, $19.99 'starts with 19,' so it feels much cheaper than $20.00, even though it's just one cent less. Benítez tried four prices for the same book. To show this effect, you need evidence that the one-cent change that switches the first digits (20 to 19) made a much bigger difference than other, larger price cuts that don't.
choices: Incorrect. True but irrelevant: $19.00 did sell the most (520), but you'd expect the lowest price to sell the most even without any left-digit effect.

Correct. A 1-cent cut that changed the first digits raised sales from 412 to 498 (86 more copies). A much bigger 49-cent cut that left them at '19' raised sales only from 498 to 505 (7 more). The tiny cut had a far bigger effect, which is exactly what the left-digit effect predicts.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: revenue at $19.00 was $9,880, less than the $9,955 at $19.99.
Incorrect. This misreads the table: the increases were 86, then 7, then 15 copies, which are far from equal.

passage.text: Shell middens—ancient heaps of discarded shells—record what coastal peoples gathered to eat. At Punta Verde, archaeologist Javier Robles excavated a midden whose layers span 2,000 years. Over that period, mussel shells became less common and smaller, while shells of small sea snails, which provide far less meat per shell, became more common. Robles argues that a growing human population overharvested the local mussel beds, removing large mussels faster than they could be replaced and forcing people to turn to less rewarding snails.

figure.title: Shells in the Punta Verde Midden by Layer

question: Which consideration, if true, should make Robles most hesitant to rely on what the table suggests about human overharvesting of mussels at Punta Verde?
choices: Sediment cores show that nearby coastal waters grew steadily warmer between 5,000 and 3,000 years ago, and in warmer water mussels grow more slowly, stay smaller, and become scarcer.
The average length of mussel shells at Punta Verde was smaller in each layer than in the layer beneath it.
At Punta Verde, both mussels and small sea snails were gathered by hand from the same intertidal rocks.
Studies at several other coastal sites have found that heavy human harvesting reduces both the abundance and the average size of the shellfish that people collect from intertidal beds.

explanation.passage: A shell midden is basically an ancient trash pile of shells. At Punta Verde, the older layers are full of big mussels, and the newer layers have fewer, smaller mussels and more tiny snails. Robles blames people: a growing population ate the mussels faster than they could regrow. To make him hesitant, look for a different cause that could produce the same pattern (fewer and smaller mussels) without overharvesting.
choices: Correct. Warming water would make mussels smaller and scarcer on its own, producing the same pattern in the table (78% to 31% mussels; 64 mm to 45 mm long). So the table can't tell overharvesting apart from climate change.
Incorrect. This restates the table (64, 58, 51, 45 mm). It's part of Robles's evidence, not a reason to doubt it.
Incorrect. True but irrelevant: gathering both from the same rocks doesn't offer another explanation for why mussels declined.
Incorrect. This would make Robles more confident, because it shows overharvesting really can shrink shellfish sizes.

intro: The following text is adapted from Jane Austen's 1815 novel *Emma*. Emma Woodhouse's former governess, Miss Taylor, has recently married a neighbor, Mr. Weston.

passage.text: Emma had always considered herself the author of Miss Taylor's happiness. It was true that Mr. Weston had admired Miss Taylor for some time before Emma had thought of the match, and true that the two had met at a dozen dinners to which Emma had not contributed so much as a suggestion; but she had once remarked, on a wet afternoon four years before, that they would suit each other very well, and from that remark, in her own reckoning, everything else had followed. Success of this kind, she felt, was not to be wasted, and she resolved to bestow the same favor upon her neighbors at the earliest opportunity.

question: Which choice best describes how Emma is presented in the text?
choices: The narrator wryly suggests that Emma credits herself with an outcome she did little to bring about.
The narrator indicates that Emma is eager to arrange marriages for her neighbors despite a history of failed attempts.
The narrator portrays Emma as modest about a matchmaking talent that others in her circle readily acknowledge.
The narrator suggests that Emma regrets an offhand remark that later had consequences she did not intend.

explanation.passage: Emma believes she caused (“was the author of”) Miss Taylor's happy marriage. The long middle sentence quietly undercuts her: Mr. Weston already admired Miss Taylor before Emma thought of the match, and the couple met many times without Emma's help. Emma's only contribution was one remark made four years earlier, yet “in her own reckoning” (that is, in her own private calculation) everything followed from it. The last sentence shows her planning to “bestow the same favor” on others. The question asks for the narrator's attitude toward Emma, and the clue is the gap between what Emma believes and what the narrator tells us actually happened: the narrator is gently poking fun at her (gentle irony).
choices: Correct. The narrator lists facts showing the match happened without Emma (Mr. Weston's earlier admiration, the dinners she did not arrange) and then says that only “in her own reckoning” did everything follow from her one remark. “Wryly” captures this dry, amused tone, and “did little to bring about” matches the evidence.

Incorrect. This is half right. Emma is eager to arrange more matches (she “resolved to bestow the same favor upon her neighbors”), but nothing in the text mentions earlier failed attempts. In fact Emma considers herself successful.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Emma is the opposite of modest: she calls herself “the author” of the marriage. The text also never says that anyone else recognizes her talent.

Incorrect. Emma does not regret the remark; she is proud of it and treats it as the cause of a success. The outcome (a happy marriage) is exactly what she would have wanted, so “consequences she did not intend” does not fit.

intro: The following text is adapted from Charles Dickens's 1861 novel *Great Expectations*. The narrator, Pip, now a young gentleman living in London, recalls learning that Joe Gargery, the blacksmith who helped raise him in a country village, is coming to visit.

passage.text: Let me confess exactly with what feelings I looked forward to Joe's coming. Not with pleasure, though I was bound to him by so many ties; no, with considerable disturbance, some mortification, and a keen sense of incongruity. If I could have kept him away by paying money, I certainly would have paid money. My greatest reassurance was that he was coming to my rooms in Barnard's Inn and not to Hammersmith, where Bentley Drummle, whom I held in contempt, might have seen him. I have had little cause, throughout life, to be proud of the feelings of that morning.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about his younger self?
choices: He dreaded Joe's visit mainly because he expected Joe to ask him for money.
He resented Joe for choosing to visit him at Barnard's Inn rather than at Hammersmith.
He was embarrassed by the prospect of Joe's visit and now views that embarrassment as shameful.
He longed to see Joe again but feared that his fashionable London acquaintances would mock Joe's manners.

explanation.passage: An older Pip looks back on how he felt, as a young man, about a visit from Joe, the kind blacksmith who raised him. He admits he felt “disturbance,” “mortification” (embarrassment or humiliation), and a sense of “incongruity” (Joe did not fit his new gentleman's life). He would even have paid money to keep Joe away, and he was relieved that Drummle, a man he looked down on, would not see Joe. The last sentence is the key: “I have had little cause... to be proud of the feelings of that morning.” So the question asks you to combine two things: how young Pip felt (embarrassed) and how older Pip judges that feeling (ashamed of it).
choices: Incorrect. This reverses the money detail. Pip says he would have paid money to keep Joe away; nothing suggests Joe wanted money from him.
Incorrect. Pip says the opposite: his “greatest reassurance” was that Joe was coming to Barnard's Inn and not to Hammersmith, where Drummle might see him. He was relieved, not resentful.

Correct. Words such as “mortification” and the wish to pay to keep Joe away show young Pip's embarrassment, and “I have had little cause... to be proud of the feelings of that morning” shows the older narrator judging those feelings harshly. This answer captures both layers.
Incorrect. This is half right. Pip does worry about being seen with Joe (Drummle), but he explicitly says he looked forward to the visit “Not with pleasure,” so he did not long to see Joe.

intro: The following text is adapted from George Eliot's 1871-72 novel *Middlemarch*. Dorothea Brooke, a young woman eager for a life of serious purpose, has spent an evening talking with Mr. Casaubon, a much older clergyman and scholar.

passage.text: Dorothea had listened to Mr. Casaubon for an hour, and every remark he made seemed to her to open some vast corridor of learning. That his remarks were in fact rather few, and that the greater part of them concerned the dampness of his library, did nothing to lessen the impression; her own ardent imagination supplied whatever his sentences omitted. Here, she thought, was a mind that held the whole of the past, and that might, if she were patient and humble enough, admit her to some small part of it. It did not occur to her that the corridors might be dim, or that their owner had long since lost his way in them.

question: Which choice best describes how Dorothea is presented in the text?
choices: The narrator mocks Dorothea for pretending to admire a man whose learning she privately doubts.
The narrator suggests that Dorothea's admiration for Mr. Casaubon owes more to her own hopes than to anything he has said.
The narrator portrays Dorothea as an accomplished scholar who is quick to recognize the limits of Mr. Casaubon's knowledge.
The narrator emphasizes Dorothea's growing impatience with Mr. Casaubon's dull remarks about practical matters.

explanation.passage: Dorothea is deeply impressed by Mr. Casaubon, but the narrator lets us see more than she does. His remarks were “rather few” and mostly about his damp library, yet her “ardent” (passionate, eager) imagination “supplied whatever his sentences omitted.” In other words, she fills in the gaps herself. The final sentence extends the “corridor” image to hint that his learning may be “dim” and that he himself is lost in it. The question asks how Dorothea is presented, so look for an answer that explains where her admiration really comes from.
choices: Incorrect. Dorothea is not pretending; her admiration is sincere. The text says “It did not occur to her” that his learning might be weak, so she has no private doubts.

Correct. The narrator states that Mr. Casaubon said little of substance and that Dorothea's “own ardent imagination supplied whatever his sentences omitted.” Her admiration comes from her own eager hopes (to be admitted to a great mind), not from his words.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Dorothea sees herself as needing to be “patient and humble” to learn from him, and she fails to notice his limits; it is the narrator, not Dorothea, who hints at them.

Incorrect. This is a topic match with the wrong claim. The text does mention his remarks about “the dampness of his library,” but it says these remarks “did nothing to lessen the impression”; Dorothea is enchanted, not impatient.

intro: The following text is adapted from Edith Wharton's 1905 novel *The House of Mirth*. Lily Bart, a beautiful young woman with little money of her own, is a guest at a wealthy family's country house.

passage.text: Lily went up to her room that night with the pleasant fatigue of one who has been admired all day. The great house closed about her like a jewel case; the carpets swallowed her footsteps, and a maid had already laid out her dressing gown. Yet as she sat before the glass, she found herself counting: the three hundred dollars lost at bridge, the dress she had ordered in town, the tips the servants would expect when she left. Her reflection gave back the face that had won her the evening, and she studied it as a merchant studies his stock, wondering how long it would keep its value.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about Lily?
choices: She regrets having lost money at bridge and privately resolves to give up the game before she leaves the house.
She feels out of place among her wealthy hosts, who treat her more like a servant than a welcome guest.
She is confident that her beauty will continue to secure her a comfortable place in wealthy society.
Her pleasure in the evening is shadowed by worry that her position depends on resources that may not last.

explanation.passage: The passage begins with Lily enjoying luxury and admiration. The word “Yet” signals a turn: alone at her mirror, she starts adding up her expenses (gambling losses, a dress, tips for servants). Then comes the key comparison: she studies her face “as a merchant studies his stock, wondering how long it would keep its value.” A merchant's stock is something to be sold, so Lily sees her beauty as her main asset for staying in this rich world, and she worries it will fade. The question asks for what the narrator suggests about her, which means combining the pleasant surface with the worry underneath.
choices: Incorrect. Lily does count the “three hundred dollars lost at bridge,” but the text never says she regrets it or resolves to stop playing. This adds a decision that is outside the passage.
Incorrect. The text shows the opposite: she “has been admired all day,” and a maid has laid out her dressing gown for her. Nothing suggests her hosts treat her like a servant.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Lily is “wondering how long it would keep its value,” which shows doubt, not confidence, about how long her beauty will serve her.

Correct. The “pleasant fatigue” of being admired is followed by “Yet... she found herself counting” her debts and by her merchant-like study of her face, “wondering how long it would keep its value.” Her beauty is a resource that may not last, and her money worries show her position is fragile.

intro: The following text is adapted from Kate Chopin's 1899 novel *The Awakening*. All summer, Edna Pontellier has tried and failed to learn to swim. One night she finally swims on her own while friends look on.

passage.text: That night Edna was like the little tottering, stumbling child who of a sudden realizes its powers, and walks for the first time alone, boldly and with overconfidence. She could have shouted for joy. A feeling of exultation overtook her, as if some power of significant import had been given her to control the working of her body and her soul. She grew daring and reckless, overestimating her strength. She wanted to swim far out, where no woman had swum before.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about Edna?
choices: She is frightened to discover how far from the shore she has drifted.
Her first success gives her an exhilarating sense of power that the narrator implies is partly misjudged.
She is determined to prove to the friends watching her that she has finally become a stronger swimmer than any of them.
She is embarrassed that her first attempts in the water looked as clumsy as a child's.

explanation.passage: Edna has finally learned to swim. The narrator compares her to a toddler walking alone for the first time, “boldly and with overconfidence.” She feels “exultation” (intense joy and triumph) and a new sense of control over “her body and her soul.” But notice the warning words: “overconfidence,” “reckless,” “overestimating her strength.” The question asks what the narrator suggests about Edna, so the best answer must capture both her thrill and the narrator's hint that her confidence goes beyond her real ability.
choices: Incorrect. Nothing in the passage shows fear. Edna “could have shouted for joy” and “wanted to swim far out,” the opposite of being frightened.

Correct. “Exultation” and the sense of a new power to “control the working of her body and her soul” show the thrill; “overconfidence” and “overestimating her strength” show the narrator signaling that her confidence is partly mistaken.
Incorrect. Her friends are mentioned only in the intro, and she wants to swim “where no woman had swum before,” not to beat her friends. Competing with them is outside the passage.
Incorrect. This misreads the comparison. The child image is about the joy of a first independent success, not about embarrassment; Edna feels triumphant, not ashamed.

intro: The following text is adapted from Willa Cather's 1918 novel *My Antonia*. The narrator, Jim Burden, recalls arriving at night, as a ten-year-old orphan, at his grandparents' farm on the Nebraska prairie.

passage.text: There seemed to be nothing to see; no fences, no creeks or trees, no hills or fields. If there was a road, I could not make it out in the faint starlight. There was nothing but land: not a country at all, but the material out of which countries are made. I had the feeling that the world was left behind, that we had got over the edge of it, and were outside man's jurisdiction. Between that earth and that sky I felt erased, blotted out. I did not say my prayers that night: here, I felt, what would be would be.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about his feelings that night?
choices: The emptiness of the land made him feel so insignificant that he surrendered any sense of control over what would happen to him.
The strangeness of the dark land frightened him so much that he prayed that night to be returned to the familiar home he had left behind.
The openness of the land excited him, since he saw in it a chance to build a new life free of others' rules.
The bareness of the land made him resent his grandparents for bringing him to a place without towns or neighbors.

explanation.passage: Young Jim looks out at the prairie and sees nothing he recognizes: no fences, trees, roads, or fields. He calls it “the material out of which countries are made,” meaning it is raw, unshaped land. He feels he has gone “over the edge” of the world and “outside man's jurisdiction” (beyond the reach of human rules and authority).
