He feels “erased, blotted out,” and he skips his prayers because “what would be would be.” The question asks about his feelings, so focus on “erased” (he feels tiny, almost nonexistent) and on his giving up prayer (he accepts that he cannot influence what happens).
choices: Correct. “I felt erased, blotted out” shows how insignificant he felt, and “I did not say my prayers that night: here, I felt, what would be would be” shows him giving up any attempt to influence his fate.
Incorrect. This is a reversal: the narrator explicitly says “I did not say my prayers that night.” He also never expresses a wish to go back.
Incorrect. “Outside man's jurisdiction” might sound like freedom, but the surrounding words (“erased, blotted out”) show he felt diminished, not excited. Building a new life is outside the passage.
Incorrect. His grandparents are mentioned only in the intro, and the narrator never blames them. Resentment is not shown anywhere in the passage.

intro: The following text is adapted from Paul Laurence Dunbar's 1899 poem “Sympathy.”

passage.text:
I know why the caged bird sings, ah me,
When his wing is bruised and his bosom sore,
When he beats his bars and he would be free;
It is not a carol of joy or glee,
But a prayer that he sends from his heart's deep core,
But a plea, that upward to Heaven he flings;
I know why the caged bird sings!

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker describes a bird that has learned to find contentment despite its captivity.
The speaker contrasts the beauty of the outdoors in spring with the harshness of winter.
The speaker regrets having caged a bird whose song he once mistook for an expression of contentment and joy.
The speaker claims to understand that a captive's song expresses longing for freedom rather than happiness.

explanation.passage: The poem has two stanzas. In the first, the speaker imagines a caged bird watching a beautiful spring scene (sunny slopes, soft wind, a clear river) that it cannot reach, and says, “I know what the caged bird feels.” In the second, the bird is bruised from beating against its bars, and the speaker explains its song: “It is not a carol of joy or glee, / But a prayer... a plea.” A “carol” is a joyful song. So the main idea is that the bird's song, which listeners might assume is happy, is really a cry for freedom, and the speaker says he understands this (“I know”). The repeated “I know” also hints that the speaker feels trapped too, which is where the title “Sympathy” comes from.
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. The bird “beats his bars,” is “bruised” and “sore,” and “would be free”; it has not found contentment.
Incorrect. The first stanza does describe a spring landscape, but there is no winter in the poem. The contrast is between the free world outside and the bird's cage.

Incorrect. The speaker never says he caged the bird or that he once misunderstood its song. “I know” presents him as someone who understands, not someone who regrets a mistake. This adds a story that is outside the poem.

Correct. The speaker repeats “I know why the caged bird sings” and explains that the song “is not a carol of joy or glee, / But a prayer... a plea” from a bird that “would be free.” The song expresses longing, not happiness.

intro: The following text is adapted from Charles W. Chesnutt's 1898 short story “The Wife of His Youth.” Mr. Ryder, a respected leader of a social club in a Northern city, is preparing a toast for a ball he will host that evening.

passage.text: Mr. Ryder had selected his quotations with care. He opened his Tennyson to “A Dream of Fair Women” and read the lines aloud to the empty parlor, pausing after each to judge its effect upon an audience that had not yet arrived. He had been, he reflected, a fortunate man: he had come to the city with nothing, had made his way by industry, and now kept a house whose furnishings were the envy of the club. If he was a little proud of these things, it was a pride he believed he had fairly earned, and he could not see that it did anyone any harm.

question: Which choice best describes how Mr. Ryder is presented in the text?
choices: As a man whose financial success has made him arrogant enough to openly scorn those who are less fortunate.
As a man who secretly feels unworthy of the comfortable position he has achieved in the city.
As a man who takes a complacent pride in his achievements, which the narrator treats with mild irony.
As a man more devoted to reading poetry than to the practical affairs of his household and club.

explanation.passage: Mr. Ryder rehearses his toast by reading poetry aloud to an empty room and imagining an audience's reaction. He then reflects on his life: he started with nothing, worked hard, and now owns a house the other club members envy. The final sentence is told from inside his own head: he admits he is “a little proud” but believes the pride is earned and “could not see that it did anyone any harm.” The phrase “he could not see” is a quiet signal from the narrator that there may be something he is missing. The question asks how he is presented, so you need both his attitude (self-satisfied) and the narrator's slightly ironic distance from it. “Complacent” means pleased with oneself in an uncritical way.
choices: Incorrect. This is too strong. Mr. Ryder is proud, but the passage never shows him openly scorning anyone; he believes his pride does no “harm.”
Incorrect. This is a reversal. He calls himself “a fortunate man” who “fairly earned” his pride, so he does not feel unworthy.

Correct. He reflects with satisfaction on his rise and his envied house, and he “could not see that it did anyone any harm.” The comic detail of performing for an absent audience and the phrase “he could not see” show the narrator's gentle irony toward his self-satisfaction.

Incorrect. This is a topic match with the wrong claim. He does read Tennyson, but only to prepare a toast for his own ball, and he is proud of his house's furnishings, so he is clearly not neglecting practical affairs.

intro: The following text is adapted from Thomas Hardy's 1874 novel *Far from the Madding Crowd*. The narrator is introducing Gabriel Oak, a young farmer.

passage.text: On working days he was a young man of sound judgment, easy motions, proper dress, and general good character. On Sundays he was a man of misty views, rather given to postponing, and hampered by his best clothes and umbrella: upon the whole, one who felt himself to occupy, morally, that vast middle space of lukewarm neutrality which lay between the devout people of the parish and the drunken section; that is, he went to church, but yawned privately by the time the congregation reached the creed, and thought of what there would be for dinner when he meant to be listening to the sermon.

question: Which choice best describes how Gabriel Oak is presented in the text?
choices: The narrator affectionately suggests that Oak is far more at ease in his everyday work than on the formal occasion of Sunday.
The narrator criticizes Oak for neglecting his religious duties in favor of joining the drunken section of the parish.
The narrator portrays Oak as a man whose judgment and habits are unreliable in nearly all circumstances.
The narrator suggests that Oak deliberately conceals his true religious opinions in order to win the approval of his neighbors in the parish.

explanation.passage: The narrator describes Oak in two settings. On working days he is sensible, moves easily, dresses properly, and has good character. On Sundays he becomes vague (“misty views”), puts things off, and is “hampered” (held back, made awkward) by his best clothes and umbrella. Morally he sits in the “middle space” between very religious people and drinkers: he goes to church but yawns and thinks about dinner. The tone is warm and amused rather than harsh. The question asks how Oak is presented, so look for the contrast between his two “selves” and the narrator's friendly tone.
choices: Correct. The contrast between “sound judgment, easy motions” on working days and being “hampered by his best clothes and umbrella” on Sundays shows he is more comfortable at work. Small comic details, like yawning at the creed and thinking of dinner, show the narrator's affection rather than scorn.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Oak sits “between the devout people of the parish and the drunken section,” so he is not one of the drinkers, and he does go to church.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The narrator praises his “sound judgment” and “general good character” on working days; only on Sundays is he vague.
Incorrect. “Misty views” means his opinions are vague, not hidden. Nothing suggests he is concealing anything or trying to win approval; this is outside the passage.

intro: The following text is adapted from Elizabeth Gaskell's 1853 novel *Cranford*. The narrator is describing the women who make up most of the respectable households of Cranford, a small English town.

passage.text: Their dress is very independent of fashion; as they observe, “What does it signify how we dress here at Cranford, where everybody knows us?” And if they go from home, their reason is equally convincing: “What does it signify how we dress here, where nobody knows us?” The materials of their clothes are, in general, good and plain, and most of them are as careful with them as if each gown were expected to outlast its owner.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about the women of Cranford?
choices: They take great care with their appearance whenever they travel, hoping to impress strangers.
They defend their indifference to fashion with reasoning that is amusingly convenient.
They are embarrassed that they cannot afford the fashionable clothing worn in larger towns.
They openly disapprove of women elsewhere who spend their money on fashionable dress.

explanation.passage: The narrator explains that the Cranford ladies ignore fashion. At home, they say it does not matter how they dress because “everybody knows us.” Away from home, they say it does not matter because “nobody knows us.” Notice that these two reasons are opposites, yet both lead to the same conclusion. The narrator calls the second reason “equally convincing,” which is said with a straight face but is clearly a joke. The question asks what the narrator suggests about the women, so think about the tone: affectionate teasing about how they can always find a reason to do what they wanted anyway.
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. When they “go from home,” they say, “What does it signify how we dress here, where nobody knows us?” They do not dress up to impress strangers.

Correct. The women use opposite reasons (“everybody knows us” and “nobody knows us”) to reach the same conclusion, and the narrator's comment that the second reason is “equally convincing” gently mocks how conveniently their logic works.
Incorrect. The text never mentions what they can afford or any embarrassment. Their clothes are “good and plain,” and they speak confidently, not with shame. This is outside the passage.
Incorrect. The women talk only about their own dress; they never comment on other women. Disapproval of others is outside the passage.

intro: The following text is adapted from Rabindranath Tagore's 1916 novel *The Home and the World*, translated by Surendranath Tagore in 1919. Bimala, the narrator, recalls the early years of her marriage to Nikhil, a wealthy landowner. In his family, as was customary, the women lived in separate inner rooms of the house.

passage.text: My husband was not content that I should remain within the inner rooms, as the women of his family always had. “You have made a whole world out of this little corner,” he would say, “but I would have you come out into the larger world and meet it as it is. Then, if you still choose me, I shall know that you have truly chosen.” I laughed at him. What did I want with any world beyond my devotion to him? Yet I see now that he was offering me something I did not yet know how to want, and that his gift frightened me more than any command could have done.

question: Based on the text, what does Bimala most strongly suggest about Nikhil's wish that she enter the larger world?
choices: She resented it at the time as an attempt to control how she should spend her days.
She welcomed it at once, since she had long wished to escape the confines of the household.
She now regrets refusing it, since she believes that accepting it would have greatly strengthened her marriage.
She did not understand it at first, and she now recognizes that the freedom it offered unsettled her.

explanation.passage: Bimala, looking back, describes how her husband Nikhil urged her to leave the secluded inner rooms and “meet” the larger world. He wanted her love for him to be a real choice made with full knowledge. At the time she “laughed at him” and thought she needed nothing but her devotion to him. The last sentence shows her present-day understanding: he was offering “something I did not yet know how to want,” and this gift “frightened” her more than an order would have. The question asks what she suggests about his wish, so you need both her original reaction (she did not take it seriously or understand it) and her later insight (it scared her).
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. Nikhil wanted to free her, not control her, and Bimala says his “gift” frightened her “more than any command could have done,” which shows she did not see it as a command.
Incorrect. She “laughed at him” and asked, “What did I want with any world beyond my devotion to him?” She did not welcome the idea.
Incorrect. Bimala does reflect on the past, but she never says she regrets her response or that accepting would have helped her marriage. This adds a judgment that is outside the passage.
Correct. She was offered “something I did not yet know how to want,” so she did not understand it at the time, and she now says that “his gift frightened me,” showing that the freedom unsettled her.

intro: The following text is adapted from Anton Chekhov's 1899 short story “The Lady with the Dog,” translated by Constance Garnett in 1917. Dmitri Gurov is a Moscow banker on vacation at a seaside resort.

passage.text: Bitter experience, he believed, had taught him what women were, and when they were discussed in his presence he always called them “the lower race.” He felt that he had suffered enough to have the right to call them what he liked. And yet he could not get on for two days together without “the lower race.” In the society of men he was bored and not himself; with them he was cold and uncommunicative. But when he was in the company of women he felt free, and knew what to say to them and how to behave.

question: Which choice best describes how Gurov is presented in the text?
choices: The narrator praises Gurov for his honesty in admitting his low opinion of women.
The narrator suggests that Gurov prefers the company of men because he finds women tiresome.
The narrator exposes a contradiction between Gurov's dismissive talk about women and his reliance on their company.
The narrator portrays Gurov as a shy and awkward man who struggles to speak comfortably with anyone, whether men or women.

explanation.passage: Gurov says insulting things about women, calling them “the lower race,” and believes his past experiences give him the right to do so. Then the narrator turns with “And yet”: he “could not get on for two days together” without women. With men he is bored and cold; with women he feels free and at ease. The narrator does not comment directly but simply places these facts side by side, which quietly reveals that his words do not match his behavior. The question asks how Gurov is presented, so look for the answer that names this mismatch.
choices: Incorrect. The narrator does not praise Gurov. Putting his insults next to his dependence on women makes him look inconsistent, not admirably honest.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. With men he is “bored and not himself”; it is with women that he “felt free.”
Correct. He calls women “the lower race,” yet “he could not get on for two days together” without them and feels free only in their company. The narrator's “And yet” highlights this contradiction.
Incorrect. This is half right. He is “cold and uncommunicative” with men, but with women he “knew what to say to them and how to behave,” so he does not struggle with everyone.

intro: The following text is adapted from Zitkala-Ša's 1900 memoir essay “The School Days of an Indian Girl.” The narrator, a Yankton Dakota girl, describes her first days at a boarding school run by missionaries far from her home, where a staff member is cutting the students' long hair.

passage.text: I cried aloud, shaking my head all the while, until I felt the cold blades of the scissors against my neck and heard them gnaw off one of my thick braids. Then I lost my spirit. Since the day I was taken from my mother I had suffered extreme indignities. People had stared at me. I had been tossed about in the air like a wooden puppet. And now my long hair was shingled like a coward's! In my anguish I moaned for my mother, but no one came to comfort me. Not a soul reasoned quietly with me, as my own mother used to do; for now I was only one of many little animals driven by a herder.

question: Based on the text, what does the narrator most strongly suggest about the cutting of her hair?
choices: It upset her chiefly because the scissors physically hurt her as she struggled.
It was the latest in a series of humiliations that left her feeling that her individuality had been ignored.
It became bearable once a teacher patiently explained to her why it was necessary.
It mattered less to her than the shame she felt at having cried and moaned in front of the other students at the school.

explanation.passage: The narrator describes having her braids cut against her will. She says, “Then I lost my spirit,” and lists earlier “indignities” (insults to her dignity): being stared at and tossed about “like a wooden puppet.” The haircut is the final blow (“And now...”). She cries for her mother, but no one comforts her or reasons with her. The last image is the most important: she is “only one of many little animals driven by a herder,” meaning she is treated as one of a herd, not as a person. The question asks what she suggests about the haircut, so connect it to the list of humiliations and the herd image.
choices: Incorrect. This is a topic match with the wrong claim. She mentions “the cold blades of the scissors,” but she never says they hurt; her pain is about dignity and loss (“I lost my spirit”), not physical injury.

Correct. “And now” presents the haircut as the latest of the “extreme indignities” she had suffered, and her feeling of being “only one of many little animals driven by a herder” shows she felt treated as part of a herd rather than as an individual.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The text says “Not a soul reasoned quietly with me,” so no one explained anything to her.
Incorrect. She cries and moans openly, but she never expresses shame about it. The text says nothing about the other students' reactions, so this is outside the passage.

intro: The following text is adapted from Virginia Woolf's 1925 novel *Mrs Dalloway*. Clarissa Dalloway, a London society hostess in her fifties, is walking through the city on a June morning.

passage.text: She would not say of any one in the world now that they were this or were that. She felt very young; at the same time unspeakably aged. She sliced like a knife through everything; at the same time was outside, looking on. She had a perpetual sense, as she watched the taxi cabs, of being out, out, far out to sea and alone; she always had the feeling that it was very, very dangerous to live even one day. Not that she thought herself clever, or much out of the ordinary.

question: Which choice best describes how Clarissa is presented in the text?
choices: As someone who experiences herself in contradictory ways, at once fully engaged in life and detached from it.
As someone who is confident that she understands other people and their motives far better than they understand themselves.
As someone so fearful of the dangers of the city that she avoids going anywhere alone.
As someone who privately considers herself exceptionally clever but conceals this from others.

explanation.passage: This passage takes us inside Clarissa's thoughts. It is built on pairs of opposites joined by “at the same time”: she feels “very young” and “unspeakably aged”; she “sliced like a knife through everything” (cutting right into life) and yet is “outside, looking on” (watching from a distance). She also feels “far out to sea and alone,” even in a busy street, and senses that simply living is “very, very dangerous.” The first sentence shows she refuses to label people. The question asks how she is presented, so look for the answer that captures these contradictions.
choices: Correct. The repeated “at the same time” pairs (“very young” and “unspeakably aged”; slicing “through everything” and being “outside, looking on”) show that she feels both deeply involved in life and separate from it.

Incorrect. This is a reversal. “She would not say of any one in the world now that they were this or were that” shows she refuses to sum people up, which is the opposite of claiming to understand them completely.
Incorrect. This reads the images too literally. Being “far out to sea” and feeling it is “dangerous to live even one day” describe an inner feeling; she is in fact walking alone through London.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The text says, “Not that she thought herself clever, or much out of the ordinary.”

intro: The following text is adapted from Zora Neale Hurston's 1926 short story “Sweat.” For fifteen years Delia Jones has supported herself and her husband, Sykes, by washing clothes for wealthy families in a Florida town. Sykes has just kicked over the laundry she was sorting on the kitchen floor.

passage.text: Delia's habitual meekness seemed to slip from her shoulders like a blown scarf. She seized the iron skillet from the stove and struck a defensive pose, which act surprised him greatly, coming from her. “Looka heah, Sykes, you done gone too fur. Ah been married to you fur fifteen years, and Ah been takin' in washin' fur fifteen years. Sweat, sweat, sweat! Work and sweat, cry and sweat, pray and sweat! Mah sweat is done paid for this house and Ah reckon Ah kin keep on sweatin' in it.”

question: Which choice best describes how Delia is presented in the text?
choices: As a woman who has always openly challenged her husband whenever he has mistreated her during their marriage.
As a woman who regrets the years of labor she has spent working for other families.
As a usually submissive woman who, when provoked, asserts her right to a home her work has paid for.
As a woman who has finally decided to leave her husband and the house they share.

explanation.passage: Delia is normally meek (quiet and submissive), but here that meekness slips off “like a blown scarf.” She grabs a skillet to defend herself, which “surprised him greatly, coming from her,” showing this is new behavior. She then lists fifteen years of marriage and fifteen years of washing, repeating “sweat” to stress how hard she has worked. Her final line claims the house: her sweat “paid for this house,” and she will “keep on sweatin' in it.” The question asks how she is presented, so focus on the change from her usual meekness and on what she claims.
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. The text calls her meekness “habitual” and says her defiance “surprised him greatly, coming from her,” so she has not always challenged him.
Incorrect. Her repetition of “sweat” stresses how hard she has worked, but she uses it to claim the house, not to express regret. She plans to “keep on sweatin',” so regret is not shown.
Correct. Her “habitual meekness” slips away when Sykes kicks the laundry, and she declares, “Mah sweat is done paid for this house,” asserting her claim to the home her labor bought.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. She says she will “keep on sweatin' in it,” meaning she intends to stay in the house, not leave.

intro: The following text is a poem by Emily Dickinson, written around 1861 and first published in 1891.

passage.text:
“Hope” is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -

And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -

I've heard it in the chillest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of me.

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hope, like a small bird, is fragile and is easily silenced when life becomes difficult.
The speaker has traveled through harsh lands and over strange seas in a long and unsuccessful search for hope.
Hope offers comfort in hard times but demands a great deal from those who depend on it.
Hope persists through the harshest conditions and comforts people while asking nothing of them.

explanation.passage: Dickinson compares hope to a small bird living in the soul. Stanza 1: it sings constantly and “never stops - at all.” Stanza 2: its song sounds “sweetest” in a “Gale” (a strong storm), and only a terribly severe storm could “abash” (silence or shame) the bird that “kept so many warm.” Stanza 3: the speaker has heard it in the coldest places, yet even in “Extremity” (the worst situations) it never “asked a crumb” of her, meaning it never asked for anything in return. The question asks for the main idea, which combines all three stanzas.
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. The bird “never stops - at all” and is heard “sweetest” in a storm, so the poem shows hope as lasting, not fragile.
Incorrect. The speaker has “heard it in the chillest land” and “on the strangest Sea,” which means she found hope even there; the search was not unsuccessful.
Incorrect. This is half right. Hope does comfort (“kept so many warm”), but the last lines say it never “asked a crumb - of me,” the opposite of demanding a great deal.

Correct. Hope “never stops,” is “sweetest - in the Gale,” and is present “in the chillest land,” and yet “never - in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of me.” It endures and gives comfort without asking anything in return.

intro: The following text is adapted from Walt Whitman's 1868 poem “A Noiseless Patient Spider.” A promontory is a point of high land that juts out over water or open space.

passage.text:
A noiseless patient spider,
I mark'd where on a little promontory it stood isolated,
Mark'd how to explore the vacant vast surrounding,
It launch'd forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself,
Ever unreeling them, ever tirelessly speeding them.

And you O my soul where you stand,
Surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space,
Ceaselessly musing, venturing, throwing, seeking the spheres to connect them,
Till the bridge you will need be form'd, till the ductile anchor hold,
Till the gossamer thread you fling catch somewhere, O my soul.

question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The speaker likens his soul's persistent efforts to reach beyond its isolation to a spider casting threads into empty space.
The speaker admires a spider's tireless skill at spinning threads, which he contrasts with his own soul's inability to act at all.
The speaker describes how a spider traps its prey and warns his soul that it may be trapped in a similar way.
The speaker celebrates his soul's freedom from any need to form connections with the world around it.

explanation.passage: The poem has two stanzas that mirror each other. In the first, the speaker watches a spider standing alone (“isolated”) on a point of land, sending out thread after thread (“filament, filament, filament”) into the “vacant vast surrounding” to explore it. In the second, he turns to his own soul, which is also “Surrounded, detached” in endless space, and is also “Ceaselessly... venturing, throwing, seeking” to “connect.” He hopes the soul's “gossamer thread” (a very fine, delicate thread) will “catch somewhere.” The question asks for the main idea, so the key is the comparison between the two stanzas: both the spider and the soul are alone and keep reaching out.
choices: Correct. The spider “stood isolated” and “launch'd forth filament” into empty space; the soul likewise is “detached” and keeps “seeking the spheres to connect them” until its “thread... catch somewhere.” The poem compares the two efforts to overcome isolation.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The soul is not inactive; it is “Ceaselessly musing, venturing, throwing,” just like the spider. The stanzas show a likeness, not a contrast.
Incorrect. The spider's threads are used to “explore,” not to trap prey, and the speaker gives no warning. This idea is outside the poem.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The soul is “seeking the spheres to connect them” and hopes its thread will “catch somewhere,” so it clearly wants connection.

intro: The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare's play *Twelfth Night*, first performed around 1602. Viola, a young woman disguised as a man named Cesario, works for Duke Orsino, who loves the countess Olivia. Viola has just been handed a ring that Olivia claims Viola left with her.

passage.text:
I left no ring with her. What means this lady?
Fortune forbid my outside have not charmed her!
She made good view of me; indeed, so much
That methought her eyes had lost her tongue,
For she did speak in starts distractedly.
She loves me, sure. Disguise, I see thou art
A wickedness. How will this fadge? My master
Loves her dearly; and I, poor monster, fond
As much on him; and she, mistaken, seems
To dote on me. O Time, thou must untangle this, not I;
It is too hard a knot for me t' untie.

question: Based on the text, what does Viola most strongly suggest about her situation?
choices: She is pleased that Olivia loves her, since Olivia's affection may help her win the Duke's favor.
She realizes that her disguise has produced a tangle of misdirected love that she feels powerless to resolve.
She intends to reveal her disguise to Olivia at once so that the confusion among the three of them can be brought to an end.
She suspects that Olivia has sent the ring as a way of mocking the Duke's attempts to court her.

explanation.passage: Viola, disguised as a man, realizes that Olivia's story about the ring is an excuse: Olivia stared at her and spoke “distractedly,” so “She loves me, sure.” Viola then blames her disguise (“thou art / A wickedness”) and lays out the triangle: the Duke loves Olivia, Viola loves (“fond as much on”) the Duke, and Olivia, “mistaken,” loves Viola. “How will this fadge?” means “How will this turn out?” She ends by handing the problem to Time: “It is too hard a knot for me t' untie.” The question asks what she suggests about her situation, so focus on the love triangle and on her feeling that she cannot fix it.
choices: Incorrect. Viola wishes the opposite (“Fortune forbid my outside have not charmed her!”, meaning “I hope my appearance has not charmed her!”) and calls her disguise “a wickedness.” She is not pleased.

Correct. She traces how the Duke loves Olivia, she loves the Duke, and Olivia loves her because of the disguise, and she concludes, “O Time, thou must untangle this, not I; / It is too hard a knot for me t' untie.” The love is misdirected, and she feels powerless.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Viola says Time must untangle the problem, “not I,” so she does not plan to act at once.
Incorrect. Viola concludes that Olivia sent the ring out of love (“She loves me, sure”), not to mock the Duke.

passage.text: Hummingbirds have the highest metabolic rate of any vertebrate, and to survive cold nights in the Andes, some species enter torpor, a state in which body temperature and heart rate drop sharply to conserve energy. Researchers long assumed that torpor was an emergency measure, used only when a bird's fat reserves had fallen dangerously low. In a 2020 study, however, Blair Wolf and colleagues recorded the nighttime body temperatures of six hummingbird species at high elevation in Peru and found that many individuals entered torpor even when they were well fed. One species, the black metaltail, lowered its body temperature to 3.3°C, the lowest ever recorded in a bird.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It explains why hummingbirds have unusually high metabolic rates and then describes how this affects what they eat.
It presents a disagreement between two research teams about hummingbird metabolism and then explains why one team's measurement methods were seriously flawed.
It describes a survival strategy, presents a long-held view about when that strategy is used, and then reports findings that challenge that view.
It describes a survival strategy, reports findings that confirm a long-held view about it, and then notes a striking exception to that view.

explanation.passage: The passage is about torpor, a deep energy-saving state (body temperature and heart rate drop) that some hummingbirds use on cold nights. Sentence 2 gives the old assumption: torpor was only an emergency move for birds low on fat. Sentence 3 begins with “however,” which signals a challenge: Wolf's team found that well-fed birds used torpor too. Sentence 4 adds a striking detail about how low one species' temperature went. For structure questions, label each sentence's job and then match the sequence: strategy, old view, challenging evidence.
choices: Incorrect. The high metabolic rate is mentioned only as background in the first sentence, and the passage never discusses diet.
Incorrect. Only one research team (Wolf and colleagues) is described, and no one's methods are criticized. The contrast is between an old assumption and a new study.

Correct. Sentence 1 describes torpor, sentence 2 gives the long-held view (“an emergency measure, used only when a bird's fat reserves had fallen dangerously low”), and sentences 3-4 report the 2020 findings, introduced by “however,” that well-fed birds also used torpor.

Incorrect. This is a reversal. The 2020 study contradicts the old view rather than confirming it: birds entered torpor “even when they were well fed.” The black metaltail detail is a record low temperature, not an exception to the view.

passage.text: Katsushika Hokusai's woodblock print *Under the Wave off Kanagawa* (c. 1831) is often described as a quintessentially Japanese image, an expression of a national artistic tradition. Art historian Christine Guth observes, however, that the print's striking blue comes from Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment imported from Europe, and that its low horizon and deep perspective draw on techniques Japanese artists had learned from Dutch engravings. The print's fame, moreover, owes much to the European collectors who eagerly sought it out in the late nineteenth century. For Guth, the image is best understood not as the product of an isolated tradition but as a product of global exchange.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes an artwork's techniques, explains why critics initially rejected the work, and then traces the work's later rise to fame.
It presents a scholar's interpretation of an artwork and then offers evidence suggesting that the scholar significantly overstates the role that foreign influence played in it.
It compares two artworks from different cultures and then argues that one of the works directly inspired the other.
It introduces a common characterization of an artwork, presents details that complicate that characterization, and then states a scholar's alternative view.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 gives the usual view of Hokusai's famous wave print: it is “quintessentially Japanese” (the purest example of Japanese art). Sentence 2 starts with “however” and gives Guth's evidence against that view: the blue pigment came from Europe and the perspective came from Dutch prints. Sentence 3 adds that European collectors helped make it famous. Sentence 4 states Guth's conclusion: the print is a product of “global exchange” (trade and influence between cultures). For the structure question, notice that the common view comes first and Guth's view comes last, with the evidence in between.
choices: Incorrect. Nothing in the passage says critics rejected the print. The European collectors “eagerly sought it out,” which suggests the opposite.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The passage presents Guth's evidence in support of foreign influence; it never argues that she overstates it.
Incorrect. Only one artwork is discussed. The Dutch engravings are a source of technique, not a second artwork being compared.

Correct. Sentence 1 gives the common view (“quintessentially Japanese”), sentences 2-3 provide complicating details (imported Prussian blue, Dutch perspective techniques, European collectors), and sentence 4 states Guth's alternative view that it is “a product of global exchange.”

passage.text: In the 1920s geologist J Harlen Bretz proposed that the Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington, a landscape of dry canyons, enormous gravel bars, and giant ripple marks, had been carved by a single catastrophic flood. Most geologists rejected the idea, partly because the prevailing view held that landscapes are shaped gradually over vast periods of time, and partly because Bretz could not identify a source for so much water. Decades later, researchers showed that Glacial Lake Missoula, in present-day Montana, had burst through its ice dam and released water at a rate far exceeding that of any modern river. Bretz's explanation is now widely accepted, though most geologists today conclude that the region was struck by dozens of such floods rather than one.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a hypothesis, explains why the hypothesis was initially resisted, describes evidence that later supported it, and notes a modification to it.
It describes a landscape, presents two competing hypotheses about how that landscape formed, and then explains why both hypotheses were eventually abandoned by geologists.
It presents a hypothesis, describes the evidence that led to its immediate acceptance, and then explains why later researchers came to doubt it.
It explains a geological process and then argues that the same process continues to reshape the landscape of eastern Washington today.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 states Bretz's hypothesis: one huge flood carved the Scablands. Sentence 2 explains why other geologists rejected it (it clashed with the belief that landscapes change slowly, and Bretz could not say where the water came from). Sentence 3 supplies the missing piece: a glacial lake suddenly broke through its ice dam. Sentence 4 says the idea is now accepted, with one change: many floods, not just one. A structure question wants each of these four moves in the right order.
choices: Correct. Sentence 1 presents the hypothesis, sentence 2 explains why “Most geologists rejected the idea,” sentence 3 describes the Lake Missoula evidence that supported it, and sentence 4 notes the modification: “dozens of such floods rather than one.”
Incorrect. The gradual-change view is a reason for rejecting Bretz, but the passage does not say it was abandoned, and Bretz's hypothesis was not abandoned at all; it is “now widely accepted.”
Incorrect. This is a reversal. Bretz's idea was first rejected and only accepted “Decades later,” so it was not immediately accepted and then doubted.
Incorrect. The passage describes floods that happened long ago and never claims they are still reshaping the region. This is outside the passage.

passage.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca, accompanied by thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold. According to the Egyptian official al-Umari, who wrote about the visit about a decade later, Musa spent and gave away so much gold that its value in Cairo fell sharply and had still not recovered twelve years afterward. News of Mali's wealth traveled far: on the *Catalan Atlas*, a map made in Spain in 1375, Musa appears seated on a throne, holding a large golden nugget.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a journey, questions the reliability of an official's account of that journey, and then offers a different explanation for an economic change.
It describes a journey, presents one of its consequences as recorded by an official, and then indicates how widely the traveler's reputation spread.
It describes the rise of an empire, explains how the empire acquired its wealth, and then describes the causes of the empire's decline.
It describes a journey, explains why its economic effects were short-lived, and then compares it to later journeys by European rulers.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 describes Mansa Musa's journey through Cairo with huge amounts of gold. Sentence 2 reports what al-Umari, an Egyptian official, wrote about one effect: Musa spent so much gold that gold lost value in Cairo for over a decade. Sentence 3 shows that Musa's fame reached Europe: a Spanish map from 1375 shows him holding gold. Match these three steps to the choices.
choices: Incorrect. The passage reports al-Umari's account without questioning it, and it offers no alternative explanation.

Correct. Sentence 1 describes the journey, sentence 2 gives a consequence recorded by al-Umari (gold's value “fell sharply and had still not recovered twelve years afterward”), and sentence 3 shows his reputation reaching Spain via the *Catalan Atlas*.
Incorrect. The passage focuses on one journey, not on the empire's rise or fall. Neither how Mali acquired its wealth nor its decline is discussed.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The effects were long-lasting (“had still not recovered twelve years afterward”), and no European rulers' journeys are discussed.

passage.text: Linguists once assumed that whistled languages, such as Silbo Gomero of the Canary Islands, were simple signaling systems capable of conveying only a limited set of messages, much like a shepherd's call. Research by Julien Meyer and others, however, has shown that Silbo is a whistled form of Spanish: whistlers convert the vowels and consonants of spoken Spanish into changes in pitch and loudness, so that in principle any sentence can be whistled. Brain-imaging studies have further found that experienced whistlers process Silbo in the same brain regions that handle spoken language. Silbo nonetheless nearly vanished in the twentieth century, as roads and telephones made whistling across the island's deep ravines unnecessary; since 1999, it has been a required subject in the island's schools.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a language, explains how the island's geography led to the language's invention, and then argues that it should be taught more widely.
It presents an earlier view of a form of communication, offers evidence supporting that view, and then describes efforts to preserve one example of it.
It compares whistled and spoken languages and then concludes that the brain processes the two in fundamentally different ways.
It presents an earlier view of a form of communication, offers evidence against that view, and then turns to the recent history of one example of it.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 gives an old assumption: whistled languages were simple signal systems with few possible messages. Sentence 2 (“however”) presents Meyer's research showing that Silbo is a full whistled version of Spanish that can express any sentence. Sentence 3 adds brain evidence that whistlers process Silbo like spoken language. Sentence 4 shifts topics with “nonetheless”: Silbo almost died out in the twentieth century but is now taught in schools. For the structure question, notice that sentences 2-3 argue against the old view and that sentence 4 moves to history.
choices: Incorrect. The ravines are mentioned only to explain why Silbo was once useful, not how it was invented, and the passage never argues that it should be taught more widely; it just reports that it is required in schools.

Incorrect. This is half right. The passage presents an earlier view and later mentions preservation, but the evidence goes against the earlier view: Silbo is a full language in which “any sentence can be whistled,” not a limited signaling system.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The brain-imaging studies found that whistlers process Silbo “in the same brain regions that handle spoken language.”

Correct. Sentence 1 states the earlier view, sentences 2-3 provide evidence against it (Silbo can express “any sentence,” and it is processed like speech), and sentence 4 describes Silbo's near disappearance and its place in schools since 1999.

passage.text: In 1912 Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working at the Harvard College Observatory, examined 25 variable stars (stars that brighten and dim in regular cycles) in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a star system so distant that all of its stars could be treated as lying at roughly the same distance from Earth. Leavitt noticed that the brighter a star appeared, the longer its cycle lasted. Because the stars were all about equally far away, differences in how bright they appeared had to reflect real differences in how much light they emitted, so a star's cycle length revealed its true brightness. Comparing a star's true brightness with how bright it looks from Earth allows astronomers to calculate its distance, a method Edwin Hubble used in the 1920s to show that the Andromeda nebula lies far outside our own galaxy.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes an astronomical discovery, explains why the discovery was overlooked for many years, and then describes its eventual rediscovery.
It presents a hypothesis about variable stars, describes an observation that disproved it, and then offers an alternative hypothesis.
It describes a pattern a researcher observed, explains why a feature of the stars studied made that pattern meaningful, and then indicates how the resulting relationship was later used.
It describes a researcher's method for studying variable stars, identifies a significant limitation of that method, and then explains how a later astronomer was able to overcome that limitation.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 introduces Leavitt's study and an important detail: the stars she studied were all about the same distance from Earth. Sentence 2 gives her observation: brighter-looking stars had longer cycles. Sentence 3 explains why that matters: since distance was equal, “appearing brighter” really meant “giving off more light,” so cycle length tells you a star's true brightness. Sentence 4 explains the payoff: comparing true and apparent brightness gives distance, which Hubble used to show Andromeda is outside our galaxy. The key structural point is that the “same distance” detail is what makes the pattern useful.
choices: Incorrect. Nothing in the passage says Leavitt's discovery was overlooked or rediscovered. It moves straight from her 1912 work to Hubble's use of it in the 1920s.
Incorrect. The passage presents no hypothesis that was disproved. Leavitt made an observation, and the passage explains its meaning.

Correct. Sentence 2 gives the pattern (brighter stars had longer cycles), sentence 3 explains why the stars' equal distance made the pattern meaningful (“Because the stars were all about equally far away...”), and sentence 4 shows Hubble later using it to measure distance.
Incorrect. The equal distance of the stars is presented as what made Leavitt's finding valid, not as a limitation, and Hubble applied her method rather than correcting it.

passage.text: When Florence Price's Symphony in E Minor won first prize in the Wanamaker Foundation's composition competition in 1932 and was performed by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra the following year, Price became the first Black woman to have a symphony played by a major American orchestra. Reviewers praised the work, noting how it joined the European symphonic form to melodies and rhythms drawn from African American spirituals and the juba, a dance rooted in plantation traditions. After Price's death in 1953, however, her music was seldom performed, and many of her manuscripts were presumed lost. In 2009 dozens of her scores were discovered in an abandoned house in St. Anne, Illinois, prompting renewed interest in her work.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It identifies a milestone in a composer's career, describes how the work behind it was received, and then explains how her music faded from view before drawing new attention.
It describes a composer's musical training, explains her influence on later composers, and then evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of her best-known symphony.
It identifies a milestone in a composer's career, describes critics' objections to the work behind that milestone, and then explains how those objections were eventually overcome by her supporters.
It describes the discovery of a set of musical manuscripts and then explains why scholars have questioned whether the composer actually wrote them.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 states Price's milestone: her symphony won a prize and made her the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra. Sentence 2 describes how reviewers responded: with praise for its blend of European form and African American musical traditions. Sentence 3 (“however”) says her music was neglected after her death. Sentence 4 describes the 2009 discovery of her scores, which renewed interest. Look for a choice that follows this sequence: achievement, reception, decline, revival.
choices: Correct. Sentence 1 names the milestone (first Black woman to have a symphony played by a major American orchestra), sentence 2 describes its reception (“Reviewers praised the work”), sentence 3 explains that her music was “seldom performed” after 1953, and sentence 4 describes the renewed interest after the 2009 discovery.
Incorrect. The passage never discusses her training or influence on later composers, and it does not evaluate weaknesses of her symphony.
Incorrect. This is half right. The milestone is correct, but reviewers “praised the work”; they did not object to it.
Incorrect. The discovery is mentioned only in the last sentence, and no one questions whether Price wrote the scores. This is outside the passage.

passage.text: Researchers long assumed that complex tool use required a large brain, which is why such behavior seemed to be confined mainly to great apes and humans. New Caledonian crows challenge that assumption. These birds, whose brains are about the size of a walnut, shape twigs and leaves into hooked tools that they use to pull insect larvae from holes in dead wood. In 2016, however, neuroscientist Seweryn Olkowicz and colleagues reported that the forebrains of crows and parrots pack neurons far more densely than primate brains do, so that a crow's forebrain can contain as many neurons as a much larger monkey brain. The capacity for tool use, the researchers suggest, may depend less on the size of a brain than on the number of neurons it contains.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a long-standing assumption, describes a behavior that seems to contradict it, and then reports research suggesting that the assumption should be refined rather than abandoned.

It presents a long-standing assumption, describes a behavior that seems to contradict it, and then reports new research showing that the behavior has been widely misunderstood by most researchers who observed it.
It describes an unusual behavior in a bird species, explains how researchers first came to observe that behavior, and then questions whether those early observations were reliable.
It presents a long-standing assumption, describes a behavior that supports it, and then reports research that extends the assumption to several animals other than great apes.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 gives an old assumption: you need a big brain to use complex tools. Sentences 2 and 3 describe a challenge: crows with tiny brains make hooked tools. Sentence 4 begins with 'however' and adds a twist: crow brains are small but packed with neurons (brain cells), as many as a bigger monkey brain. Sentence 5 draws the lesson: what matters may be the number of neurons, not brain size. So the old idea is not thrown out; it is adjusted.
choices: Correct. This matches all three steps: the old assumption (big brain needed), a behavior that seems to contradict it (small-brained crows making tools), and research suggesting the idea should be refined (number of neurons, not size) instead of dropped entirely.
Incorrect. The first two steps are right, but the third is not. The 2016 research does not say people misunderstood the crows' tool use; it explains how crows can do it. This is half right.
Incorrect. The text never explains how the behavior was first observed, and it never doubts that the crows really make tools. This misses the text's focus on the brain-size assumption.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The crows' tool use with walnut-sized brains challenges the big-brain assumption; it does not support it.

passage.text: Violins made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona, Italy, in the late 1600s and early 1700s are prized for their brilliant tone, and for centuries many players and instrument makers attributed that tone to a secret varnish. In a 2016 study, however, chemist Hwan-Ching Tai and colleagues analyzed tiny shavings from the maple wood inside several Stradivari instruments and found traces of borax, zinc, and copper, substances rarely found in untreated maple. The researchers suggest that the wood was soaked in these minerals, probably to protect it from woodworm, and that the treatment also stiffened the wood in ways that may have shaped the instruments' sound.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes how Stradivari's violins were made and then argues that their tone is no better than that of violins being made today.
It presents a traditional explanation for the violins' tone and then reports chemical evidence proving that the varnish on the instruments had no effect at all on their sound.
It describes a chemical treatment applied to the violins' wood and then explains how that treatment caused the instruments to deteriorate over time.
It notes a traditional explanation for the violins' tone, reports a finding about their wood, and suggests that a protective treatment may have affected their sound.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 introduces Stradivari's famous violins and the old explanation for their sound: a secret varnish (the shiny coating on the outside). Sentence 2, starting with 'however,' reports a chemical study that found unusual minerals inside the wood. Sentence 3 interprets the finding: the wood was probably treated to keep worms out, and that treatment may also have changed the sound.
choices: Incorrect. The text never explains how the violins were made step by step, and it never compares them with modern violins. This is outside the scope of the passage.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The study suggests the wood treatment 'may have shaped' the sound; it does not 'prove' that the varnish had 'no effect at all.'
Incorrect. The text says the treatment may have improved the sound, not that it made the violins deteriorate. This reverses the passage's point.

Correct. This follows the three steps in order: the traditional explanation (varnish), the finding about the wood (borax, zinc, copper), and the suggestion that a treatment meant to protect the wood may have affected the sound.

passage.text: Economists have traditionally assumed that people value a product according to the benefits it provides, regardless of how much effort they put into obtaining it. In a series of experiments, Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely asked participants to assemble simple storage boxes or fold origami figures and then state how much they would pay for the results. Participants offered significantly more for items they had built themselves than for identical items assembled by others, and they valued their own amateur origami nearly as highly as figures folded by experts. When participants began building the boxes but were not allowed to finish them, however, the extra value disappeared.

question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It states an economic assumption, describes experiments whose results confirm that assumption, and then notes an exception to the experiments' findings.
It describes a series of experiments and then explains why the participants in those experiments may not represent typical consumers.
It states an economic assumption, describes experiments whose results conflict with it, and then argues that the assumption should be abandoned in all economic research.
It states an economic assumption, describes experiments whose results conflict with it, and then reports a condition under which the observed effect did not appear.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 gives the traditional economic view: a product's value depends only on its benefits, not on the effort spent getting it. Sentences 2-3 describe experiments in which people valued things they built themselves more highly than identical things built by others. That goes against sentence 1, because the products were the same and only the effort differed. Sentence 4 (“however”) adds a limit: if people were not allowed to finish building, the extra value disappeared. Three choices begin similarly, so check carefully what the last sentence actually does.
choices: Incorrect. This is a reversal. People valued items more because they had put effort into them, which conflicts with the assumption that effort does not matter.
Incorrect. The passage never questions whether the participants were typical. This is outside the passage.

Incorrect. This is half right and too strong. The results do conflict with the assumption, but the passage ends by reporting a limiting condition, not by arguing that the assumption should be abandoned “in all economic research.”

Correct. Sentence 1 states the assumption, sentences 2-3 report results that conflict with it (more value for self-built but identical items), and sentence 4 reports a condition (unfinished boxes) under which “the extra value disappeared.”

passage.text: Why zebras have stripes has been debated since Darwin's time, with proposals ranging from camouflage to heat regulation. In 2019 Tim Caro and colleagues dressed horses in black-and-white striped coats and filmed horseflies, biting insects that spread disease among grazing animals, as they approached. The flies flew toward striped and plain coats alike, but near the striped coats they failed to slow down and often bumped into the fabric or flew past without landing. [u]Exactly what it is about the stripes that prevents the flies from landing, however, the study could not determine.[/u] Some researchers have since proposed that the stripes confuse the motion-detecting system in the flies' eyes, which judges how fast a surface is approaching by tracking its moving edges.

question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It casts doubt on the accuracy of the observations that Caro and colleagues made of horseflies approaching the striped coats.
It explains why earlier proposals about the purpose of zebra stripes, such as camouflage and heat regulation, have been abandoned.
It identifies a question left unresolved by the study, which a later proposal described in the text attempts to answer.
It suggests that the striped coats were less effective at keeping horseflies away than Caro and colleagues had expected them to be.

explanation.passage: The passage starts with an old puzzle: why do zebras have stripes? Caro's team put striped coats on horses and found that horseflies did not land on them properly. The underlined sentence admits a limit: the study showed THAT the stripes stopped flies from landing, but not WHY. The final sentence then offers a possible 'why': the stripes may confuse how flies' eyes judge an approaching surface. The question asks what job the underlined sentence does between those two parts.
choices: Incorrect. The underlined sentence does not question what Caro's team saw; it accepts the result (flies did not land) and points out what remained unexplained. This misreads a limitation as a doubt about accuracy.

Incorrect. Camouflage and heat regulation are mentioned only in the first sentence. The underlined sentence is about the horsefly study, not about why other ideas were dropped. The passage never says they were abandoned.

Correct. The sentence points out an open question (what about the stripes stops the flies from landing?), and the next sentence gives a proposal that tries to answer it (the stripes confuse the flies' motion detection). It links the study to the later proposal.

Incorrect. The study found the stripes did keep flies from landing, and nothing in the text mentions what the researchers expected. The underlined sentence is about the cause of the effect, not its strength.

passage.text: Between 1940 and 1941 Jacob Lawrence painted the *Migration Series*, sixty small panels depicting the movement of African Americans from the rural South to Northern cities in the early twentieth century. Rather than complete the panels one at a time, Lawrence worked on all sixty at once, applying a single color across every panel where it was needed before moving on to the next. This method, he later explained, ensured that the panels would read as one continuous work rather than as sixty separate pictures, an effect reinforced by the recurring shapes and limited palette that carry a viewer's eye from one panel to the next.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how an artist's working method helped give a multipart work a sense of unity.
To argue that a series of paintings is more valuable as a historical record than as a work of art.
To describe the historical events depicted in a series of paintings and their effect on Northern cities.
To contrast the method an artist used early in his career with the method he used later.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 introduces the *Migration Series*, sixty panels about African Americans moving from the South to the North. Sentence 2 describes Lawrence's unusual method: he painted all sixty panels at once, one color at a time. Sentence 3 explains why: so the series would read as “one continuous work,” helped by repeated shapes and a limited palette (a small set of colors). The question asks for the main purpose, so ask what most of the passage is doing. It mentions the history only briefly and spends most of its length on the method and its effect on unity.
choices: Correct. Most of the passage explains Lawrence's method (working on “all sixty at once,” one color at a time) and its effect: the panels “read as one continuous work rather than as sixty separate pictures.”
Incorrect. The passage never compares the series' historical and artistic value or makes any such argument. This is outside the passage.

Incorrect. This is true but irrelevant. The migration is mentioned in the first sentence as the subject of the paintings, but the passage does not describe these events or their effects in any detail.
Incorrect. Only one method is described, the one used for this series. Nothing is said about different stages of his career.

passage.text: Loggerhead sea turtles that hatch on Florida's beaches swim out into the North Atlantic gyre, a vast circular system of currents, and spend years circling the ocean before returning to the coast. Straying outside the gyre's warm waters can be fatal, yet the young turtles rarely do. Biologist Kenneth Lohmann proposed that hatchlings read the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field, which differ from place to place, to tell where they are. [u]Other researchers suggested that the young turtles simply drift with the currents, which would carry them around the gyre without any need for navigation.[/u] In 2001 Lohmann and colleagues placed hatchlings in a tank of still water surrounded by coils that reproduced the magnetic fields found at different points along the gyre's edge; in each field, the hatchlings swam in the direction that would have kept them inside the gyre.

question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents a competing explanation that the experiment described later in the text helps to rule out.
It summarizes the evidence that first led Lohmann to propose his explanation of how the hatchlings navigate.
It describes a flaw in the design of the tank experiment that Lohmann and colleagues conducted in 2001.
It explains why straying outside the gyre's warm waters is so often fatal to young loggerhead turtles.

explanation.passage: Young loggerhead turtles ride a giant loop of ocean currents for years and almost never leave it. Lohmann's idea is that they use Earth's magnetic field like a map. The underlined sentence gives a rival idea: maybe they do not navigate at all and just drift with the currents. Then the experiment puts turtles in STILL water (no currents) with magnetic fields from different spots, and they still swim the right way.
choices: Correct. The underlined sentence offers a different explanation (passive drifting). The experiment then tests it: in still water, with no current to carry them, the hatchlings still swam the right way when given only magnetic cues. That result works against the drifting explanation.
Incorrect. The underlined sentence describes other researchers' rival idea, not the evidence behind Lohmann's own proposal.
Incorrect. The sentence comes before the experiment and does not mention its design. In fact, the experiment's still water was set up to deal with the drifting idea, not to show a flaw.
Incorrect. The passage says straying can be fatal but never explains why, and the underlined sentence is about how the turtles stay in the gyre, not the dangers outside it.

passage.text: During the hot summer of 1858, the stench of untreated sewage in the River Thames grew so overpowering that the curtains of the Houses of Parliament, which stand on the river's bank, were soaked in chemicals in an attempt to block it. Engineers had warned for years that London's drainage system was inadequate, and repeated cholera outbreaks had killed tens of thousands of residents, but proposals to rebuild the system had repeatedly stalled over their cost. Within weeks of the “Great Stink,” however, Parliament approved Joseph Bazalgette's plan for a vast network of sewers. The episode suggests that a widely recognized problem may go unaddressed until it becomes impossible for those with the power to solve it to ignore.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that nineteenth-century engineers misunderstood the causes of the cholera outbreaks in London.
To trace the engineering difficulties that delayed the construction of London's sewer system for many years before Parliament finally approved a plan.
To use a historical episode to illustrate how a long-recognized problem may be addressed only when it directly affects those able to solve it.
To criticize Parliament for approving an expensive sewer plan without fully considering its cost.

explanation.passage: The passage tells the story of the “Great Stink” of 1858: the Thames smelled so bad that Parliament, right on the river, soaked its curtains in chemicals. Sentence 2 explains that the problem was not new: engineers had warned about it and cholera had killed many people, but plans stalled because of cost. Sentence 3 says Parliament acted “within weeks” once the smell reached them. Sentence 4 states the lesson: problems may be ignored until decision-makers themselves cannot ignore them. A main-purpose question usually points to the passage's overall point, which here is stated in the last sentence.
choices: Incorrect. The passage never says engineers misunderstood cholera; in fact, it says they had correctly warned that the drainage system was inadequate. This is outside the passage.
Incorrect. This is a topic match with the wrong claim. The delay was due to cost (“stalled over their cost”), not engineering difficulties, and tracing the delay is not the main point.

Correct. The passage shows a problem known “for years” being solved only “Within weeks” of the smell reaching Parliament, and it ends with the general lesson that problems may wait until “those with the power to solve it” cannot ignore them.
Incorrect. This is a reversal of the passage's view. It presents the approval as a long-overdue response, not as a mistake, and it does not criticize the cost.

passage.text: When Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë published a volume of poems in 1846, they did so under the names Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. Charlotte later explained that they had chosen names that did not reveal their sex, because they had noticed that critics often judged women writers by their sex rather than by their work. [u]The volume sold only two copies in its first year.[/u] Yet the sisters' choice proved consequential: when Charlotte's novel *Jane Eyre* appeared the following year under the name Currer Bell, reviewers debated the author's identity, and many praised the novel's power in terms they rarely applied to books known to be by women.

question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It indicates that the pseudonyms did not bring the sisters immediate success, which contrasts with the later outcome described in the text.
It provides evidence that critics judged the sisters' poems harshly because they suspected that the authors behind the pseudonyms were actually women.
It explains why the sisters decided to publish their poems under names that did not reveal their sex.
It suggests that the sisters' choice of pseudonyms was the main reason their volume of poems failed.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 says the Brontë sisters published poems under male-sounding or neutral pen names (pseudonyms). Sentence 2 gives Charlotte's reason: critics judged women by their sex, not their work. The underlined sentence reports that the poems sold just two copies. The next sentence begins with “Yet,” a contrast word: the pen names did matter, because reviewers praised *Jane Eyre* in ways they rarely praised women's books. So the underlined sentence describes an early disappointment that the “Yet” sentence contrasts with a later, more significant result.
choices: Correct. The underlined sentence shows that the poems, published under pseudonyms, sold almost nothing, and the following sentence, beginning “Yet the sisters' choice proved consequential,” contrasts this with the reception of *Jane Eyre*.
Incorrect. The passage says nothing about how critics reviewed the poems or what they suspected. Low sales are not the same as harsh reviews. This is outside the passage.
Incorrect. The reason for the pseudonyms is given in the previous sentence (critics “judged women writers by their sex rather than by their work”), not the underlined one.
Incorrect. The passage never connects the low sales to the pseudonyms, and the next sentence says the choice proved beneficial. This reverses the passage's emphasis.

passage.text: When touched or jostled, the leaves of the plant *Mimosa pudica* fold inward, a response thought to deter plant-eating insects. In a 2014 experiment, Monica Gagliano and colleagues repeatedly dropped potted mimosas a short distance onto a cushioned surface. At first the plants folded their leaves after every drop, but after several drops many stopped responding. The same plants, however, still folded their leaves promptly when they were shaken, a different kind of disturbance. Because the plants had not lost the ability to respond, the researchers argued that the change was not caused by fatigue but reflected a simple form of learning: the plants had stopped reacting to a stimulus that had proved harmless.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To present evidence that *Mimosa pudica* folds its leaves primarily to protect itself from plant-eating insects.
To describe a study suggesting that a plant can learn and to explain how the researchers ruled out another explanation for its behavior.
To argue that plants are capable of forms of intelligence and memory comparable to those found in animals, including the ability to anticipate danger.
To describe a study of plant behavior and to explain why its results were later attributed to fatigue.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 introduces a plant whose leaves fold when disturbed. Sentences 2-3 describe the experiment: plants dropped repeatedly at first folded every time, then stopped. Sentence 4 (“however”) is the clever part: those same plants still folded when shaken. Sentence 5 explains why this matters: if the plants were simply tired out (fatigue), they would not have responded to shaking either, so the researchers concluded the plants had “learned” that drops were harmless. A main-purpose answer should cover both the learning claim and how the shaking test supports it.
choices: Incorrect. This is true but irrelevant. The insect explanation appears in the first sentence as background (“thought to deter”), but the passage presents no evidence about it.

Correct. The passage reports that the plants stopped responding to drops (suggesting learning) and explains that because they “still folded their leaves promptly when they were shaken,” the change “was not caused by fatigue.” This covers both the finding and how an alternative was ruled out.
Incorrect. This is too strong. The researchers claim only “a simple form of learning”; animals and intelligence comparable to theirs are never mentioned.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The researchers ruled out fatigue (“not caused by fatigue”), and nothing indicates their results were later reinterpreted.

passage.text: When construction of Florence's cathedral began in 1296, its planned dome was wider than any built since ancient times, and no one knew how to raise it: the usual method of supporting a dome on wooden scaffolding until the mortar set would have required more timber than the region could supply. The problem remained unsolved for more than a century. In 1418 Filippo Brunelleschi proposed building the dome without such supports, laying bricks in a herringbone pattern that locked each new layer in place. [u]Brunelleschi had trained as a goldsmith and had no formal training as an architect.[/u] His design nonetheless succeeded, and the dome, completed in 1436, remains the largest brick dome ever constructed.

question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains how Brunelleschi came up with the idea of laying the dome's bricks in an interlocking herringbone pattern.
It suggests that Brunelleschi's lack of training led to structural weaknesses in the completed dome.
It identifies the main reason the cathedral's dome remained unbuilt for more than a century.
It provides a detail about Brunelleschi's background that makes the success of his design more remarkable.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 explains the challenge: Florence's planned dome was enormous, and the normal building method needed more wood than was available. Sentence 2 says the problem went unsolved for over a century. Sentence 3 describes Brunelleschi's solution: herringbone brickwork (bricks laid in a zigzag, like fish bones) that did not need wooden supports. The underlined sentence tells us he was a goldsmith with no formal architectural training. The next sentence says his design “nonetheless succeeded.” “Nonetheless” means “in spite of that,” so the underlined detail is something that might have made success seem unlikely.
choices: Incorrect. The passage never connects his goldsmith training to the herringbone idea. This assumes a link the text does not make.
Incorrect. This is a reversal. The design “succeeded,” and the dome “remains the largest brick dome ever constructed,” so no weaknesses are suggested.
Incorrect. The reason the dome went unbuilt is given in sentence 1 (the usual method needed too much timber), not in the underlined sentence.

Correct. The underlined sentence notes that he “had no formal training as an architect,” and the next sentence says his design “nonetheless succeeded,” so the detail makes his achievement more striking.

passage.text: Many people who frequently juggle several streams of media at once, such as texting while watching videos and browsing the web, believe that the habit has made them skilled at shifting their attention. In a 2009 study, Eyal Ophir, Clifford Nass, and Anthony Wagner compared heavy and light media multitaskers on a series of attention tasks. Surprisingly, the heavy multitaskers performed worse at switching between tasks and were more easily distracted by irrelevant information. The researchers suggested that frequent multitasking may train people to take in everything around them rather than to focus on what matters.

question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that people should never use more than one form of media at the same time.
To present research suggesting that a habit does not build the skill that many who practice it believe it does.
To explain why people who use several forms of media at once tend to find the experience more enjoyable.
To compare how different types of media, such as videos, text messages, and websites, compete for people's attention.

explanation.passage: Sentence 1 describes a common belief: people who multitask with media a lot think it has made them good at switching attention. Sentences 2 and 3 describe a study that found the opposite: heavy multitaskers were worse at switching and more distracted. Sentence 4 offers the researchers' explanation. The whole passage is built around a belief and the research that contradicts it.
choices: Incorrect. This is too strong. The text reports research findings; it never tells people what they should do, and 'never' goes far beyond what it says.

Correct. The 'habit' is media multitasking and the 'skill' is shifting attention. People believe the habit builds the skill, but the study found heavy multitaskers were actually worse at it. The text exists to present that research.
Incorrect. The text never discusses whether multitasking is enjoyable. This is outside the scope of the passage.
Incorrect. Videos, texts, and websites are mentioned only as examples. The text compares heavy and light multitaskers, not different types of media.
